glossary.def: Media name for Florida's Parental Rights in Education bill, signed into law by Gov. Ron DeSantis, barring classroom instruction on sexual orientation or gender identity in K-3 or in a manner not age- or developmentally appropriate. The lecture treats it as a language ideology enacted as law, noting the statute does not define 'age appropriate' and that consequences have included AP Psychology not being offered in Florida.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

glossary.def: The pronunciation pattern of a later-learned language, shaped by transfer from the learner's first language's phonology.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

glossary.def: Coined by Rubin (1992): hearing something in speech that is not there in reality, usually a stereotypically attributed feature, through top-down processing. Teachers in the UCD study reported slang words, filler 'umms and ahhs', and a stutter in the African American guise when the recording contained none of these.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: A broad cover term for any linguistic ill- or well-formedness, encompassing grammaticality, interpretability, and felicity.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A speaker's/signer's judgment about whether a form is possible in their language; an empirical observation used as data. Also called a grammaticality judgment.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The case marking a grammatical object. Latin 'Canem fêlis vîdit' — canem is dog-ACC, so the dog is the one seen, and the meaning flips without any change in word order.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The subfield studying the physical sound waves of spoken language (no comparable light-wave subfield exists yet for signed languages).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A word derived from the initials of several words and pronounced as a word: scuba, FOMO, NASA.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The moving (lower) articulator in a consonant — e.g., the lower lip or a part of the tongue (tip/blade/front/back/root) or the epiglottis.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A modifier attached at an extra bar level — neither a specifier nor a complement (e.g., a modifying PP).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: The cover term for prepositions and postpositions. English has prepositions (to school, on the table); Turkish has postpositions (evim de, 'house-my at' = 'at my house'). Some languages have both.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: Someone acquiring a language after childhood; adults differ from child learners in cognition, existing language knowledge, and motivation.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

glossary.def: A bound morpheme that must attach to a base (prefix, suffix, circumfix, infix, or simultaneous affix).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: A plosive with a slow, fricated release (e.g., the start of jet); counts as a single phone.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A rule-governed variety of English spoken largely by African Americans. The lecture stresses it is not 'improper English' but a different variety with its own systematic grammar, and that the ideology framing it as improper links language to race and power.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: The convention year;month for a child's age (e.g., 2;6 = two years, six months).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: The age at which someone begins learning a language; earlier onset is generally associated with more native-like attainment, especially for phonology/accent.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

glossary.def: The thematic role of an animate participant that does something on purpose (e.g., 'The pirate sank the ship').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A synthetic type where words are built from many easily separated affixes, each with one consistent meaning (e.g., Japanese tabe-sase-rare-ta).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: When the form of the verb depends on properties of the subject or object — number (singular, plural, dual), person (1st, 2nd, 3rd), or gender. English 'be': I am / we-you-they are / she-he-it is. Arabic agrees for number, person, and gender.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: One of the three features classifying consonants: how the moving air that carries the sound is initiated. The airstream may be initiated by the diaphragm and lungs (pulmonic) or by some other mechanism (non-pulmonic).
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: A vervet monkey vocalization warning of a specific predator (snake, eagle, leopard), each triggering a different escape response; appears learned and can even be used deceptively, but lacks discreteness and duality of patterning.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: One of the variant forms of a morpheme (e.g., English plural -s/-z/-ɪz/-(r)en/internal change/-∅).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: When one morpheme with a consistent meaning appears in different forms depending on its environment.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: One of the physical phones that realize a phoneme in a particular environment (e.g., [ɾ] and [tʰ] are allophones of English /t/).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: A place of articulation produced when the tongue touches the alveolar ridge: [t], [d], [s], [z], [n], [l], [ɹ].
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: The nasal consonant [n], produced with the tongue at the alveolar ridge. In Standard Italian it is the underlying phoneme /n/, with [ŋ] as its conditioned allophone.
glossary.source: [Language Files, Ch. 3, Exercise 25: Standard Italian - instructor walkthrough & answer key]

glossary.def: [ɾ] — a single rapid contact of the tongue tip against the alveolar ridge, shorter than a trill. In Farsi it appears only between vowels.
glossary.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

glossary.def: [r] — a consonant produced by rapid vibration of the tongue tip against the alveolar ridge. In the Farsi data it is the voiced trill appearing word-initially and next to consonants, and is taken to be the underlying phoneme.
glossary.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

glossary.def: When a word shifts to match a pattern found in other words — typically from a rare pattern toward a common one; often reduces the number of allomorphs in a paradigm.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: Signaling systems used by non-human animals; they may share some hallmarks (communication, systematicity, limited displacement) but lack the full set that defines human language.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: A constituency test: a constituent can serve as the complete answer to a wh-question. 'That is my brother' → Who is that? 'My brother.' 'The keys are on the table' → Where are the keys? 'On the table.'
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The relation between words that are opposites with respect to at least one aspect of their meaning: young/old, boy/girl, hot/cold, come/go.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: A regional variety spoken in the Appalachian Mountains (crossing North Carolina, Tennessee, West Virginia and others), frequently stigmatized as uneducated or lower-class — a judgment the lecture identifies as classist rather than linguistic.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: Inferring language change by comparing speakers of different ages at one time (older vs. younger as a proxy for earlier vs. later).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: A consonant with articulators far enough apart to give little/no frication. Central (e.g., yet, wet) vs. lateral, where air flows around the tongue sides (e.g., let).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The property that, for most words, the pairing between a word's form and its meaning is conventional rather than inherent (e.g., 'pumpkin' vs. Nishnaabemwin 'kosmaan').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A phrase (usually a noun phrase) corresponding to a participant in the predicate's event.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: The set of arguments a predicate requires and the thematic roles it assigns; can be changed by operations like the passive.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: Using parts of the body to give a message physical reality — the movements/configurations that produce a linguistic signal (sound waves for speech, light waves for sign).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: Knowledge of how the articulators (mouth, tongue, lips; or hands, fingers, wrists) are used to produce the sounds or signs of a language.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A stop released with an audible puff of air, transcribed with a superscript h - e.g., 'pie' is [pʰaɪ]. In English, aspirated stops appear word-initially.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A puff of air on a plosive, transcribed [ʰ] (e.g., aspirated [tʰ] in 'atomic').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: An illocutionary act of putting forward a proposition as true (a statement).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

glossary.def: The most common rule type: a phoneme changes to match a property of its environment (e.g., French sonorant devoicing; nasal-place assimilation; vowel nasalization).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: The main, literal, 'surface' meaning of a sentence — the primary issue being conveyed; targeted by sentential negation ('it is not the case that…'). Often called truth-conditional meaning.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

glossary.def: The subfield of phonetics concerned with speech reception and perception. (Your textbook uses the label 'perceptual phonetics' for this same subfield — know both names.)
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: A functional verb carrying tense/aspect/mood (have, be, will, can); analyzed as the head T (tense).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: An early stage where babies practice producing the units of language; vocal babbling begins ~0;6 in hearing and deaf babies, and babies in signing environments babble on the hands (manual babbling).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: A new word created by removing what is mistakenly taken to be an affix: cran-apple, whelmed (from 'underwhelmed'), tamale (from tamales, Spanish tamal).
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: Horizontal tongue position: front (beat), central (but), or back (boot). Do not confuse central (backness) with mid (height).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The intermediate node (X') between the head (X) and the full phrase (XP) in X-bar structure.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: The unit an affix attaches to; can itself be simple or complex (library → librarian → librarianship).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: The order of subject, object, and verb in a neutral declarative clause. English is SVO; the most common type worldwide is SOV; all six orders are attested.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: The semantic role of an NP for which an action is performed: I baked a cake for [my brother]; Cristiano Ronaldo bought a car for [me].
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: A place of articulation produced by bringing both lips together: [p], [b], [m].
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: Combining parts of two words into one: smog, blog, podcast, brexit, mocktail, affluenza, cronut, dramedy, chillax, jeggings.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: Adopting a word from another language (e.g., English 'falcon' from Old French 'faucon'); borrowed words may later be respelled or re-pronounced.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: Information that flows from the physical signal up to the brain during perception (the incoming acoustic/visual input).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

glossary.def: Revitalization from the GRASSROOTS at the community level: starting a daycare in an endangered language, study groups, family language policies.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

glossary.def: A morpheme that must occur with other morphemes (all affixes, plus bound roots like -whelmed); shown with a hyphen on its attaching side.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: A way of showing syntactic grouping with nested brackets instead of a tree: [S [NP [N Alice]] [VP [V eats] [NP [N cake]]]].
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: Transcription written between slashes / /, representing phonemes - the abstract, psychological sound categories - rather than fine phonetic detail. Also called phonemic or phonological transcription.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The property of an implicature that it can be explicitly denied or suspended without contradiction — distinguishing it from an entailment.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

glossary.def: Repeated consonant-vowel syllables like [bababa] or [dadada] that emerge as babies gain articulatory control.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: The distinctive dialect of the North Carolina Outer Banks, documented by the Language and Life Project at NC State; used in lecture to show dialect variation within a single state.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: Inflectional morphology marking the grammatical relationship between nouns and verbs. Common cases: nominative (grammatical subjects), accusative (grammatical objects), dative (indirect objects), locative, and instrumental.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A change fully determined by the linguistic environment (not free social choice), which therefore does NOT count as a sociolinguistic variable.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: Any natural force that brings about a change of state. Causes do NOT require agents — no intention, no volition: [The snow] caved in the roof.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: Language change that speakers are consciously aware of, often spreading from higher-prestige speech (e.g., importing 'r-fulness' into NYC English).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: Language change below conscious awareness, spreading through the vernacular.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: A variety of English associated with Latino/a communities, one of the three varieties John Baugh used in his housing-discrimination studies.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: The special register caregivers often use with infants (exaggerated prosody, simplified forms), which can support acquisition.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: An affix attached around its base — part before and part after (e.g., Meskwaki ne-…-ena·n 'our').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: An obligatory grammatical element used with nouns when counting in many languages, similar to English 'five ears of corn' or 'five pieces of bread'. The choice is usually based on semantic properties of the noun — Indonesian orang for people, ekor for animals, biji for small round objects, helai for thin flat objects.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: A constituent containing a subject and a predicate; some clauses are embedded inside others, so not every clause is an independent sentence.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: Shortening a longer word while keeping its meaning and word class: phone (telephone), gym, fax, ad, exam, app, totes, obvs.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The set of grammatical categories that rarely gain or change members — prepositions, determiners, conjunctions, pronouns, auxiliary verbs.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The consonant(s) after the nucleus. A syllable with a coda is closed; without one, open. A syllable with no onset is onsetless.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A term that is secretly derogatory only to those with in-group knowledge (e.g., 'Monday' used as a coded racial slur) — derogatory without necessarily causing offense to the unaware target.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: A word in one language that descends from the same ancestor word as a word in a related language (e.g., English 'gift' and German 'Gift', which are true cognates despite different meanings).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: The core historical method: comparing multiple related languages and their systematic sound correspondences to reconstruct their common ancestor.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: A phrase selected by (required by) a head, sitting close to it (e.g., the object NP that a verb selects).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: Antonyms where if one is true the other is false, with no middle ground: dead/alive, pass/fail, off/on.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: When two phones never occur in the same environment (non-overlapping). They may be allophones of the SAME phoneme (if phonetically similar) or of different phonemes.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: A functional category (C) introducing an embedded clause (that, if, whether).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A sentence containing a subordinate embedded clause (a clause inside a clause) — an instance of recursion.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A sentence with two or more clauses joined by a coordinator (and, or, but).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: Building a word from two or more roots (e.g., blackboard, dog-tired); in English, compounds are stressed on their first member.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: Two sides of proficiency; learners often understand more than they can produce, and both improve as proficiency grows.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

glossary.def: A sound change that applies only in a particular phonological environment.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: A phone made with a relatively narrow constriction somewhere in the vocal tract.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A diagnostic showing that a string of words is a constituent: substitution/pro-form replacement, movement, it-cleft, stand-alone (fragment) answer, and (less reliably) coordination.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A group of words that functions as a single unit in the structure of a sentence; identified with constituency tests.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A question formed with a wh-word (who, what, where…), also called a wh-question; involves wh-movement to the front.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A word carrying core lexical meaning: mug, cup, bowl, glass. Contrasted with function words. Lexical-semantic relations such as antonymy, polysemy, and homonymy apply mainly to these.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: The shared situation and common ground (what participants mutually take to be established) against which utterances are interpreted and update the conversation.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

glossary.def: The class with continuous oral airflow: fricatives and approximants (sometimes trills).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A tone category involving pitch movement within the syllable: High-Low, Low-High, and so on.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: Antonyms occupying opposite regions of a SCALE that has intermediate values: young/old, thin/thick. Something can be neither clearly young nor clearly old.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: When two phones can occur in the same environment (overlapping distributions); proven by a single minimal pair. Contrastive phones belong to different phonemes.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: An agreed-upon, community-shared link between a form and its meaning; because the link is not natural or causal, it must be shared and learned rather than deduced.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: An inference a listener draws from an utterance in context, beyond its literal meaning, by assuming the speaker is being cooperative; cancellable.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

glossary.def: Grice's principle that, in conversation, participants generally cooperate toward the accepted purpose of the talk; the basis for calculating implicatures.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

glossary.def: Joining two elements with a coordinator (and, or, but); also called conjunction. Coordinated elements are usually the same type of constituent.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A large database collecting real examples of language use (books, newspapers, message boards, video, audio) used as a tool for making observations.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A noun that can be counted and pluralized and take numerals/'many' (e.g., three cats).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: Hidden, in-group prestige attached to a non-standard variety, indexing values like toughness or local solidarity.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: A projection of C (complementizer); embedded clauses are CPs, and the landing site for moved auxiliaries (T-to-C) and wh-phrases.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A window early in life during which language is acquired most readily and to native-like attainment; acquisition is harder afterward.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: The property that (at least part of) a language must be learned from the surrounding community rather than inherited genetically; which language you speak depends on your environment, and no one person can change the shared code alone.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: The earliest known writing system, developed in Mesopotamia about 5,000 years ago; part of the lecture's point that writing is very recent compared with speech.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.term: de jure vs. de facto (language status)
glossary.def: De jure = official by law; de facto = official in practice/effect even without a law. The lecture noted that, at the federal level, the U.S. has historically had no de jure official language, while English functions de facto because government business is conducted in it.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Video Lecture 1 (parts 1-2): What Is Language & Linguistics?]

glossary.def: Using a trans person's former (pre-transition) name, whether accidentally or deliberately; a way names are used to enforce power.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: A clause type used to make a statement (true or false).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: Conscious, fact-like knowledge (e.g., explicitly knowing a grammar rule); one of two memory systems relevant to later language learning (Paradis).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

glossary.def: The marking of the orientation or position of entities and events with respect to certain points of reference. Deictic words require CONTEXT to be understood — 'Meet me here tomorrow' versus 'Meet John at the library on Tuesday, February 19th'. They are both SYMBOLIC (conventional) and INDEXICAL (context-dependent); often called 'pointing words'.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: What a linguistic expression points to in the world (more precisely, in our cognitive model of the world); written ⟦x⟧. The denotation of 'pencil' is the set of all pencils.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: Morphology that changes the meaning or the lexical category of its base (e.g., -er turns the verb teach into the noun teacher).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: Harm in which a linguistic expression disparages people; expresses the utterer's condemnation of a referent.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: Describing expressions that disparage people. Offense (impact on hearers) and derogation (utterer's attitude) are distinct: an expression can be one, both, or neither.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: Describing what people actually do with their language, without judging it — the goal of scientific linguistics.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The set of core properties that define human language; in this lecture called the "eight hallmarks." A communication system that shows all of them counts as a true language.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: A functional category (D) marking a noun phrase (the, a, this, my, 's-possessors); determiners are in complementary distribution with each other.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A mark added to an IPA symbol to indicate additional phonetic detail, such as aspiration, length, or an unreleased stop.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: A variety of a language associated with a region or group; note that everyone speaks a dialect and no dialect is linguistically better than another.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: The older study of variation across regional dialects, producing dialect maps; early work was biased toward N.O.R.M. speakers (non-mobile older rural males).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: A theory of word meaning in which mental representations resemble dictionary entries — words defined using other words plus usage examples. PRO: useful and can genuinely help people learn meanings. CON: circular — if every word is defined by other words, nothing connects to anything more basic.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: A vowel that shifts from one quality to another within a single phone (e.g., the vowel in toy).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The argument that (in English) appears after the verb; accusative case if a pronoun (me, us, them).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A word or phrase that structures talk by breaking an utterance into units, such as 'like' in 'I went to the store and then like, I went to the mall'. The lecture contrasts this descriptive term with the prescriptive, negatively loaded label 'filler word'.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: The property that language is built from a small set of separable, elemental units (sounds/signs) that can be pulled apart and recombined; e.g., "tap" breaks into t–a–p.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: The ability to communicate about things and events that are not physically or temporally present — the past, the future, the hypothetical, the absent.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: A phonological process in which sounds that are close together become MORE different from each other. Lecture examples: 'surprise' and 'February' (where one /r/ is commonly changed or dropped).
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A phonetic property is distinctive when changing it can change the meaning of a word in that language. Aspiration is NOT distinctive in English, because making a stop aspirated or unaspirated never changes which word it is.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The overall set of environments in which a given phone can occur.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: A verb taking a subject, a direct object, and an indirect object: 'I gave her the gift'.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The hand used more for daily tasks and one-handed signs; the other is the nondominant hand (often the location in two-handed signs).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A language that no longer has living first-language speakers but can be revived from documentation and community effort — as with Hebrew, Cornish, and Manx.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

glossary.def: The use of two modal verbs in sequence, e.g. 'might could'. Grammatical in African American English and Southern American English, ungrammatical in California English — a grammatical, not merely lexical, dimension of variation.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: The English pattern in which an indirect object shifts to sit directly after the verb: 'I taught French to three students' → 'I taught three students French'. Obliques cannot shift this way: 'She drove her car to Portland' → *'She drove Portland her car'. This shift is the key evidence distinguishing indirect objects from obliques.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: "Complexly patterned at multiple levels": meaningless elemental units (sounds) at a lower level combine into meaningful units at a higher level; the same sounds t–a–p yield tap, apt, and pat.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: Evidence (e.g., from EEG) that the brain registers phonological contrasts very early in perceptual processing, before higher-level areas engage.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

glossary.def: Testimony or judgment based on identifying a speaker by voice alone; paired with linguistic profiling in the lecture because both rest on the assumption that a listener can reliably infer a speaker's race or identity from speech.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: A phonological process involving the deletion of a sound. Lecture example: 'laboratory', commonly reduced by dropping a syllable/vowel.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The allophone that appears in every environment not claimed by a more specific rule. Because it is defined by default rather than by a stated condition, it is normally the one chosen as the underlying phoneme. In Farsi, [r] is the elsewhere case.
glossary.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

glossary.def: Placing one clause inside another; the outer clause is the matrix/main clause and the inner one is the embedded (subordinate) clause.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: Based on systematic observation of data as evidence for theories.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A language with a shrinking community of speakers, at risk of falling out of use — often the legacy of colonial policies.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

glossary.def: The process by which a set of linguistic features becomes recognized as a distinct, socially meaningful register or 'way of speaking' (e.g., Canadian 'eh').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: A relation where if sentence p is true, q is necessarily true. Tested with the contradiction test: negating an entailment while asserting the original yields a contradiction.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: The surrounding context (usually the phone(s) immediately left and/or right) that determines which allophone of a phoneme is used.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: A phonological process involving the insertion of an extra sound. Lecture example: the instructor's own name being pronounced with an inserted sound ('Chlowe').
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A word created from a proper noun or name: achilles, freudian, scrooge, xerox, kleenex.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The thematic role of an animate participant that perceives or undergoes a mental state (e.g., 'Pirates frighten me').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: An expression used for emotional outbursts (e.g., damn). An expression can be both a vulgarity and an expletive.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: A person's public self-image, the concept underlying politeness theory. It has two aspects: NEGATIVE face (not being burdened or inconvenienced) and POSITIVE face (being praised and complimented).
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

glossary.def: An act that challenges someone's face. A NEGATIVE FTA imposes on another person; a POSITIVE FTA insults them. Politeness strategies exist to mitigate FTAs.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

glossary.def: The default principle that a phoneme is pronounced as its matching default allophone in any environment not covered by a rule ('faithful' to the phoneme).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: Words in two languages that look/sound similar but differ in meaning (and may or may not be cognates) — a trap when comparing languages.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: Whether a sentence is appropriate for the context in which it was used — distinct from whether it is grammatical or interpretable.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A phonological process in which a voiced sound loses its voicing at the end of a word. The Farsi rule /r/ → [r̥] / ___ # is an instance: the voiced trill devoices word-finally.
glossary.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

glossary.def: A language learned from the people around you in early childhood; a person may have more than one L1. (Contrast with L2, introduced in Ch. 2.)
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A child's earliest vocabulary (~0;12 for speech, often ~0;8-0;9 in sign), similar across children; nouns for things and verbs for actions like 'cry' or 'eat'.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: Blatantly and obviously failing to observe a maxim in order to trigger an implicature (the listener assumes cooperation and infers extra meaning) — e.g., sarcasm.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

glossary.def: Someone who can readily use a language in conversation; fluent Elders and first-language speakers are central mentors in reclamation work.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

glossary.def: An inanimate entity or natural phenomenon that instigates a change of state without intent: [The heavy gale] shattered the window panes. The reference table's name for what the lecture calls CAUSE.
glossary.source: [ANTH 4 semantic roles reference table - Inventory of Standard Semantic Roles]

glossary.def: A language L defined as a SET of sentences. Eng = {They are happy, Bob is in the room, The cat ran, ...} versus Not-Eng = {*is happy he, *cat the ran, ...}.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A frequency at which the energy of a vowel peaks. Vowels are made up of a wide range of frequencies, and where those frequencies peak we have formants — these determine vowel quality.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: A morpheme that can stand alone as a word (e.g., cat). Only roots can be free.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: When more than one allophone is possible in the SAME environment and the choice does not change meaning, but is also not predictable. Example: the final /p/ in 'leap' may be released [lip] or unreleased [lip̚]. Conventionally marked with a tilde (~) between the two variants.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A consonant with a narrow constriction causing turbulent, noisy airflow (frication) — e.g., the start of set and vet.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A word serving a grammatical function rather than carrying core meaning: she, the, is, will, there. Deixis and tense/mood are the semantic phenomena that apply here.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: A closed-class category providing grammatical 'glue' (determiner, auxiliary/tense, complementizer, pronoun, conjunction), as opposed to lexical categories.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A synthetic type where a single affix fuses several grammatical meanings (e.g., Spanish -áramos = person+number+tense+aspect+mood).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: A system of rules that generates all and only the sentences of a language L. A language can be defined as a set of sentences; the grammar must produce every sentence in that set and no sentence outside it.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A framework (Chomsky & Halle 1968) in which URs are inputs 'generated' into SRs by ordered phonological rules; phonemes/rules may reflect cognitive reality.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: A manner of articulation with a very minimal amount of obstruction, very vowel-like; involves movement from one position to another.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: The spread of English across the world, which the lecture stresses is NOT of neutral value or coincidental — it is the direct result of colonization, and it continues to put many Indigenous and minoritized languages at risk.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

glossary.def: A morpheme-by-morpheme translation line pairing each piece with its meaning/function, using abbreviations (1=first person, PL=plural, etc.).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: A place of articulation produced by air flowing through an open glottis, or by stopping and releasing air there: [h], [ʔ].
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: The opening between the vocal folds; the glottal place of articulation involves the vocal folds (e.g., the first sound of he/who).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The endpoint, final destination, or TARGETED STATE toward which an action or movement is directed: They walked over to [the campus library]. Note that it covers abstract targeted states as well as physical destinations.
glossary.source: [ANTH 4 semantic roles reference table - Inventory of Standard Semantic Roles]

glossary.def: In linguistics, the mental system of knowledge underlying a language — not a book of 'proper-usage' rules. Every human language has a grammar.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A morpheme that serves a function in the utterance rather than carrying core meaning: prepositions, determiners, conjunctions, pronouns, auxiliary verbs. In 'John is going to the store for the third time', these are is, to, the, for.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A classification system for nouns. Related to but NOT the same as sociocultural gender: German has three genders and 'Mädchen' (girl) is NEUTER, not feminine, because the suffix -chen patterns as neuter. Assignment is also affected by phonetics/phonology, morphosyntax, semantic features (human, animate, object type), and processing.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: Whether a form could be generated by the mental grammar of a language. 'Ungrammatical' (marked with *) means the grammar cannot produce it — about what is possible, not merely what exists.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: When an ordinary word gradually becomes a grammatical marker (e.g., the adjective 'stille' becoming the adverb/particle 'still').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: A large chain of changes to English long vowels (after spelling had settled), which is why English spelling and pronunciation often mismatch; analysed as push and/or pull chains.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: In a matched-guise study, the varying label or presentation applied to the stimulus (e.g., the name on a résumé, an accent, a face shown with a voice).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The static configuration of the base knuckles and interphalangeal joints (e.g., the ASL '5' or 'B' handshape); may be unmarked (common, basic) or marked.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The central word of a phrase that determines its category and is obligatory; every phrase is a projection of a head (e.g., a noun heads an NP).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: Movement of a head into the next higher head position (e.g., T-to-C movement, which derives English yes-no questions).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: The organization of words into nested constituents rather than a flat string. A change in meaning corresponds to a change in constituency — 'more intelligent leaders' can mean 'more leaders who are intelligent' or 'leaders who are more intelligent' depending on how the words group.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The ancient Egyptian writing system that appeared around the same time as cuneiform; one of several independently invented scripts (alongside Mayan).
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: An experimental paradigm using an infant's sucking rate: a novel stimulus raises the rate; habituation lowers it; a change back up (dishabituation) shows the infant perceives a difference.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: The study of how languages change over time and how related languages descend from a common ancestor.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: The one-word stage, where a single word conveys a whole utterance's worth of meaning.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: Two words identical in form but with NO relation in meaning — the formal identity is pure coincidence: ail~ale, assent~ascent, bier~beer, dough~doe, past~passed, bank~bank.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: A Coast Salish language of British Columbia, the focus of family- and community-based reclamation work described in the chapter.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

glossary.def: The more general term in a hyponymic relation — the superset. 'Dog' is the hypernym of 'poodle'; 'cook' is the hypernym of 'fry', 'boil', and 'roast'.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: The more specific term in a hyponymic relation — the subset. 'Poodle' is a hyponym of 'dog'; 'stir-fry' and 'sauté' are hyponyms of 'fry'.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: A relation between two words, one more general and one more specific. Word X is a HYPONYM of word Y if X is a subset of Y; Y is the HYPERNYM. dog (hypernym) / poodle (hyponym); shirt ~ tank top; cook ~ fry; child ~ baby.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: A resemblance between a form and its meaning; iconic (representational) words like onomatopoeia are relatively rare because most language is arbitrary.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: The unique language variety of a single individual.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: A multi-word expression whose meaning is non-compositional and must be stored as a whole (e.g., 'let the cat out of the bag').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: The meaning of an utterance in terms of what the speaker is doing with it (asserting, questioning, ordering) — the act performed in making the utterance.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

glossary.def: A teaching setting where learners are surrounded by and use the target language (e.g., the Six Nations immersion program for Mohawk).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

glossary.def: A clause type expressing a request or command (e.g., 'Open the door!').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A meaning a sentence suggests but does not necessarily make true; unlike an entailment, an implicature is cancellable (can be negated without contradiction).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: Unconscious knowledge a fluent user has about their language that they cannot easily articulate (contrast: explicit knowledge).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The belief that people should be able to choose the labels and gendered pronouns used for them, and that speakers should monitor their own and others' language accordingly. Includes coming-out narratives as a genre, pronoun sharing, and debate over terms such as Latinx.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

glossary.def: A person-deixis distinction in first person plural: 'we including you' versus 'we not including you'. English does not mark this; many other languages do.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: Replacing or mispronouncing someone's name to make it 'sound more English/white,' stripping their connection to family, community, and language (Bucholtz).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The way linguistic forms point to social meaning. Referential indexicality points to something in context; non-referential indexicality signals social identity/stance.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: Institutions to which thousands of Indigenous children across North America were sent, roughly 1870–1970, where English was imposed and Indigenous languages suppressed. Andy Windyboy describes his experience in 'Our Spirits Don't Speak English'. The lecture frames this under English as a 'killer language'.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

glossary.def: In a ditransitive, the (often recipient) argument, frequently marked by 'to'; accusative in English (dative in languages with dative case).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A predicate expressing a stable, more-or-less permanent property (e.g., 'is tall', 'is intelligent').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: An affix inserted inside another morpheme (e.g., Tagalog -um- in t-um-akbuh 'ran').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: Morphology expressing grammatical information appropriate to a word's category; it never changes the category (e.g., -s plural, -ed past, agreement).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: A shortening pronounced letter by letter rather than as a word: lol, fyi, diy, IRS, CIA, FBI, DC.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The countries where English is the primary, native language of most of the population — the US, UK, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand. The lecture ties their English dominance directly to settler colonialism, which brought large numbers of English speakers.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

glossary.def: The semantic role of the means by which an event is carried out — the intermediary through which an agent performs the action. There is usually an agent present: Michel cut the bread with [the knife]; The child broke the window with [a hammer].
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: The property that any competent user of the code can both send and receive messages, switching freely between producing and understanding.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: A place of articulation produced by placing the tongue between the teeth: [θ], [ð].
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: A learner's own evolving language system, distinct from both the L1 and the target L2, with its own rule-governed patterns (Selinker 1972).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

glossary.def: A morphological change that alters sounds inside a root rather than adding an affix (e.g., mouse→mice, sit→sat); irregular in modern English.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: A standard transcription system (est. 1886) with one symbol per phone; its underlying structure (like the periodic table) matters more than memorizing symbols.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: Whether a sentence can receive a coherent interpretation. Independent of grammaticality: 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously' is grammatical but not interpretable, while “Chomsky's idea are exciting” is ungrammatical but perfectly interpretable.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A clause type used to ask a question — either a yes-no question or a content (wh-) question.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: Occurring between two vowels (V ___ V). The conditioning environment for the Farsi tap [ɾ].
glossary.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

glossary.def: Pitch manipulated across phrases/sentences for conversational functions (e.g., statement vs. question). Such a language is intonational.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A verb taking only a subject: 'John walked'; 'Sarah listened to the radio'.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A man of the Yahi nation of California. No one has spoken the Yahi language since Ishi died in 1916 — the lecture's example of a language lost entirely.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

glossary.def: A language where words tend to be morphologically simple, expressing grammar via separate function words (e.g., Mandarin, Cantonese; English is fairly analytic).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: A test using the frame 'It is/was ___ that ___'; only a constituent can go in the blank.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: Linguist (1884–1961) whose life's work was audio-recording Indigenous languages of North America. In the last year of Ascención Solórzano's life she shared Mutsun with him, and those recordings now enable Indigenous people to reclaim ancestral languages.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

glossary.def: The language of the Kanien'kehá:ka (Mohawk); an Iroquoian language discussed by Dr. David Kanatawakhon-Maracle (Turtle Clan Mohawk).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

glossary.def: A classic demonstration of sound symbolism: across cultures, people match the sharp nonsense word "kiki" to a spiky shape and the round word "bouba" to a curvy shape, showing non-random sound–meaning associations.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: A place of articulation produced by touching the bottom lip to the teeth: [f], [v].
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: The process by which children implicitly and subconsciously gain their first language(s) simply from exposure, without explicit instruction - contrasted with writing, which must be deliberately taught.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Video Lecture 1 (parts 1-2): What Is Language & Linguistics?]

glossary.def: The principle, stressed by the chapter's contributors, that a language carries cultural knowledge and cannot be taught apart from its culture (e.g., Mohawk nyaweh means far more than English 'thank you').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

glossary.def: A documentary and research project at North Carolina State University, led by Walt Wolfram, that records speakers across North Carolina. Source of the Carolina Brogue and Mountain Talk excerpts used in lecture.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

glossary.def: The gradual, systematic change all living languages undergo across time, at every level (sound, morphology, syntax, meaning, lexicon).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: The mental process of perceiving and understanding linguistic input.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

glossary.def: The specialized work of linguists and linguistic anthropologists who go to (often remote) communities to record a language that has not been documented, aiming to preserve it and to add to linguistic knowledge.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

glossary.def: A group of languages descended from a common proto-language (daughter languages of one ancestor).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: Beliefs or attitudes, held beyond the individual level, concerning what types of languages should be spoken, by whom, and in which contexts. Lecture examples: prescriptivism in schools, the belief that African American English is 'improper', and the belief that only English should be spoken in public in the US. All are tied to power. 'Language attitudes' is used more or less interchangeably in this course, though attitudes skew individual and ideologies are community-held.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: A typical developmental achievement reached around a certain age (babbling, first words, two-word stage, etc.).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: Governmental/institutional rules that encourage or force the use (or non-use) of languages, require proficiency, or regulate languages in public space — usable to erase OR reinforce identities.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The mental process of planning and generating linguistic output (speech or sign).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

glossary.def: A community's work to reclaim and bring back use of its heritage language, especially after colonial suppression; the theme uniting this chapter (Mohawk, Michif, Hul'q'umi'num', Nishnaabemwin).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

glossary.def: Efforts to restore vitality to an endangered or dormant language by growing its number of speakers and its everyday use.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

glossary.def: Attempts to halt or reverse the decline of a language or to revive a DORMANT one — used interchangeably with language revitalization in the lecture. Participants may be community members, linguists, government parties, and others.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

glossary.def: The finding that a person's native language influences how they process linguistic input (e.g., which phonological contrasts the brain responds to).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

glossary.def: A program trained on a vast corpus that calculates the probability that pieces of language relate to one another, used to generate statistically plausible text; it has no mind or communicative intent.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The 'voice box' at the top of the trachea; a set of cartilages surrounding the airway, housing the vocal folds.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A manner of articulation in which air flows along the sides of the mouth or tongue, as in [l].
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: A vowel produced with a less constricted, less peripheral tongue position: /ɪ/, /ɛ/, /æ/, /ə/, /ʌ/, /ʊ/. Contrasted with tense vowels.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: The historical suppression of Indigenous languages (including through residential schools), which made speaking them feel shameful and drove language endangerment — the backdrop reclamation responds to.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

glossary.def: A phonological process in which a sound becomes 'weaker' over time. Lecture example: English /t/ becoming a flap [ɾ], as in the casual pronunciation of words like 'butter'.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A tone category with a steady pitch target: High, Mid, or Low.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: A morpheme with a core meaning of its own: nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs. In 'Bill watches all his favorite shows on Mondays', the lexical morphemes are Bill, watch, favorite, shows, Mondays.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A word's grammatical class (part of speech: noun, verb, adjective, adverb), defined by distribution (grammatical context), not meaning.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: Change in a language's vocabulary — adding, losing, borrowing, or shifting words.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: The study of the meaning of individual words (the semantic information stored with a lexical item, alongside its form and syntactic category).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: Stress whose placement is unpredictable and memorized per word; can create minimal pairs. Contrast with predictable (rule-governed) stress.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The encoding of concepts in the words of a language. Different languages lexicalize different concepts — Inuktitut aput 'snow on the ground', qana 'falling snow'; Pennsylvania German fedderschei 'the condition of being reluctant to write letters'; French flâner 'to wander around aimlessly but enjoyably'. ⚠ This is NOT in itself evidence for language relativism: speakers of other languages can still understand the concept.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: Allomorph choice determined by the specific root, which must be memorized (e.g., ox→oxen, sheep→sheep).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: The 'mental dictionary' — the large store of words and word parts available to the users of a language to choose from.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A visual symbol on a keyboard used by trained apes (e.g., Kanzi) to "say" words; Kanzi answered complex questions by selecting lexigrams.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: A rating scale (e.g., 1-5 or 1-6) between opposed descriptors, used in matched-guise experiments to quantify listeners' judgments: educated/not educated, friendly/unfriendly, employable/unemployable.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: The 'killing' of a language through policy (e.g., residential-school prohibitions on Indigenous languages).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: Judgments people (including linguists) make about others based on how they use language.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A speaker's or community's anxiety that their own way of speaking is incorrect. Dennis Preston describes a long-standing American linguistic insecurity rooted in English having been inherited rather than invented, held in tension with American populism and a desire not to sound stuffy.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

glossary.def: The meaning encoded by linguistic expressions themselves (words/sentences), as opposed to non-linguistic 'meaning' (e.g., 'those clouds mean rain').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: The denial of goods or services based on a person's way of speaking and the assumed characteristics of people who sound a particular way. Per Baugh, it has a detrimental impact on the collective quest to advance equal access to fair housing and fair lending, and courts are ill equipped to offer adequate legal redress against housing providers, lending institutions, or insurance companies.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: A point in a language where speakers have two or more ways of expressing the same thing in the same linguistic environment (e.g., the -ing variable: walking vs. walkin').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: The scientific study of human language: describing the patterns of languages and drawing conclusions about the shared systems in speakers' and signers' minds.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A manner of articulation involving obstruction of the airflow, but less than a fricative: [l] and [ɹ].
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: A word borrowed from another language: pizza, blitz, czar, bagel, taco.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: Where in space or on the body a sign is articulated (default = neutral signing space in front of the torso).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The semantic role referring to the location of an action or state: [Midwest] is cold in winter; I live in [Europe]; We will meet at [the lounge].
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: How air flows through the vocal tract, based on the size/shape of the constriction (stop, fricative, approximant, affricate, tap, trill).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: Rhythmic, syllable-like babbling on the hands by babies acquiring a signed language — evidence that babbling reflects the ambient language, not just random motor activity.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: The modality of signed languages: articulated by the hands/arms (manual), transmitted by light waves (photic), received by sight (visual).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A noun treated as an uncountable substance, taking 'much' and resisting plural/numerals (e.g., water, furniture).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: A revitalization model begun through collaboration between several California Native tribes and UC Berkeley linguists. It pairs young learners with older fluent speakers, works outside a classroom, and is adaptable to each community; it has since been used by Indigenous communities worldwide. One version pairs a fluent speaker with a committed learner for over 300 hours across three years, using only the heritage language.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

glossary.def: A technique for revealing hidden attitudes: hold a STIMULUS constant and vary its GUISE; any difference in participant ratings is attributed to the guise, not the stimulus.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: A conversational maxim: be clear — avoid obscurity and ambiguity, be brief and orderly.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

glossary.def: A conversational maxim: be truthful — do not say what you believe to be false or lack evidence for.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

glossary.def: A conversational maxim: be as informative as required, but not more informative than needed.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

glossary.def: A conversational maxim (relevance): make your contribution relevant to the conversation.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

glossary.def: The shared cognitive system in a language user's mind that lets them produce and understand a language and be understood by others who know it.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A theory in which word meaning is stored as a mental image, a prototype. PRO: we really do use mental images when conceptualizing. CON: different people have different experiences and images (think of 'mom'), the images are prototypical, and some concepts are hard to visualize (e.g. 'reciprocity', 'from').
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: The part of the grammar that links forms (sounds, signs, or symbols) to meanings — a kind of dictionary in the mind.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: Conscious knowledge you have about your grammar, as distinct from the (often unconscious) grammatical knowledge itself.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A phonological process that swaps the order of two phonemes. Lecture example: the historical development of 'Wednesday'.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A distinct Indigenous people whose historically multilingual communities are associated with Michif and a homeland spread across the Prairies and northern US.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

glossary.def: A mixed language of the Métis people combining Algonquian (e.g., Cree/Ojibwe/Saulteaux) and French elements; spoken across the western provinces and into North Dakota.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

glossary.def: The dialect region spanning much of the Midwest (Ohio, Michigan, Indiana, Wisconsin, and neighboring states) that Americans across regions — including Southerners — most often identify as 'normal', accent-free, or correct English, and treat as the broadcast target.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

glossary.def: Two signs (or, in Ch.4, two words) that differ in exactly one parameter/property — e.g., ASL SORRY vs. PLEASE differ only in handshape.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The period of Spanish missions in California, 1769–1834. Native Americans were brought to the missions, baptized, then forcibly kept there; language loss resulted from population loss and repression of language and culture.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

glossary.def: A language whose grammar and lexicon draw substantially from two source languages (Michif is a well-known example).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

glossary.def: The physical channel of a language: whether it is vocalized (spoken) or signed.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A vowel with a stable quality from start to finish.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The smallest systematic pairing of form (sound/sign) and meaning or grammatical function (e.g., cat, -s, inter-).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]
