glossary.def: The method for identifying morphemes in unfamiliar data: compare similar words, look for pairs where one has a particular sequence of sounds and one does not, then hypothesize that the additional sounds carry the additional meaning. A form in isolation ([grapho] 'I write') cannot be analyzed — only comparison reveals structure.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The strategy taught in the Chickasaw walkthrough: rather than attacking all the data at once, take groups of similar forms with similar meanings, extract what is shared across every form and every meaning in that chunk, link the leftovers, then use the remaining data to CONFIRM conclusions already reached.
glossary.source: [ANTH 4 Morphology walkthrough: Chickasaw problem (adapted from Fromkin et al., An Introduction to Language, 8e) - instructor answer key]

glossary.def: Change in a language's word-building system, often via analogy.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: A word containing more than one morpheme (e.g., cats, non-renew-abil-ity); a one-morpheme word is morphologically simple.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: The part of grammar dealing with the meaningful pieces inside words and how they combine (e.g., adding -s to make a plural).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: How the manual articulators move: path movement (elbow/shoulder, moving through space) vs. local movement (wrist/radioulnar/knuckles).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: An Ohlone/Costanoan language of people missionized at San Juan Bautista. Its last first-language speaker, Ascención Solórzano, died in 1929; most Mutsun people today speak only English, some Spanish and English. It is now being reclaimed from archival documentation.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

glossary.def: A sequence of N items occurring in a given order in a corpus (bigram = 2, trigram = 3), used to model co-occurrence probabilities.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: Transcription written between square brackets [ ], representing allophones and the actual phonetic detail of how a sound is produced. Also called phonetic transcription.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: Whether a vowel is oral (raised velum) or nasal/nasalized (lowered velum, e.g., the vowel in bent).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A set of phones that share phonetic properties AND share phonological behaviour; must be exhaustive for the language (e.g., English voiceless plosives [p t k]).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: The area of computational linguistics concerned with programming computers to understand and produce human language (e.g., how a voice assistant like Siri interprets speech).
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Video Lecture 1 (parts 1-2): What Is Language & Linguistics?]

glossary.def: Two words that would be a minimal pair except for extra difference(s) elsewhere; weaker evidence, so several are needed.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: A classical theory of word meaning: the minimal set of conditions that something must meet (necessary) and that suffice (sufficient) to belong to a category (e.g., defining 'doe').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: The desire not to be burdened, imposed on, or inconvenienced.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

glossary.def: An expression (e.g., 'any', 'ever', 'lift a finger') that is only licensed in negative or similar downward-entailing environments.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: A strategy mitigating a negative FTA by minimizing the imposition — hedging, apologizing for intruding, offering an easy way out. 'Would you mind shutting the window?' rather than 'Shut the window'; 'If it's not too much trouble, could you get me a glass of water, please?'
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

glossary.def: When an existing-language feature differs from the target and interferes (a common source of L2 accent and errors).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

glossary.def: A completely novel coinage: zany and grovel (Shakespeare), scrumptdittilyumptious (Roald Dahl), boo, fleek, poggers.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The study of how the brain supports language, using brain measures (e.g., electrical activity/EEG) to test where and when linguistic processing happens.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

glossary.def: Learning a language in an unfamiliar modality (e.g., a hearing speaker learning a signed language as an M2 learner), where learners transfer existing iconic gesture at first.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

glossary.def: An Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) language variety; the chapter describes learning it in a university/community setting.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

glossary.def: The case marking a grammatical subject. Latin 'Canis fêlem vîdit' — canis is dog-NOM, so the dog is the one who saw.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: Meaning that is not part of the literal surface content (e.g., implicatures and presuppositions); not targeted by 'it is not the case that…'.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

glossary.def: An invented word used for testing; speakers' acceptance of a nonce word can show two phones contrast without a real minimal pair.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: Signing articulators other than the hands/arms — torso, head, face (brow, eyes, cheeks, lips) — which carry essential meaning.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A phrase headed by a noun, functioning as a unit: Bobbi, them, the dog, our wonderful pet, that scary spider on my leg. English rule: NP → (Det) (Adj) N (PP).
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The loudest, most prominent core of a syllable, usually a vowel (or a syllabic consonant, e.g., the second syllable of bottle).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A morpheme realized by no overt material, written ∅. In Chickasaw, 'he/she' is signaled by the absence of any subject prefix, so it is a null morpheme. (Your textbook calls this a zero affix.)
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: Any argument that is not a subject, direct object, or indirect object. Most obliques are NPs inside prepositional phrases (from the bank, under the table). Obliques have no grammatical relation with the verb and no shared behavior defining them as a class.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The methodological problem that to study natural vernacular speech, linguists must observe it — but observation makes speech less natural.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: The class of consonants with significant obstruction to airflow: oral stops, fricatives, and affricates.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: Social/psychological harm done to discourse participants (hearers/viewers) by an expression in a given context; can occur regardless of the speaker's intent.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: A predicate taking a single argument; its denotation is the set of things that satisfy it (⟦sour⟧ = the set of all sour things).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: Words that imitate the actual sound they name (buzz, slurp, clank, woof, meow); a partial exception to arbitrariness, though even these vary across languages and stay somewhat arbitrary.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: The consonant(s) before the nucleus. A margin (onset or coda) is simple with one phone, complex with two or more.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The set of lexical categories that readily accept new members — nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs. 'I googled the totally hip ipod on my computer' shows new open-class items entering the language.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The view that vocal language is more important than signed language — a bias that has caused harm to deaf people and to the study of sign languages.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The direction the hand faces (palm orientation + finger orientation), set by the wrist, radioulnar, elbow, and shoulder joints.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A language's writing system. Lecture stresses that orthography does NOT represent sounds accurately: one sound can have many spellings (18 ways to spell the vowel in 'he'), one spelling can map to different sounds (car, cell, cello), some letters have no sound (debt, knot, receipt) and some sounds have no letter (colonel, soldier).
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: Using a word too broadly, applying it to things outside its adult meaning (e.g., calling anyone with a beard 'Dada', or a motorcycle by one's word for a car).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: Applying a regular pattern to an irregular form (e.g., 'goed', 'foots') — evidence the child has learned the rule.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: Prestige attached to a standardized, socially dominant variety, openly recognized as 'correct.'
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: A place of articulation produced by raising the front of the tongue to the palate: [ʃ], [j].
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: The four categories describing a sign: handshape, orientation, location, and movement.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A derogatory term (jerk, idiot, asshole; also called a general pejorative) condemning a specific person for specific behavior, rather than an entire group.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The target (upper) articulator a consonant moves toward — e.g., upper lip, teeth, alveolar ridge, palate, velum, uvula, pharyngeal wall.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The trajectory, route, or ground covered over the course of a MOVEMENT event: The runner sped along [the gravel track]. Path requires motion through space.
glossary.source: [ANTH 4 semantic roles reference table - Inventory of Standard Semantic Roles]

glossary.def: The semantic role of the entity that undergoes a change of state or is directly affected by an event: I cleaned [the car]; Hyun-ju broke [the glass]; Mike burned [the cake].
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: The language of the Yocha Dehe nation. The Patwin people lived along Putah Creek (where UC Davis now stands) until the 1830s, when Mexican soldiers captured them and took them to the Solano mission. Many descendants now live along Cache Creek.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

glossary.def: Improved comprehension of an unfamiliar talker or accent as a result of more listening experience; extends across speakers and even across different accents.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The study of where non-linguists believe dialect boundaries lie and how they evaluate those areas. Dennis Preston's research asked people to draw and label regions on blank maps, revealing widely shared beliefs about 'correct' and 'incorrect' English.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: The process by which infants, initially sensitive to many phonemic contrasts, tune to the contrasts of their ambient language(s) and lose sensitivity to unused ones.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: The subfield studying how the body perceives and processes linguistic signals (works for both signed and spoken languages).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: An utterance that not only conveys information but performs an action that changes reality (e.g., 'I concede,' 'I now pronounce you married') — provided the right authority, sincerity, and audience uptake exist.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The property of language by which utterances (and other social practices) can perform actions and affect reality, including constructing identity (Austin; extended by Butler).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: Deixis marking participant roles: I, she, he, they. The most basic opposition found across languages is speaker (1st person 'I') versus hearer (2nd person 'you'). Third person pronouns are common but not universal. Other distinctions: formal vs. informal (you/thou), inclusive vs. exclusive 'we', and singular/dual/trial/paucal/plural.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: The general category of manipulating airflow with the vocal folds. In this book limited to voiced vs. voiceless.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: An individual unit of speech that can be part of a word in a language; what counts as a phone depends on whether the sound appears in ordinary words of that language.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: An abstract sound category that speakers treat as a single unit; notated in slashes / /. A phoneme is a set of allophones that appear in different environments (e.g., English /t/ = {[ɾ],[tʰ]…}).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: The process of determining a language's phonemes, their allophones, and each allophone's distribution; the result is a phonemicization.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: How much two phones share in articulation; used (with complementary distribution) to decide whether they're allophones of the same phoneme.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: The area of grammar concerned with the physical production and perception of the sounds or signs of language.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The lecture's step-by-step procedure for solving a phonology problem: (1) identify the sounds under investigation, (2) identify any minimal pairs, (3) list the environments for each sound and check for overlap, (4) generalize the environments using natural classes, (5) determine which sound is underlying (the one with the wider distribution), (6) write a rule.
glossary.source: [Language Files, Ch. 3, Exercise 25: Standard Italian - instructor walkthrough & answer key]

glossary.def: The process turning a UR into an SR by applying phonological rules; shown in a derivation table (UR on top, rules down the side, SR on the bottom; — = rule didn't apply).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: A statement A → B / C _ D: a target natural class (A) changes (B) in a stated environment (C _ D). Notation uses → , / , _ (target position), and # (word boundary).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: Allomorph choice determined by surrounding sounds (e.g., a/an; English plural [s]/[z]/[ɪz] by the final sound).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: The part of grammar governing how the physical units of a language can be combined and how they change in different contexts.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A language-specific restriction on which combinations of sounds are possible. English permits the onset clusters in 'bring', 'clean', and 'fly' but not *bming, *cgean, or *fvy; Persian requires a vowel between such consonants (berim 'let's go', kilid 'key', felan 'something/somebody').
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: Language-specific restrictions on which combinations of units are allowed in which positions (e.g., English bans [tl]/[dl] onsets).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: A syntactic category at the phrase level rather than the word level: noun phrase, verb phrase, adjective phrase, prepositional phrase, adverbial phrase.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The study of meaning patterns conveyed in phrases and sentences, as opposed to lexical semantics, which studies meaning patterns in individual words.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: A set of words that act together as a single unit and can occupy the same structural position.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A rule (e.g., S → NP VP) specifying how a constituent breaks into smaller constituents; equivalent to a tree diagram.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A change in fundamental frequency at the END of a phrase. Statements typically take a falling phrase tone, questions a rising one; phrase tone also marks phrasal boundaries.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: The auditory perception of vocal-fold vibration rate (the physical rate is the fundamental frequency, f0).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A mid-utterance change in fundamental frequency that highlights a particular word. Shifting it across 'I never said she stole my money' yields seven different meanings.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: The overall combination of an active and a passive articulator (e.g., bilabial, labiodental, alveolar, velar, glottal). Named active-first (e.g., labiodental).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A process in which a sound takes on the place of articulation of a neighboring sound. In Standard Italian, the alveolar nasal /n/ is realized as the velar nasal [ŋ] before velar stops - the nasal assimilates to the following consonant's place.
glossary.source: [Language Files, Ch. 3, Exercise 25: Standard Italian - instructor walkthrough & answer key]

glossary.def: The most common oral stop: lung air trapped behind the closure, then released in an explosive burst (e.g., English p, t, k, b, d, g).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: Behavior governed by pragmatic competence and strongly culture-specific: when you can accept a gift, who pays for dinner. What counts as polite in one cultural context can be rude in another.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

glossary.def: Brown and Levinson's 1970s framework dividing politeness into NEGATIVE and POSITIVE types, both built on the concept of FACE. Politeness seeks to mitigate face-threatening acts.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

glossary.def: A single word having multiple meanings that are distinct but RELATED — typical for most lexemes. rent (payment) ~ to rent (as tenant) ~ to rent (as landlord); eye (body part) ~ eye (verb); wood (from a tree) ~ wood (place of many trees). Often a shift from one semantic frame to another: surf (ocean → Internet), attack (war → problems), foot (body → landscape), head (body → organization).
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: A language in which several stems and affixes combine into a single word, often expressing a whole sentence. Sora (India): nenadʒdʒadarsiem 'I will not receive cooked rice from your hands'.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The desire to be praised, complimented, and approved of.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

glossary.def: A strategy mitigating a positive FTA by affirming the other person's worth — compliments, praise, expressions of solidarity. 'You're doing so well in this class, you're a brilliant student.'
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

glossary.def: When an existing-language feature matches the target and helps learning (e.g., the new language has a phoneme contrast the learner already has).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

glossary.def: The language- and culture-dependent knowledge of how to use language appropriately: how to greet someone, thank them, say goodbye, give a compliment, flirt. 'How are you?' is an Anglophone greeting that English speakers know does not literally request information — which can cause issues for non-native speakers.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

glossary.def: The part of grammar concerned with how meaning arises in context (e.g., how 'I have some news' can be read as good or bad).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The state, event, or activity a sentence attributes to its subject (in this chapter, a single head — usually a verb or adjective — that combines with a subject and objects).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: An affix attached before its base (e.g., inter- in international).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: A phrase headed by a preposition: around, under the bridge, from Ohio, by the rowdy stadium parking lot. English rule: PP → PREP (NP).
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: Prescribing how people should or should not use language (e.g., style-guide 'rules'). Not the goal of linguistics.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The social value attached to a language variety; higher-prestige forms are often those used by more powerful or privileged groups, not objectively superior ones.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A special kind of entailment that a sentence takes for granted / assumes to be true already (e.g., 'again' presupposes a prior occurrence).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: The meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts AND how those parts are combined (not just which words, but their structure).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: When two analyses fit the data equally, prefer the simpler one (fewest statements/rules).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: Automatic, skill-like knowledge used without conscious effort (fluent real-time use); the other memory system relevant to language learning.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

glossary.def: A rule that applies to EVERY form meeting its target and environment, with no exceptions (typical of spoken-language phonological rules; signed languages seem to lack these).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: The property that a language can produce an infinite number of new words and sentences from a finite vocabulary and finite set of combining principles. Also called creativity.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: How well a learner can use the language; gaining proficiency means moving from limited toward more native-like comprehension and production.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

glossary.def: A standardized scale for rating proficiency (e.g., ACTFL Proficiency Guidelines, the CEFR/Canadian Language Benchmarks), used by programs including language-reclamation schools.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

glossary.def: A constituency test: a constituent can be replaced by a pronoun such as s/he, they, it, that, them, then, there, do that. 'A man with dark glasses (He) is following us'; 'Annette went to Brazil (there)'.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The content of a declarative sentence that can be true or false.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: The reconstructed common ancestor language, spoken roughly 5,000-10,000 years ago, from which many modern languages descend (English, German, Spanish, Italian, Russian, and more). Used in lecture to illustrate what historical linguistics studies: how one language diverges into hundreds of related ones.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Video Lecture 1 (parts 1-2): What Is Language & Linguistics?]

glossary.def: The reconstructed common ancestor of a set of related languages (reconstructed forms are marked with * ; unknown forms may be marked with ?).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: A theory/observation that categories have fuzzy boundaries and better/worse examples; the 'cup or bowl' experiments show categorization isn't captured by strict necessary-and-sufficient conditions alone.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: The study of the mental processes involved in language production and comprehension, using experiments (e.g., reaction times) to test theories of how linguistic knowledge is deployed in real time.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

glossary.def: The idea that abstract linguistic units (like phonemes) are not just analysts' constructs but are actually used by the mind/brain — supported by psycho- and neurolinguistic evidence.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

glossary.def: A chain shift in which one sound moves away, leaving a gap that 'pulls' another sound in (e.g., [iː]>[ai] pulling others up).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: Describing sounds whose airstream is initiated by the lungs and diaphragm. All English consonants are pulmonic; some other languages use non-pulmonic mechanisms.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: A chain shift in which one sound moves into another's space, 'pushing' it to move too.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: An illocutionary act of inviting the addressee to supply information.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

glossary.def: An ideology formed in reaction against social progress. Lecture examples: 'I don't have pronouns', opposition to singular they as ungrammatical, and 'Don't Say Gay' legislation.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

glossary.def: Studying change by comparing a community's speech at two actual points in time.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: The semantic role of an NP that receives a physical object: Ivan gave a banana to [Amanda]; Suzanna brought [me] a cake.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: Repurposing a slur as a marker of shared identity and solidarity against oppression (e.g., 'queer'); not all targeted members may be ready to embrace a reclaimed term.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The property that a structure can contain another instance of the same kind of structure (e.g., a clause inside a clause), allowing infinitely long sentences.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: Repeating part or all of a word as a morphological process (e.g., Halq'eméylem qwélqwel 'talkative'; English 'salad-salad').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: The actual thing in the world (or cognitive model) that a linguistic expression points to on a given use.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: The ability to use language to talk about language itself (metalanguage) — e.g., "How do you pronounce that?" or "I don't like what you just said."
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: A language variety associated with a particular geographic area, differing in words, pronunciations, and grammar.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: A variety of language chosen to express formality (or informality) appropriate to a situation; part of how language signals social identity.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: A sound change that applies systematically to all eligible words (often in a specific conditioning environment).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: Antonyms denoting movement in opposite directions (come/go) or change between reversible states (melt/freeze).
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: A manner/class description for sounds that are 'r-like' in some way.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: A pitch rise at the end of an utterance. In English it typically marks questions, but it also occurs on declaratives, where it is stereotyped as part of the Valley Girl persona.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: The smallest possible base — the indivisible core of a word (e.g., cat, library, nation).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: A honey bee behavior signaling simply that a food source is present (nearby), as opposed to the more detailed waggle dance.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: Lip shape in a vowel: rounded (boot) vs. unrounded (spread as in beat, or neutral as in but).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: Any language learned after one already has an L1 (even if it is one's third or fourth language). One's L2 accent is shaped by the phonology of one's L1.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The study of how people learn an additional language after early childhood (SLA); this book frames it broadly to include later language learning of any kind, including reclamation contexts.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

glossary.def: A head's requirement about what complement it combines with (e.g., a transitive verb selects an object).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: Change in the meaning of words over time (broadening, narrowing, shift, amelioration, pejoration).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: The meaning relationship holding between a verb and its NP arguments — the way a referent noun contributes to the state, action, or situation in a phrase. A fairly small, abstract set, and INDEPENDENT of grammatical roles.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: Change in a word's meaning over time, which often reflects changing attitudes toward a social phenomenon. Lecture examples trace gay, girl, harlot, hussy, and Cantonese tongzhi.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: The process by which a pragmatic inference becomes part of a word's semantic meaning over time. 'Since' used to refer only to time, was used pragmatically to indicate causality, and can now be used like 'because'.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

glossary.def: The part of grammar that calculates the meanings of words, phrases, and sentences; works together with syntax.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: The meaning of a word that language users store in their heads — the concept associated with the expression (e.g., what you know when you know the word strawberry).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: A softer version of the critical-period idea: a span of heightened (but not strictly all-or-nothing) readiness for language learning.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: A string of words expressing a complete statement, question, or command; a clause that stands on its own as an utterance. A statement expresses a proposition (true or false).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A Cherokee man who, in the early 19th century, created a writing system for Cherokee. It let people read and write the language, leading to extensive documentation and making Cherokee the most published Indigenous language in the US.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

glossary.def: The arrival of politically and militarily powerful new inhabitants in an area where they intend to STAY, and where displacing the original inhabitants is essential to their goals — usually farming. Practiced by the British in the eastern United States, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, and by the United States in California.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

glossary.def: The basic independent meaningful unit of a signed language (equivalent to a spoken word); analyzed by parameters rather than phones.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: An indicator that stands for something else. Linguistic signs are arbitrary and used by convention, like a traffic light or a wedding ring, with no inherent or causal link between form and meaning.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: A sentence with only one clause.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: An affix realized at the same time as its base — common in signed languages (added motion) and tone languages (tonal morphemes).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: Acquiring two (or more) languages from early childhood at the same time; children can separate the systems and reach native competence in each.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: An insult that denigrates a specific marginalized group; targets a person BECAUSE of group membership. Power imbalance is essential — insults aimed at high-status groups lack the same force.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: A language variety associated with a particular social group (class, ethnicity, community) rather than a geographic region.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: A statistical association between a linguistic variable and a social factor such as class, gender, age, or ethnicity.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: Variation within a single language/variety (and even within one speaker), as opposed to cross-linguistic variation between different languages.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: The subfield of linguistics that studies language in its social contexts — how language varies with and signals social identity.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: Traits measured in matched-guise studies that index social closeness: friendly, helpful, trustworthy. The pattern reverses here, with lower-status guises rated HIGHER on these than higher-status guises.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: The class of consonants with relatively free airflow: nasal stops, approximants, taps, and trills.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: An abstract measure of a phone's relative prominence (roughly loudness); a sonority hierarchy orders phones (vowels highest, obstruents lowest).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The tendency for sonority to rise through the onset, peak at the nucleus, and fall through the coda (e.g., [plænt] obeys it; *[lpætn] violates it).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A change that specifically affects the phonology of a spoken language; may add, lose, merge, or simply re-pronounce phonemes.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: A regular match between sounds in related languages (e.g., a sound in one language regularly corresponds to another), used as evidence in reconstruction.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: A tendency for certain sound combinations to become associated with certain meanings within a language (English gl-: glisten, gleam, glare, glow, glitter); still only weakly, not fully, non-arbitrary.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: The starting point, initial physical location, or prior state from which an entity moves: We traveled all the way from [Oakland].
glossary.source: [ANTH 4 semantic roles reference table - Inventory of Standard Semantic Roles]

glossary.def: Deixis marking location: here, there, this, that. 'Here' = near the speaker; 'there' = away from the speaker. Many languages have three-term systems (near speaker / near hearer / far from both), as in Fijian oŋgo, oŋgori, oya.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: Use of 'they/them' to refer to a single, known individual (e.g., 'Samnang told me they needed an extension'); an in-progress grammatical change resisted by prescriptivists.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: A phrase in a designated structural position at the top edge of a phrase (e.g., the subject is the specifier of TP).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: An act performed by producing an utterance (asserting, questioning, promising, pronouncing); performatives are one kind. Applies across modalities.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

glossary.def: An irregular sound change affecting only some words (e.g., changes driven by stereotypes about pronunciation).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: A predicate expressing a temporary state or stage (e.g., 'is available', 'is being restless right now').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: The belief that one variety — standardized American English, following prescriptive rules — is the proper or correct form, and that other varieties are deficient. The lecture's core counterargument: nothing about the standard is linguistically better; its authority comes from its association with power.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

glossary.def: The variety of a language that most closely matches dictionaries, textbooks, and high-status media; its status comes from social/economic/political power, not from being linguistically 'better.'
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: Traits measured in matched-guise studies that index social standing: educated, intelligent, attractive. Speakers in lower-status guises are rated LOWER on these, even by judges who speak the same variety.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: Anything a morpheme can attach to. All roots can be stems, but stems are not always roots: in 'un-tru-th-ful-ly', 'tru' is the root while 'truth' and 'truthful' act as stems for further affixation.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: Negative attitudes and expectations attached to a non-standard accent or variety (the variety itself is neither good nor bad); can cause real harm in jobs, housing, courts, and education.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: In a matched-guise study, the element held constant across conditions (e.g., the résumé, the sales script, the recorded voice).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The entity, event, or concept that triggers a mental or sensory response in an Experiencer: [The loud alarm] startled the horse. Stimulus and Experiencer are a pair. (Not to be confused with 'stimulus' in a matched-guise study.)
glossary.source: [ANTH 4 semantic roles reference table - Inventory of Standard Semantic Roles]

glossary.def: The first major sign-notation system (Stokoe 1960), which analyzed signs into parameters and showed signed languages have full linguistic structure.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A consonant with complete closure blocking airflow. Oral stops (raised velum) include plosives, ejectives, implosives, clicks; nasal stops (lowered velum) send air through the nose.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: Extra prominence on a syllable (via loudness, duration, and/or pitch). Levels: primary [ˈ], secondary [ˌ], and unstressed.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: When one string of morphemes (or words) has more than one possible structure and therefore more than one meaning (e.g., unlockable).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: Switching between registers (levels of formality) depending on audience and context - e.g., an instructor speaking formally in a lecture versus casually with friends. Everyone does it, constantly.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Video Lecture 1 (parts 1-2): What Is Language & Linguistics?]

glossary.def: Varying one's speech across situations; in Labov's attention-paid-to-speech model, more careful speech goes with more attention (other motivations exist too).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: The argument that (in English) appears before the predicate and controls verb agreement; nominative case if a pronoun (I, we, they).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: The English yes-no-question process that reverses subject and auxiliary (You have left → Have you left?); analyzed as T-to-C head movement.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: An affix attached after its base (e.g., -s in cats).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: An irregular pattern that replaces a morpheme's form entirely (go→went, good→better→best); always memorized, often on very frequent words. A type of allomorphy.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: A sound property laid on top of and across segments rather than occurring as a discrete unit: stress, tone, intonation, and length. Contrasted with segments (vowels and consonants), which appear one after another.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: The (relatively concrete) phonetic form of a word, made of phones, written in [ ]. Also called the phonetic representation.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: Associating phones to positions in syllable structure, based partly on sonority.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A layer of structure (abbreviated σ) between the word and the phone; every syllable has a nucleus and optional onset/coda.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: An ASL phonotactic constraint: a two-handed sign with both hands moving must use the same handshape and move the same way (rare exceptions exist).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: The relation between words or expressions that have the same meaning in some or all contexts. Synonyms usually have slightly different meanings and frequently have overlapping — but not identical — senses: vacation/holiday, automobile/car, remember/recall, purchase/buy, big/large.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: When the grammar can assign at least two structures to the same sentence, and those structures sometimes correspond to different interpretations. 'I saw the man in my car' and 'black coffee drinkers' are lecture examples. (Your textbook calls this structural ambiguity.)
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The class a word or constituent belongs to, defined by DISTRIBUTIONAL properties. Members of the same syntactic category can substitute for one another without loss of grammaticality, and show similar distribution in sentences.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: Change in a language's sentence structure/word order over time.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

glossary.def: A transformation that moves an element from its base position to another position in the tree (e.g., head movement, wh-movement); shown by striking the base position and drawing an arrow (trace notation is an alternative).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: The part of grammar that determines how words can and cannot be combined into phrases and sentences.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: A language with much word-internal morphology; subtypes are agglutinative and fusional.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: A word or expression whose use is avoided except in certain circumstances; using it in the wrong context breaks the taboo and causes offence. Taboos can arise for negative OR positive (respect) reasons.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: A strategy of replacing a taboo word with another word — either to avoid resembling it (e.g., Kambaata in-law names) or to evoke it via a similar form (e.g., 'sugar,' 'shoot' for a swear).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The multi-layered structure created by nested hyponymic relationships: cook → fry, boil, roast → stir-fry, sauté, blanch, simmer.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: An early multiword stage containing mostly content words (nouns, verbs) and omitting function words like obligatory determiners — like a telegram.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: The semantic role referring to the time at which an action or state occurred: She left home [yesterday]; I graduated from high school in [2002].
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: Deixis marking time: yesterday, before, after, now. In many languages it is marked through tense affixes on the verb — English has a two-term past/non-past system, Kusaiean a future/non-future system, and Lithuanian a three-term past/present/future system.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: Tongue-root position distinguishing tense (advanced root, e.g., beat) from lax (retracted root, e.g., bit) vowels.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The role a participant plays in an event (agent, experiencer, theme/patient, instrument, goal, source, etc.); also called theta role.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: The thematic role of a participant that something happens to; a patient is a theme that is also changed by the event.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: An organizing history: 1st wave correlates variables with broad social categories; 2nd wave adds locally meaningful community facts; 3rd wave treats variation as active identity/style construction.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: In an LLM, a unit of language — a letter, word, piece of a word (morpheme), or punctuation mark — whose co-occurrence probabilities are calculated.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

glossary.def: Pitch manipulated at the syllable/word level to change meaning (high/low/mid). A language using it is a tone/tonal language.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The effect of a person's existing knowledge (e.g., of words) on how they perceive incoming input — knowledge shaping perception.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

glossary.def: Revitalization that is INSTITUTIONAL, flowing from a government or other institution down to people: language policies, standardization, compulsory education, bilingual education. Often happens simultaneously with bottom-up efforts.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

glossary.def: The especially offensive emotional power of slurs, arising from the power differential and the invocation of historical violence against the targeted group; so strong that even mentioning some slurs can cause harm.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The X-bar analysis of a sentence: a projection of T (tense/auxiliary), with the subject in its specifier and the VP as its complement. (Also called IP.)
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: Notating the phones of a word unambiguously; can be broad (minimal detail) or narrow (fine detail). Written in square brackets [ ].
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The influence of a learner's existing language(s) on the new one.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

glossary.def: A verb taking both a subject and an object: 'John ate five hamburgers'; 'Sarah plays the piano'.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The number of arguments a predicate takes (also called valency): intransitive (1: subject), transitive (2: subject + object), ditransitive (3: subject + two objects).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A branching representation of constituency in which the elements under a node form a constituent. Equivalent alternatives are bracket notation and box diagrams.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: Command of three dialects. John Baugh was a tridialectal speaker of standard American English, AAVE, and Chicano English, which allowed him to vary only intonation and prosody across his test calls.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: A manner of articulation involving rapid vibrations of the articulator.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: A vowel phone that moves through three qualities (e.g., Vietnamese rượu 'alcohol').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The conditions under which a sentence would be true; at-issue (literal) meaning is often called truth-conditional meaning.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

glossary.def: A stop released without a puff of air, written with no superscript h - e.g., 'spy' is [spaɪ]. In English, unaspirated stops appear after [s].
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: Using a word too narrowly, applying it to fewer things than the adult meaning covers.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: The abstract phonemic form of a word, made of phonemes, written in / /. Also called the phonemic representation; the input to a derivation.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: A stop produced without releasing the closure (lips or tongue stay in place), transcribed with a corner diacritic - e.g., 'soap' as [sop̚]. In English this alternates freely with the released version.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A theory in which word meaning is stored together with the ways and contexts in which the word is used. The same vessel is a 'bowl' with rice in it and a 'cup' with a hot drink in it.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

glossary.def: The difference between USING a word to refer to something in the world vs. MENTIONING the word itself as a linguistic object (conventionally shown in italics).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: A place of articulation produced by raising the back of the tongue to the uvula: [ʀ], [q], [ɢ]. Not used in English.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: A stereotyped speech persona associated with young, wealthy white women of the San Fernando Valley, indexed by frequent 'like', creaky voice, and rising intonation on declaratives.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

glossary.def: One of the alternative forms of a linguistic variable (e.g., [ɪŋ] vs. [ɪn] for -ing).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: The study of language variation and change that counts and quantifies variants of linguistic variables to uncover social patterns; grew out of dialectology (Labov).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: A neutral term for any subdivision of a language (used in this chapter to avoid the loaded connotations of 'dialect').
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: A place of articulation produced by raising the back of the tongue to the velum: [k], [g].
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

glossary.def: The nasal consonant [ŋ], produced with the back of the tongue at the velum. In Standard Italian it is an allophone of /n/; in English (as in 'ringing') it is a phoneme in its own right.
glossary.source: [Language Files, Ch. 3, Exercise 25: Standard Italian - instructor walkthrough & answer key]

glossary.def: A stop consonant produced with the back of the tongue against the velum (soft palate): [k] (voiceless) and [g] (voiced). This pair forms the natural class that conditions the Italian [ŋ] allophone.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: A phrase headed by a verb: ran, played the piano, watched the big game on Saturday. English rule: VP → V (NP) (PP).
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: The natural, everyday way a person uses language when not monitoring their speech (e.g., when not being recorded by a linguist).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

glossary.def: Quietly failing to observe a maxim (e.g., lying), without intending the listener to derive an implicature — unlike flouting.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

glossary.def: Two membranes in the larynx that can vibrate; the space between them is the glottis.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A voice quality produced by very low-frequency vocal-fold vibration, sounding creaky; a normal part of many languages' phonetics/prosody, disproportionately criticized in women's voices.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: The lips, tongue, and other parts of the mouth and throat used to articulate spoken language, often shown in a midsagittal diagram.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The modality of spoken languages: articulated with the vocal tract (vocal), transmitted by sound waves (acoustic), received by hearing (auditory).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: [r̥] — an alveolar trill produced without vocal-fold vibration, marked by the under-ring diacritic. In Farsi it appears only in word-final position.
glossary.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

glossary.def: Vocal-fold vibration. A phone with vibration is voiced (e.g., buzz's [z]); one without is voiceless/unvoiced (e.g., bus's [s]).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: A phone made with a wider opening than a consonant; described by quality (height, backness, rounding) rather than place/manner.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: An assimilation process in which the vowels within a word become more similar on some feature. In Finnish, suffix vowels agree in backness with the stem: töllö (front vowels) takes -ltä, while sisko (back vowels) takes -lta.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: Vertical tongue position: high (beat), mid (bet), or low (bat).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: Duration contrast between long and short vowels (phonemic in Japanese; sub-phonemic in English). Long/short consonants = geminates/singletons.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: The overall configuration of tongue and lips in a vowel; more of a continuum than consonant categories.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

glossary.def: An expression involving taboo bodily references (e.g., shit, ass).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

glossary.def: A honey bee behavior encoding the distance, direction, and quantity of a food source; a striking but limited, largely genetic communication system.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

glossary.def: A sign process where the nondominant hand is dropped entirely (a kind of deletion) in a two-handed sign.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: A sign process where the moving nondominant ('weak') hand stops moving in a two-handed sign.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

glossary.def: Whether a string conforms to the structural requirements of the language. The lecture's cline runs from fully well-formed ('The dog is sleeping under the blanket') through agreement errors ('The dog are sleeping...') to word-salad ('Is the the under sleeping Dog blanket').
glossary.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

glossary.def: Movement of a wh-phrase to the front of the clause (into the specifier of CP) to form a content question.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A framing in which outsiders cast themselves as rescuing a community. The lecture lists it among the ethical risks of language documentation, alongside exploitation and power differentials.
glossary.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

glossary.def: In phonemic analysis, the allophone appearing in the greater number of environments - and in the less easily specified ones - is taken to be the underlying phoneme. In the Italian data [n] appears in more environments than [ŋ], so /n/ is the phoneme.
glossary.source: [Language Files, Ch. 3, Exercise 25: Standard Italian - instructor walkthrough & answer key]

glossary.def: The smallest separable unit of language — the smallest unit that can stand on its own in an utterance and move independently in a sentence.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

glossary.def: The order of words in a sentence; fixed in some languages (English) and flexible in others (Latin, Kanien'kéha, ASL), where order is often set by topic/focus.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A method (Berko 1958) using nonce words like 'wug' to show children apply morphological rules productively (one wug, two wugs).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

glossary.def: A theory constraining tree structure: every phrase (XP) is the projection of a head (X) through an intermediate bar level (X'), with positions for a specifier, complement(s), and adjuncts.
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

glossary.def: A morpheme with no overt form, written ∅ (e.g., the plural of sheep/deer).
glossary.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: What is linguistics?
flashcards.back: The scientific (descriptive, empirical) study of human language and the shared mental systems behind it.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: What is 'mental grammar'?
flashcards.back: The shared system in users' minds that lets them understand and be understood — not prescriptive 'rules.'
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: Name the components of mental grammar.
flashcards.back: Phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics (plus the mental lexicon).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: Descriptive vs. prescriptive?
flashcards.back: Descriptive = describe what users actually do; prescriptive = dictate what they 'should' do. Linguistics is descriptive.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: What does the '*' (asterisk) mark?
flashcards.back: An ungrammatical form — one the mental grammar cannot generate (e.g., *'lbitfer').
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: Form–meaning link: what property?
flashcards.back: Arbitrariness — the pairing is conventional, not inherent (with some iconic exceptions).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: What is productivity/generativity?
flashcards.back: A finite vocabulary + finite rules can generate infinitely many new words and sentences.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: Modality of a language means…
flashcards.back: Whether it is vocalized (spoken) or signed.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: Is reading/writing part of core mental grammar?
flashcards.back: No — it's a secondary skill; users have full grammars without literacy, and some languages have no written form.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: What is metalinguistic awareness?
flashcards.back: Conscious knowledge about your grammar, vs. the unconscious grammatical knowledge itself.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: Three accessible tools of language science?
flashcards.back: Acceptability judgments, surveys, and corpora (plus experiments, phonetic software, neuroimaging).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: How does an LLM 'generate' text?
flashcards.back: By combining tokens in statistically probable sequences from training data — combinatorial, with no meaning or intent of its own.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: Human language vs. LLM output — key difference?
flashcards.back: Human language is generative and shared to communicate meaning; LLM output is combinatorial with no communicative intention.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 1]

flashcards.front: What is a performative speech act?
flashcards.back: An utterance that performs an action and changes reality (e.g., 'I now pronounce you married'), given proper authority, sincerity, and audience uptake.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: Whose ideas underlie performativity?
flashcards.back: J. L. Austin ('How to Do Things With Words') and Judith Butler (who extended it to gender/identity).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: Offense vs. derogation?
flashcards.back: Offense = harm to the hearers/viewers (impact); derogation = the utterer's disparaging attitude. An expression can be one, both, or neither.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: Vulgarity vs. expletive?
flashcards.back: Vulgarity = taboo bodily reference (shit, ass); expletive = outburst term (damn). Some words are both.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: What makes something a slur (vs. a particularistic insult)?
flashcards.back: A slur denigrates a whole marginalized GROUP and depends on a power imbalance; a particularistic insult condemns one person for specific behavior.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: Why are slurs 'toxic'?
flashcards.back: Their emotional power comes from a power differential and the invocation of historical violence — even mentioning some can harm.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: What is the use–mention distinction?
flashcards.back: Using a word refers to a thing; mentioning a word treats the word itself as a linguistic object (shown in italics).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: How does a matched-guise study work?
flashcards.back: Hold the STIMULUS constant, vary the GUISE; any rating difference is due to the guise (the label), revealing hidden attitudes.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: In the résumé study, what were stimulus and guise?
flashcards.back: Stimulus = the (constant) résumé; guise = the name at the top (English- vs. non-English-sounding).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: What is indexical bleaching?
flashcards.back: Replacing/mispronouncing a name to make it 'sound more English/white,' erasing identity (Bucholtz).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: Singular 'they' — new or old?
flashcards.back: Unspecified singular 'they' is ~600 years old; the NEW change is SPECIFIC singular 'they' for a known person.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: Can anyone stop language from changing?
flashcards.back: No. Language change is inevitable; prescriptive complaints don't stop it.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: What is linguicide?
flashcards.back: The killing of a language through policy (e.g., residential schools forbidding Indigenous languages).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: Why do L2 users have accents?
flashcards.back: Their L2 mental grammar is shaped by their L1's phonology; accent 'reduction' is hard after childhood — but comprehension adapts more easily.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 2]

flashcards.front: Modality of spoken vs. signed languages?
flashcards.back: Spoken = vocal-auditory; signed = manual-visual.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Three parts of a full consonant description (and order)?
flashcards.back: Phonation – Place – Manner (e.g., voiced bilabial nasal stop).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Active vs. passive articulator?
flashcards.back: Active = the moving/lower articulator; passive = the target/upper articulator.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Name the 4 core manners (this book) + affricate.
flashcards.back: Stop, fricative, approximant, (+ affricate = plosive with fricated release).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Oral vs. nasal stop — what differs?
flashcards.back: Velum position: raised = oral stop; lowered = nasal stop (air through the nose).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Obstruents vs. sonorants?
flashcards.back: Obstruents = oral stops, fricatives, affricates (big obstruction); sonorants = nasals, approximants, taps, trills (free airflow).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Voiced vs. voiceless?
flashcards.back: Voiced = vocal folds vibrate (buzz [z]); voiceless = no vibration (bus [s]).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Three main dimensions of vowel quality?
flashcards.back: Height (vertical tongue), backness (horizontal tongue), rounding (lip shape).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Central vs. mid — don't confuse!
flashcards.back: Central = intermediate BACKNESS; mid = intermediate HEIGHT.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Tense vs. lax vowels?
flashcards.back: Tense = advanced tongue root (beat); lax = retracted tongue root (bit).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: What is the IPA and why like the periodic table?
flashcards.back: A one-symbol-per-phone transcription system; its organizing principles matter more than rote symbol memorization.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: The 4 sign parameters (primes)?
flashcards.back: Handshape, orientation, location, movement.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Path vs. local movement in signs?
flashcards.back: Path = elbow/shoulder (moves through space); local = wrist/radioulnar/knuckles.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: What is a minimal pair (signs)?
flashcards.back: Two signs differing in exactly one parameter (e.g., SORRY vs. PLEASE = handshape only).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Parts of a syllable?
flashcards.back: Onset (optional) + nucleus (required, usually a vowel) + coda (optional).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Open vs. closed syllable? Onsetless?
flashcards.back: Closed = has a coda; open = no coda; onsetless = no onset.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Sonority Sequencing Principle?
flashcards.back: Sonority rises through the onset, peaks at the nucleus, falls through the coda.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Primary vs. secondary stress marks (IPA)?
flashcards.back: Primary = upper tick [ˈ]; secondary = lower tick [ˌ]; before the syllable's onset.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Tone vs. intonation?
flashcards.back: Tone = pitch on syllables/words changing meaning; intonation = pitch over phrases/sentences for functions (question vs. statement).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 3]

flashcards.front: Phoneme vs. allophone?
flashcards.back: Phoneme = abstract category /x/; allophones = its physical realizations [ ] in specific environments.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]
