flashcards.front: Notation: / / vs. [ ] vs. < >?
flashcards.back: / / = phonemic (UR); [ ] = phonetic (SR/phones); < > = spelling/orthography.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: What proves two phones are contrastive (different phonemes)?
flashcards.back: One minimal pair — same context, one phone differs, different meaning.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: Complementary distribution means…?
flashcards.back: The two phones never share an environment. Same phoneme if phonetically similar; different phonemes if not (e.g., [h]/[ŋ]).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: Two allophones of English /t/ and their environments?
flashcards.back: [ɾ] before an unstressed vowel (atom); [tʰ] before a stressed vowel (atomic).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: What is a natural class?
flashcards.back: A set of phones sharing phonetic properties AND phonological behaviour; must include ALL such phones in the language.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: Three parts of a phonological rule?
flashcards.back: Target (A) → change (B) / environment (C _ D).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: UR vs. SR?
flashcards.back: UR = underlying/phonemic /x/ (input); SR = surface/phonetic [x] (output). Rules derive SR from UR.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: Principle of faithfulness?
flashcards.back: Absent any rule, a phoneme surfaces as its default allophone ('elsewhere' case) — so we don't write that statement.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: Principle of simplicity?
flashcards.back: Given equal data coverage, choose the analysis with fewer rules/statements.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: Most common rule type — assimilation?
flashcards.back: A phoneme changes to match a property in its environment (e.g., sonorants devoice after a voiceless obstruent).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: If no minimal pair exists, what tools help?
flashcards.back: Near-minimal pairs (need several) and nonce-word judgments.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: Do signed languages have productive phonological rules?
flashcards.back: Not the fully productive kind; they have sign-specific processes (weak hand freeze/drop, lowering) affecting individual signs.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: What is the Symmetry Condition (ASL)?
flashcards.back: In a two-handed sign where both hands move, both must share handshape and movement.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 4]

flashcards.front: What is a morpheme?
flashcards.back: The smallest systematic pairing of form and meaning/grammatical function (e.g., cat, -s).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: Linguistic definition of 'word'?
flashcards.back: The smallest separable unit — can stand alone and reorder in a sentence (not the spelling/spaces definition).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: Root vs. base vs. affix?
flashcards.back: Root = indivisible core; base = whatever an affix attaches to (can be complex); affix = bound morpheme needing a base.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: Five affix types?
flashcards.back: Prefix (before), suffix (after), circumfix (around), infix (inside), simultaneous (at the same time).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: Free vs. bound morpheme?
flashcards.back: Free = can stand alone (cat); bound = must attach (all affixes + bound roots like -whelmed). Only roots can be free.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: Three 'beyond affix' processes?
flashcards.back: Internal change (mouse→mice), suppletion (go→went), reduplication (salad-salad).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: Allomorph vs. allomorphy?
flashcards.back: Allomorphs = the variant forms of one morpheme; allomorphy = the phenomenon of a morpheme having them.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: Phonologically vs. lexically conditioned allomorphy?
flashcards.back: Phonological = chosen by nearby sounds (a/an); lexical = chosen by the specific root, memorized (ox→oxen).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: Derivational vs. inflectional — key difference?
flashcards.back: Derivation can change meaning/category; inflection expresses grammatical info and NEVER changes category.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: How are lexical categories defined in linguistics?
flashcards.back: By distribution (grammatical contexts a word appears in), not by meaning ('action word').
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: What is a compound?
flashcards.back: A word built from two or more roots (blackboard); in English, stressed on the first member.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: Isolating vs. synthetic; agglutinative vs. fusional?
flashcards.back: Isolating = few morphemes/word (Mandarin); synthetic = many. Agglutinative = separable one-meaning affixes; fusional = one affix, many meanings.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: What is a zero (∅) affix?
flashcards.back: A morpheme with no overt form (e.g., plural of sheep).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: What is structural ambiguity?
flashcards.back: One string with two possible structures → two meanings (e.g., unlockable).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 5]

flashcards.front: What are the two most common basic word orders?
flashcards.back: SOV (most common, ~41%) and SVO (~35%, incl. English). All six orders are attested.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: Sentence vs. clause?
flashcards.back: A clause = subject + predicate; a sentence = a clause that stands alone. Clauses can be embedded inside others.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: Transitivity: intransitive / transitive / ditransitive?
flashcards.back: 1 argument (subject) / 2 (subject+object) / 3 (subject + two objects).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: Simple / compound / complex sentence?
flashcards.back: Simple = one clause; compound = clauses joined by and/or/but; complex = has an embedded clause (recursion).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: What is a constituent?
flashcards.back: A group of words acting as a single structural unit, identified by constituency tests.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: Name the main constituency tests.
flashcards.back: Substitution (pro-form), movement, it-cleft, stand-alone (fragment) answer, and (weakly) coordination.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: Head, complement, specifier?
flashcards.back: Head = the obligatory central word; complement = a phrase the head selects; specifier = phrase at the phrase's top edge (e.g., subject = specifier of TP).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: Lexical vs. functional categories?
flashcards.back: Lexical (N, V, Adj, Adv) name things/events; functional (D, T/Aux, C, pronouns, conjunctions) are grammatical glue.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: What does a complementizer do?
flashcards.back: Introduces an embedded clause (that, if, whether); it's the head C of a CP.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: Name four thematic roles.
flashcards.back: Agent (does on purpose), experiencer (mental state), theme/patient (thing affected), instrument (tool used).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: Core claim of X-bar theory?
flashcards.back: Every phrase XP is a projection of a head X via an intermediate X' (bar level), with specifier, complement, and adjunct positions.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: Why is a sentence a TP?
flashcards.back: Because it's always headed by tense (an auxiliary, tense on the verb, or nonfinite 'to'); subject = specifier of TP, VP = complement.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: What is a CP?
flashcards.back: A complementizer phrase — embedded clauses are CPs, and it's the landing site for T-to-C and wh-movement.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: How are English yes-no questions formed (in X-bar terms)?
flashcards.back: Subject-Auxiliary Inversion = T-to-C head movement (the auxiliary moves from T up to C).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: How are content questions formed?
flashcards.back: With a wh-word via wh-movement — the wh-phrase moves to the front (specifier of CP).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: What is an adjunct?
flashcards.back: A modifier attached at an extra bar level — neither specifier nor complement.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: Agent vs. experiencer?
flashcards.back: Agent acts on purpose (The pirate sank it); experiencer undergoes a mental state (Pirates frighten me).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: What does the passive do to argument structure?
flashcards.back: It rearranges arguments (the theme becomes subject; the agent is demoted/optional), changing argument structure without changing the event's roles.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 6]

flashcards.front: Linguistic vs. non-linguistic meaning?
flashcards.back: Linguistic = meaning encoded by words/sentences (sense of 'swill'); non-linguistic = 'clouds mean rain', a gift 'means' I'm sorry.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.front: Sense vs. denotation?
flashcards.back: Sense = the concept stored in your head; denotation = what the expression points to in the world (⟦pencil⟧ = the set of all pencils).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.front: Principle of compositionality?
flashcards.back: A complex meaning depends on the meanings of the parts AND how they're combined — not just which words, but the structure.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.front: Entailment vs. implicature — key test?
flashcards.back: Negate it: negating an entailment (while keeping the original) is a contradiction; an implicature is cancellable (no contradiction).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.front: What is a presupposition?
flashcards.back: A special entailment the sentence takes for granted as already true (e.g., 'The professor petted a cat again' presupposes a previous petting).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.front: Why isn't meaning just necessary & sufficient conditions?
flashcards.back: The 'cup or bowl' experiments show category boundaries are fuzzy and depend on world knowledge — prototypes, not strict definitions.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.front: Count vs. mass noun?
flashcards.back: Count = countable, pluralizes, takes 'many' (cats); mass = uncountable substance, takes 'much' (water).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.front: Individual-level vs. stage-level predicate?
flashcards.back: Individual-level = stable property (is tall); stage-level = temporary state (is available / being restless now).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.front: What does ⟦x⟧ mean?
flashcards.back: 'The denotation of x' — what the expression x points to; for a one-place predicate, the set of things it's true of.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.front: What is a negative polarity item (NPI)?
flashcards.back: A word like 'any/ever' licensed only in negative/downward-entailing contexts (*'I saw anyone' vs. 'I didn't see anyone').
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.front: Are idioms compositional?
flashcards.back: No — idioms ('let the cat out of the bag') are non-compositional and stored whole.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.front: Is a dictionary the authority on meaning?
flashcards.back: No — dictionaries lag usage and don't list all senses; meaning lives in speakers' minds, not the OED.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 7]

flashcards.front: At-issue vs. non-at-issue meaning?
flashcards.back: At-issue = literal surface meaning (targeted by 'it is not the case that…'); non-at-issue = implicatures/presuppositions (not targeted).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.front: What is a conversational implicature?
flashcards.back: An inference beyond the literal meaning, drawn by assuming the speaker is being cooperative; it's cancellable.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.front: State the Cooperative Principle (Grice).
flashcards.back: In conversation, cooperate toward the accepted purpose of the talk — the basis for computing implicatures.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.front: Name Grice's four maxims.
flashcards.back: Quality (be truthful), Quantity (be appropriately informative), Relation (be relevant), Manner (be clear/brief/orderly).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.front: Flouting vs. violating a maxim?
flashcards.back: Flouting = blatantly breaking a maxim to trigger an implicature (sarcasm); violating = quietly breaking it (lying), no implicature intended.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.front: What is illocutionary meaning?
flashcards.back: What you DO with an utterance — assert, ask, order — the act performed in saying it.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.front: Assertion vs. question (illocutionary)?
flashcards.back: Assertion = put a proposition forward as true; question = invite the addressee to supply information.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.front: What is a speech act?
flashcards.back: An act performed by uttering (asserting, questioning, promising, pronouncing); works across modalities.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.front: Why is implicature 'cancellable'?
flashcards.back: Because you can deny/suspend it without contradiction — unlike an entailment.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.front: What is 'context' / common ground?
flashcards.back: The shared situation participants mutually take as established; utterances are interpreted against it and update it.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.front: Are presuppositions at-issue?
flashcards.back: No — like implicatures, presuppositions are non-at-issue (survive 'it is not the case that…').
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.front: Do all cultures apply the maxims identically?
flashcards.back: No — e.g., the Maxim of Quality is parameterized differently across communities (Mopan/Mopan Maya study).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 8]

flashcards.front: What is language reclamation?
flashcards.back: A community reclaiming active use of its heritage language, especially after colonial suppression.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.front: Reclamation vs. revitalization?
flashcards.back: Reclamation = a community reclaiming its language; revitalization = restoring its vitality by growing speakers and everyday use.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.front: Dr. Kanatawakhon-Maracle's core point about survival?
flashcards.back: For a language to survive it must be widely SPOKEN — used in daily life, not just supported in principle.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.front: Why teach language WITH culture?
flashcards.back: Language carries cultural knowledge; e.g., Mohawk 'nyaweh' means far more than English 'thank you.'
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.front: What is Michif?
flashcards.back: A mixed language of the Métis combining Algonquian (Cree/Ojibwe) and French elements.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.front: Who are the Métis (re: language)?
flashcards.back: A distinct, historically multilingual Indigenous people associated with Michif, spread across the Prairies and into North Dakota.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.front: What is an immersion program?
flashcards.back: A setting where learners are surrounded by and use the target language (e.g., Six Nations Mohawk immersion).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.front: What drove Indigenous-language endangerment in Canada?
flashcards.back: The legacy of colonialism, including residential schools, which suppressed the languages and made speaking them feel shameful.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.front: Name three languages featured in this chapter.
flashcards.back: Kanien'kéha (Mohawk), Michif, Hul'q'umi'num' (plus Nishnaabemwin).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.front: Role of fluent Elders in reclamation?
flashcards.back: They are key mentors — sources of the language and the stories/knowledge carried in it.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 9]

flashcards.front: What is a linguistic variable?
flashcards.back: A place where speakers have two+ ways of saying the same thing in the same environment (e.g., -ing: walking/walkin').
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.front: Variable vs. variant?
flashcards.back: The variable is the choice point (-ing); the variants are the alternatives ([ɪŋ] vs. [ɪn]).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.front: Cross-linguistic vs. sociolinguistic variation?
flashcards.back: Cross-linguistic = between different languages; sociolinguistic = within one language/variety (even one speaker).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.front: Dialect vs. variety — why 'variety'?
flashcards.back: 'Dialect' can carry a loaded 'lesser' connotation; 'variety' is neutral. Everyone speaks a variety; none is 'better.'
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.front: Idiolect vs. vernacular?
flashcards.back: Idiolect = one individual's variety; vernacular = natural unmonitored speech (how you talk when not being recorded).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.front: What is the observer's paradox?
flashcards.back: To study natural speech linguists must observe it — but observing makes it less natural.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.front: What is style-shifting (Labov)?
flashcards.back: Varying speech by situation; the attention-paid-to-speech model links careful speech to more attention.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.front: Overt vs. covert prestige?
flashcards.back: Overt = open prestige of the standard variety; covert = hidden in-group prestige of a non-standard form (toughness/solidarity).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.front: Apparent-time vs. real-time?
flashcards.back: Apparent-time = compare age groups at one time; real-time = compare the community at two actual times.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.front: Change from above vs. below?
flashcards.back: Above = conscious, often from higher-prestige speech; below = below awareness, via the vernacular.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.front: What are the three waves of sociolinguistics?
flashcards.back: 1st: variable × broad social category; 2nd: locally meaningful community facts; 3rd: variation as active identity/style-making.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.front: What's NOT a sociolinguistic variable?
flashcards.back: A categorical alternation fully forced by the linguistic environment (no social choice).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.front: What does indexicality mean?
flashcards.back: Forms point to social meaning: referential (points to context) vs. non-referential (signals identity/stance).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.front: What is enregisterment?
flashcards.back: When a bundle of features becomes recognized as a socially meaningful 'way of speaking' (e.g., Canadian 'eh').
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 10]

flashcards.front: When does vocal babbling begin, and what about deaf babies?
flashcards.back: ~0;6 for both hearing and deaf babies; babies in a signing environment also babble on the hands (manual babbling).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.front: What is canonical babbling?
flashcards.back: Repeated CV syllables like [bababa]/[dadada].
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.front: What does manual babbling show?
flashcards.back: Babbling reflects the ambient language (signed or spoken), not just random motor noise.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.front: Overextension vs. underextension?
flashcards.back: Overextension = word used too broadly (all bearded men = 'Dada'); underextension = word used too narrowly.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.front: What is telegraphic speech?
flashcards.back: Early multiword speech with mostly content words, omitting function words (like a telegram).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.front: How does the high-amplitude sucking method work?
flashcards.back: Sucking rate rises to novelty, falls with habituation; a rise again (dishabituation) shows the baby noticed a change.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.front: What is perceptual narrowing?
flashcards.back: Infants start sensitive to many contrasts, then tune to their ambient language's contrasts and lose unused ones.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.front: What does overregularization ('goed') reveal?
flashcards.back: The child has internalized the regular rule and is applying it.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.front: What is the wug test for?
flashcards.back: Showing children apply morphological rules productively to novel words (one wug → two wugs).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.front: What does '2;6' mean?
flashcards.back: Two years, six months (age notation = year;month).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.front: Critical vs. sensitive period?
flashcards.back: Critical = a hard window for native-like acquisition; sensitive = a softer span of heightened readiness.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.front: Can children acquire two languages natively at once?
flashcards.back: Yes — simultaneous bilinguals separate the systems and can reach native competence in each.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 11]

flashcards.front: How do adult learners differ from children?
flashcards.back: They have mature cognition, an existing language system, and different motivations — so the process differs from child acquisition.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.front: What is interlanguage (Selinker)?
flashcards.back: A learner's own evolving, rule-governed system, separate from both L1 and the target L2.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.front: Positive vs. negative transfer?
flashcards.back: Positive = an existing feature matches the target and helps; negative = a mismatch interferes (source of accent/errors).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.front: What shapes an L2 accent?
flashcards.back: Transfer from the phonology of the learner's first language.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.front: What are proficiency benchmarks?
flashcards.back: Standardized scales (ACTFL, CEFR/Canadian Language Benchmarks) for rating how well someone uses a language.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.front: Declarative vs. procedural knowledge?
flashcards.back: Declarative = conscious, fact-like (knowing a rule); procedural = automatic skill (fluent real-time use).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.front: What happens when learning a new modality (M2)?
flashcards.back: Hearing learners of a signed language at first transfer existing iconic gesture before acquiring the linguistic system.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.front: How does age of acquisition matter?
flashcards.back: Earlier onset generally means more native-like attainment, especially for pronunciation.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.front: Comprehension vs. production in proficiency?
flashcards.back: Learners usually understand more than they can produce; both grow with proficiency.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.front: Is interlanguage just 'broken' language?
flashcards.back: No — it's a systematic, rule-governed system of its own, a normal stage of learning.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 12]

flashcards.front: Psycholinguistics vs. neurolinguistics?
flashcards.back: Psycholinguistics studies the mental processes of language (via behaviour, e.g., reaction times); neurolinguistics studies the brain basis (via brain measures like EEG).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

flashcards.front: What does 'psychological reality' of phonemes mean?
flashcards.back: That phonemes are actually used by the mind/brain, not just analysts' abstractions — supported by experiments.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

flashcards.front: Bottom-up vs. top-down in perception?
flashcards.back: Bottom-up = the incoming signal flowing to the brain; top-down = existing knowledge (e.g., of words) shaping perception.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

flashcards.front: Give an example of a top-down effect.
flashcards.back: Your knowledge of real words biases how you perceive an ambiguous sound on a [d]-[t] continuum toward a real word.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

flashcards.front: What does 'language-specific processing' show?
flashcards.back: Your native language shapes how your brain processes input (e.g., which contrasts it responds to).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

flashcards.front: What do EEG studies suggest about phonological contrasts?
flashcards.back: The brain registers them very early in processing, before higher-level language areas engage.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 13]

flashcards.front: What is historical linguistics?
flashcards.back: The study of how languages change over time and how related languages descend from a shared ancestor.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

flashcards.front: What is a sound change?
flashcards.back: A change affecting the phonology of a spoken language (adding, losing, merging, or re-pronouncing phonemes).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

flashcards.front: Regular vs. sporadic sound change?
flashcards.back: Regular = systematic across all eligible words (often conditioned by environment); sporadic = irregular, affecting only some words.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

flashcards.front: Push chain vs. pull chain?
flashcards.back: Push = a sound moves into another's space, pushing it along; pull = a sound moves away, leaving a gap that pulls another in.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

flashcards.front: What was the Great Vowel Shift?
flashcards.back: A chain of changes to English long vowels (after spelling settled) — a main reason English spelling and pronunciation mismatch.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

flashcards.front: What is analogy?
flashcards.back: A word shifts to match a pattern in other words (rare → common), often reducing allomorphs in a paradigm.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

flashcards.front: What is grammaticalization?
flashcards.back: An ordinary word becomes a grammatical marker over time (e.g., 'stille' adjective → 'still').
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

flashcards.front: What is the comparative method?
flashcards.back: Comparing related languages' systematic sound correspondences to reconstruct their common ancestor (proto-language).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

flashcards.front: What is a cognate?
flashcards.back: A word descended from the same ancestor word as a word in a related language (gift/Gift are true cognates).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

flashcards.front: Cognates vs. false friends?
flashcards.back: Cognates share an ancestor; false friends look/sound similar but differ in meaning (and may not be cognates).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

flashcards.front: What is a proto-language?
flashcards.back: The reconstructed common ancestor of related languages; reconstructed forms get a *.
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

flashcards.front: What is a language family?
flashcards.back: A group of languages descended from one common proto-language (daughter languages).
flashcards.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

flashcards.front: Linguistics is the ___ study of natural human language.
flashcards.back: Scientific and empirical — it treats language as data to be observed and analyzed objectively, describing what people actually do.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

flashcards.front: Descriptive vs. prescriptive grammar — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: Descriptive grammar describes and explains what speakers actually do (subconscious, never taught, necessary for communication). Prescriptive grammar tells people what they "should" do (must be taught, easily forgotten, decided by "experts," not needed to communicate).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

flashcards.front: Name the eight hallmarks of human language.
flashcards.back: Arbitrariness, discreteness, duality of patterning (complex patterns at multiple levels), displacement, productivity, cultural transmission, reflexivity, and interchangeability.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

flashcards.front: What is arbitrariness? Give evidence.
flashcards.back: No inherent/causal link between a word's form and its meaning; the pairing is by convention. Evidence: the same concept has unrelated forms across languages (bread / pain / xleb / mian bao / kenyér).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

flashcards.front: What is discreteness?
flashcards.back: Words are built from separable elemental units you can break apart — e.g., "tap" = t + a + p.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

flashcards.front: What is duality of patterning?
flashcards.back: Language patterns at two levels: meaningless sound units at the lower level combine into meaningful units at the higher level — the sounds t, a, p recombine as tap, apt, pat.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

flashcards.front: What is displacement?
flashcards.back: We can talk about things and events not present — the absent, past, future, or hypothetical ("If I had a million dollars…").
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

flashcards.front: What is productivity (generativity)?
flashcards.back: We can produce and understand an almost infinite number of messages by recombining relatively few elements and patterns (e.g., The Cat in the Hat: ~200 unique words, endless imagination).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

flashcards.front: What are onomatopoeia and sound symbolism, and why don't they break arbitrariness?
flashcards.back: Onomatopoeia imitates real sounds (buzz, woof); sound symbolism links certain sound clusters to meanings (English gl-: gleam, glow). Both are only partially motivated and still vary across languages, so language stays mostly arbitrary.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

flashcards.front: Is the honey bee waggle dance a language? Why or why not?
flashcards.back: No. It's genuine, systematic, rule-based communication with limited displacement, but it isn't really arbitrary, has no duality of patterning, is essentially non-productive (no innovation), and is genetic rather than learned.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

flashcards.front: What did vervet monkey alarm calls show — and what did they lack?
flashcards.back: At least ~10 predator-specific calls (snake/eagle/leopard → different responses) that appear learned and can be used to "lie." But the calls lack discreteness, duality of patterning, and real productivity (no syntax).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

flashcards.front: Vicki, Washoe, and Kanzi — what did each ape achieve?
flashcards.back: Vicki (chimp): spoke only ~4 words (mama, papa, up, cup). Washoe (chimp): produced ~132 ASL signs, understood far more. Kanzi (bonobo): understood complex spoken commands and answered via a lexigram keyboard.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

flashcards.front: Physically, what adapts humans for speech? (name a few)
flashcards.back: Upright even teeth, muscular lips, a small mouth, a small muscular tongue, a velum that raises/lowers, and — most importantly — bipedalism, which puts the head above the spine and lowers the larynx, creating a long pharynx for resonance.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

flashcards.front: How is human language different from even advanced animal communication?
flashcards.back: Beyond lexical items (nouns, verbs), roughly half of human speech is purely grammatical (prepositions, conjunctions, articles, auxiliaries), and grammar lets us build infinite sentences from finite words — far beyond a 5-year-old-level any animal reaches.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

flashcards.front: Which is older, spoken or written language — and by how much?
flashcards.back: Speech is far older: spoken/signed language goes back tens of thousands of years (~50,000+), while writing is only a few thousand years old (cuneiform ~5,000 years ago). Children learn speech naturally but must be taught to write.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

flashcards.front: What is a language ideology, and how does it differ from a personal language attitude?
flashcards.back: A language ideology is a belief about what languages should be spoken, by whom, and in which contexts, held at a community rather than individual level, and tied to power. Thinking Italian sounds nice is a personal attitude; believing only standardized English belongs in classrooms is an ideology. For this course the two terms are treated as effectively the same.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: Name three language ideologies the lecture identifies, and what each is tied to.
flashcards.back: (1) Prescriptivism in schools — standardized American English is 'proper' and anything else is wrong. (2) African American English is 'improper English' — ties language ideology to race. (3) Only English should be spoken in public in the US — surfaces in viral videos of people harassed for speaking Spanish.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: Define linguistic profiling and name the linguist associated with it.
flashcards.back: Denial of goods or services based on a person's way of speaking and the characteristics assumed of people who sound that way. John Baugh. He showed it undermines fair housing and fair lending, and that courts are poorly equipped to provide redress.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: Describe Baugh's housing study design and result.
flashcards.back: Baugh, tridialectal in standard American English, AAVE, and Chicano English, called landlords about advertised apartments saying the same sentence and varying ONLY intonation and prosody, not grammar. Conducted 1988 across five Bay Area communities (Palo Alto, East Palo Alto, San Francisco, Oakland, Woodside). Appointments were far more often offered to the standard American English guise.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: How does a matched guise experiment work?
flashcards.back: A bilingual or bidialectal speaker records the same neutral material in two varieties of differing community status. Typically 8-10 speakers are used and presented randomly. Listeners rate each guise on Likert scales. Judges do not realize they have heard the same speaker twice, so any rating difference is attributable to the variety alone.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: What is the consistent split between status and solidarity variables in matched-guise results?
flashcards.back: Lower-status guises are rated LOWER on status variables (educated, intelligent, attractive) — even by judges who speak that variety. The reverse holds for solidarity variables (friendly, helpful, trustworthy), where lower-status guises are rated HIGHER.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: Summarize the Mengesha (2015) UC Davis study.
flashcards.back: Zion Mengesha recruited a bidialectal African American student to record the same weather report twice — once in African American phonology and intonation, once in 'standard' English — with grammar unchanged and both takes the same length. Teachers from three school types each heard one guise, were told the speaker was auditioning for KDVS radio, and rated his employability and traits.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: What is accent hallucination? Give two examples from the study.
flashcards.back: Rubin (1992): hearing a feature that is not actually present, stereotypically attributed via top-down processing. One teacher reported 'too many slang words' though the weather report contained none; another heard excessive 'umms and ahhs' that were not in the recording.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: What did teacher BX report, and why is it the most serious finding?
flashcards.back: BX said the African American guise seemed to stutter, was 'a little slow', 'not the smartest cookie', and sounded 'bigger and heavy set' — attributing a nonexistent speech impediment and invoking stereotypes of African American men as large and aggressive. BX then judged the same speaker in the standard guise as more intelligent and 'skinnier', reading the identical slow pace as methodical and tactful.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: Who was the speaker in the UCD study actually?
flashcards.back: A concert pianist and Sociology major at UC Davis. His reading ability was identical across both guises, so the negative judgments reflected attitudes toward AAVE, not literacy.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: What is semantic shift? Trace 'gay' and 'queer'.
flashcards.back: Change in word meaning over time reflecting shifting social attitudes. GAY: happy (c.1300) → immoral woman (1825) → homosexual (1935) → 'hopeless/ridiculous' (1980s). QUEER: originally 'weird' → a slur for non-normative sexuality → reclaimed by the community in the 1980s-90s → now common in academia and activism, though some older gay speakers still hear it as offensive.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: Trace the semantic shift of girl, harlot, and hussy — what pattern emerges?
flashcards.back: GIRL: child of either gender (1290) → unmarried female child (1530) → sweetheart (1650) → female sex worker (1711). HARLOT: low fellow/knave (1330) → male servant (1390) → unchaste woman (1450). HUSSY: housewife (1530) → playfully rude address (1600s) → woman of low behavior (1700s). The pattern: terms for women drift toward derogation tied to perceived sexual promiscuity.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: What is the tongzhi example?
flashcards.back: In Cantonese/Chinese in Hong Kong, tongzhi originally meant 'comrade' in the context of the Communist revolution, and was taken up in the 1990s to refer to members of the gay community — semantic shift outside English.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: What is perceptual dialectology, and what did Dennis Preston find?
flashcards.back: The study of where ordinary people believe dialects lie and how they judge them. Preston had people draw and label regions on blank US maps. Respondents overwhelmingly marked the US South and New York City as places where 'bad' English is spoken, and identified the Midland region (Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin, Indiana) as 'normal' or correct — even Southerners did so.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: Three levels on which language varies, with a lecture example of each.
flashcards.back: SOUND: British English speakers don't pronounce /r/ after vowels (flower). GRAMMAR: AAE and Southern American English permit double modals ('might could'), ungrammatical in California English. LEXICON: 'sigogglin'' for something crooked in Appalachian English; lift/elevator and nappy/diaper across British and American English.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: What does the soda/pop/Coke map illustrate?
flashcards.back: Lexical variation by region within the US. Soda dominates California and most of the Northeast, pop dominates the Midwest (Oregon splits), and Coke is used as a generic in the South — where a server may ask what kind of Coke you want and accept 'Sprite' as an answer.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: What is the lecture's single most important takeaway about language varieties?
flashcards.back: No language variety, language, or dialect is better than any other. All varieties are complex, logical, and rule-governed in their own ways. There is nothing linguistically superior about standardized American English — its status comes from its association with power.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: How can language ideologies cut both ways?
flashcards.back: They can harm speakers interpersonally and institutionally — teachers treating students differently or placing them in remedial classes, people being pulled over or profiled by law enforcement. But they can also uplift marginalized groups, as with inclusive language ideologies in LGBTQ communities.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

flashcards.front: What is the lecture's point about Californians and accent?
flashcards.back: Most Californians assume they have no accent and that their speech is simply normal — but it is noticeable to outsiders, and the SNL 'Californians' sketch parodies it (drawn-out vowels, slurred words, obsessive freeway directions). Everyone has an accent; believing you don't is itself a product of how unmarked your variety feels.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

flashcards.front: Why is 'filler word' a loaded term for 'like'?
flashcards.back: 'Filler word' is a prescriptive, negatively valued label, aimed especially at young women. Descriptively, sentence-medial 'like' is a DISCOURSE MARKER that segments units within an utterance — it does real work in discourse rather than merely filling space.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

flashcards.front: Who actually uses creaky voice, and why does it happen?
flashcards.back: Nearly everyone. Sociolinguistic studies find it roughly equal between men and women, and trans and non-binary speakers use it too — despite the stereotype tying it to young women and the Valley Girl persona. It arises naturally at the ends of English sentences, where pitch drops to distinguish statements from questions.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

flashcards.front: What does the Havre, Montana Border Patrol incident illustrate?
flashcards.back: Two US citizens buying milk and eggs were asked for ID by a Border Patrol agent who said it was because he heard them speaking Spanish, denying it was racial. The lecture frames it as linguistic profiling fused with racial profiling, driven by the ideology that only English belongs in public. The women sued for discrimination and reportedly received a substantial settlement.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

flashcards.front: How does Baugh's original definition of linguistic profiling differ from this case?
flashcards.back: Baugh originally conceived linguistic profiling as audio-only — over the phone, where the listener cannot see the speaker. The Montana case shows it can also occur face to face, where it combines with visual racial profiling.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

flashcards.front: Why is language often a 'proxy' in discrimination?
flashcards.back: Because it remains more socially acceptable to say 'I didn't hire her because she didn't sound educated' than to name race, class, or regional origin directly. Judgments about speech stand in for those categories while appearing neutral.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

flashcards.front: What is the troubling consequence for students who speak non-standard varieties?
flashcards.back: Their variety can be pathologized — treated as a speech impediment rather than a dialect — leading to inappropriate referral to speech-language pathologists and placement in remedial classes.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

flashcards.front: Why is singular 'they' not actually a grammatical error?
flashcards.back: Speakers have used singular they for hundreds of years and do so uncontroversially all the time, as in 'a student left their bag in the classroom'. Objections arise only because it has become associated with LGBTQ rights and inclusive language ideologies — it's an ideological reaction, not a grammatical one.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

flashcards.front: How many speech sounds exist across the world's languages, and what does each language use?
flashcards.back: Around 600 vowels and 200 consonants across world languages (Ladefoged, 2004, p. 179) — thousands of possible speech sounds. Each individual language uses only a small subset of them to build its words.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: Name the three subfields of phonetics and what each studies.
flashcards.back: ARTICULATORY phonetics — speech production. ACOUSTIC phonetics — the physical transmission of speech sounds. AUDITORY phonetics — speech reception and perception (your textbook calls this perceptual phonetics).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: Segments vs. suprasegmentals?
flashcards.back: SEGMENTS are discrete units of sound occurring one after another: vowels, consonants. SUPRASEGMENTALS are properties laid on top of and across segments: stress, tone, intonation, length.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: Give four ways orthography fails to represent sounds accurately.
flashcards.back: (1) One sound, many spellings — the vowel of 'he' has 18 spellings (believe, Caesar, see, people, seize, sea, amoeba, machine...). (2) One spelling, different sounds — father, want, many, bad, fame; car, cell, cello. (3) Letters with no sound — psychology, debt, knot, Wednesday, receipt. (4) Sounds with no letter — colonel, soldier.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: What is the 'ghoti' joke, and what does it demonstrate?
flashcards.back: 'ghoti' can be read as 'fish': GH as in enou GH, O as in w O men, TI as in na TI on. It dramatizes how unreliable English orthography is as a guide to pronunciation — exactly the problem the IPA solves.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: When and why was the IPA created?
flashcards.back: In 1888, linguists set out to create the International Phonetic Alphabet to represent the fundamental sounds of all languages. With it, a linguist can write down the words of any language and read a word in any language.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: What three features classify a consonant?
flashcards.back: Airstream mechanism, place of articulation, and manner of articulation. (Voicing and nasality are the further cross-cutting distinctions.)
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: List the places of articulation from the front of the mouth backward.
flashcards.back: Bilabial (two lips) → labiodental (lip + teeth) → interdental (between teeth) → alveolar → alveolar-palatal/post-alveolar → palatal → velar → glottal. (Uvular sits between velar and glottal but isn't used in English.)
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: Define each manner of articulation from the lecture.
flashcards.back: STOP — full closure in the mouth, then release. FRICATIVE — small opening creating turbulence/frication. AFFRICATE — a stop released as a fricative. APPROXIMANT — includes rhotics (r-like) and laterals (air along the sides). GLIDE — movement from one position to another, minimal obstruction. NASAL — oral closure with air exiting the nasal cavity. TRILL — rapid vibration of the articulator. LIQUID — obstruction, but less than a fricative.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: What is voicing, and what is nasality?
flashcards.back: VOICING: whether the vocal cords vibrate. [p], [t], [s], [k] are voiceless; [b], [d], [z], [g] are voiced. NASALITY: whether the velum is open so air passes through the nose. [m], [n] are nasal; [p], [t] are oral.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: What do these 'weird symbols' stand for: /j/ /θ/ /ð/ /ʒ/ /ʃ/ /dʒ/ /tʃ/ /ŋ/?
flashcards.back: /j/ = yellow, /θ/ = thigh, /ð/ = thy, /ʒ/ = rouge, /ʃ/ = shy, /dʒ/ = judge, /tʃ/ = chair, /ŋ/ = long.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: How are vowels produced and classified?
flashcards.back: Produced with little to no restriction of the airflow; quality depends on the shape of the vocal tract. Classified by TONGUE POSITION (front vs. back, open/low vs. close/high) and LIP SHAPE (rounded vs. unrounded).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: Which English vowels are rounded, and which are lax?
flashcards.back: ROUNDED: /u/, /o/, /ʊ/, /ɔ/ — all the rest are unrounded. LAX: /ɪ/, /ɛ/, /æ/, /ə/, /ʌ/, /ʊ/.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: Monophthong vs. diphthong, with examples.
flashcards.back: A MONOPHTHONG is a single vowel. A DIPHTHONG is a sequence of two vowels together: bate [beɪt], bite [baɪt], boat [boʊt], boy [bɔɪt]. Quick keys: /aʊ/ = ow, /aɪ/ = eye, /ɔɪ/ = oy.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: What is length, and where is it contrastive?
flashcards.back: How long a sound is held, understood relative to speech rate in context. In some languages length changes meaning — Finnish: 'mud' /muta/ vs. 'some other' /muːta/; 'come!' /tule/ vs. 'comes' /tuleː/ vs. 'is windy' /tuːleː/.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: Phrase tone vs. pitch accent?
flashcards.back: PHRASE TONE is a change in fundamental frequency at the END of a phrase — falling for statements, rising for questions — and also marks phrasal boundaries. PITCH ACCENT is a MID-utterance change in fundamental frequency that highlights a word.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: What does 'I never said she stole my money' demonstrate?
flashcards.back: Pitch accent. Stressing each of the seven words in turn yields seven different meanings from identical words — the accent alone carries the contrast.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: What is tone, and what are its two types?
flashcards.back: The pitch of a single word used to create a meaning distinction. LEVEL tone (High, Mid, Low) and CONTOUR tone (High-Low, Low-High, etc.). Tones are relative to the speaker's own pitch range and to linguistic context.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: How does stress work in English, with examples?
flashcards.back: Stress is mostly a property of syllables; stressed syllables are longer, louder, and have fuller vowels. In English it can create semantic distinctions: object /ˈɒbʤɛkt/ (noun) vs. object /əbˈʤɛkt/ (verb); produce /ˈproʊdus/ vs. produce /prəˈdus/; present /ˈprɛzənt/ vs. present /priˈzɛnt/.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: Name the five parameters of articulation for signed languages.
flashcards.back: Place/Location, Movement, Handshape, Hand Orientation, and Non-manual Markers (facial expressions or head movement).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: Give a minimal-pair example for each signed-language parameter.
flashcards.back: LOCATION: apple vs. onion; lucky vs. clever. MOVEMENT: tough vs. physics; can vs. shoes. HANDSHAPE: orange vs. color vs. wrong; like vs. white. ORIENTATION: meet vs. I-meet-you. NON-MANUAL MARKERS: late vs. not yet; hot vs. very hot.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: What three things do diacritics mark in this course?
flashcards.back: Aspiration, length, and unreleased stops.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

flashcards.front: How do linguists decide whether an utterance is "grammatical"?
flashcards.back: Descriptively: if speakers of that variety can produce and understand it, it's grammatical - regardless of prescriptive rules. "Ain't" is grammatical in varieties that use it; "me drive the car" is ungrammatical in English. Linguists avoid "correct/incorrect" because of the judgment those words carry.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Video Lecture 1 (parts 1-2): What Is Language & Linguistics?]

flashcards.front: What's the difference between an icon and an arbitrary sign?
flashcards.back: An icon RESEMBLES its meaning (an emoji face, a road sign of a person falling off a bike). An arbitrary sign has only a conventional, agreed-upon link with no inherent connection - most words, plus things like traffic-light colors and wedding rings.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Video Lecture 1 (parts 1-2): What Is Language & Linguistics?]

flashcards.front: If no one "decides" a language's rules, where do they come from?
flashcards.back: They emerge through interaction and consensus within a community over time. Dictionary writers, English teachers, and linguists REFLECT and describe existing rules - they don't invent them. Individuals can nudge usage but can't unilaterally change the shared code.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Video Lecture 1 (parts 1-2): What Is Language & Linguistics?]

flashcards.front: Why is speech (or sign) considered primary and writing secondary?
flashcards.back: Humans have spoken/signed for roughly 50,000 years but only invented writing ~4,000-5,000 years ago. Many languages have no writing system yet are fully languages, and children acquire speech implicitly while writing must be explicitly taught.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Video Lecture 1 (parts 1-2): What Is Language & Linguistics?]

flashcards.front: What does Proto-Indo-European illustrate about historical linguistics?
flashcards.back: That a single ancestor language (~5,000-10,000 years ago) can diverge into many related languages - English, German, Spanish, Italian, Russian, and others - showing how languages systematically change and split over time.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Video Lecture 1 (parts 1-2): What Is Language & Linguistics?]

flashcards.front: What is style shifting, and how does it relate to registers?
flashcards.back: A register is a level of formality; style shifting is moving between registers as the situation changes (lecturing vs. chatting with friends vs. speaking to a judge). It's part of how language expresses social identity.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Video Lecture 1 (parts 1-2): What Is Language & Linguistics?]

flashcards.front: Phonetics vs. phonology - one line each?
flashcards.back: Phonetics = the study of the PHYSICAL properties of speech sounds. Phonology = the study of the PSYCHOLOGICAL/mental properties - how sounds are represented, categorized, and structured in the mind of a speaker.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What is a minimal pair, and what does finding one prove?
flashcards.back: Two words differing in exactly one sound with different meanings (pat/bat). It proves those two sounds are CONTRASTIVE in that language, i.e., they belong to different phonemes.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Why are phonemes described as 'psychological' and 'learned'?
flashcards.back: Psychological: they are abstract categories in the mind, and physically different sounds can belong to one phoneme. Learned: your brain sorts the sounds it hears into a small, language-specific set based on experience with the ambient language.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What can babies do that adults can't, phonologically?
flashcards.back: Babies can produce and perceive the sounds of ALL human languages. They quickly learn which contrasts matter in the surrounding language and learn to ignore the ones that don't - which is why learning new sounds gets harder with age.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What causes a foreign accent, in phonological terms?
flashcards.back: Speaking a foreign language using the sound categories of your native language. Sounds outside your native set can be hard to even hear, so you perceive and produce the closest sound from your own inventory.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Transcribe 'pie' and 'spy' phonetically. What's the difference?
flashcards.back: 'pie' = [pʰaɪ] - aspirated, with a puff of air on release. 'spy' = [spaɪ] - unaspirated, no puff. The bilabial stops are phonetically DIFFERENT but phonologically the SAME (both /p/).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Is aspiration distinctive in English? Why does it matter?
flashcards.back: No. Making a stop aspirated or unaspirated never changes a word's meaning in English, so aspiration is non-distinctive - [pʰ] and [p] are allophones of one phoneme /p/, not separate phonemes.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: State the English aspiration pattern as a distribution.
flashcards.back: [pʰ] and [tʰ] occur WORD-INITIALLY (pat [pʰæt], pool, peak; thin [tʰɪn]). [p] and [t] occur AFTER [s] (spat [spæt], spool, speak; sting). Mutually exclusive environments = complementary distribution, and therefore predictable.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Complementary vs. contrastive distribution vs. free variation?
flashcards.back: Complementary = mutually exclusive environments, predictable, allophones of ONE phoneme. Contrastive = same environment / minimal pairs exist, unpredictable, DIFFERENT phonemes. Free variation = same environment, but either variant is possible with no meaning change (marked with ~).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Why are phonemes 'not predictable' while allophones are?
flashcards.back: Allophones are rule-governed: given the environment, you can predict which one appears ([pʰ] initially, [p] after [s]). Phonemes are not derivable from context - you have to memorize which phoneme goes in which word, i.e., the sound-meaning connection.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: When do you conclude FREE VARIATION rather than complementary distribution?
flashcards.back: Only when you actually see two variants in the SAME environment meaning the same thing - conventionally shown with a tilde: leap [lip] ~ [lip̚], soap [sop] ~ [sop̚]. When in doubt, don't assume free variation without that evidence.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Name the six phonological processes from lecture, with an example each.
flashcards.back: Assimilation - sounds become more similar (English nasal place assimilation). Dissimilation - become more different (surprise, February). Lenition - weakening (/t/ → [ɾ]). Metathesis - swapping two phonemes (Wednesday). Elision - deleting a sound (laboratory). Epenthesis - adding a sound (Chlowe).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What are phonotactic constraints? Give an English and a Persian example.
flashcards.back: Language-specific restrictions on possible sound combinations. English allows 'bring/clean/fly' but not *bming/*cgean/*fvy. Persian requires a vowel between such consonants: berim 'let's go', kilid 'key', felan 'something/somebody'.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What are the three parts of a syllable, and what's in 'flutes' /fluts/?
flashcards.back: Onset, nucleus, coda. In /fluts/: onset = /fl/, nucleus = /u/, coda = /ts/ - a CCVCC syllable.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: How many phonemes are in 'cough' and in 'ringing'? Why is this tricky?
flashcards.back: 'cough' = 3 (/k/ /ɔ/ /f/) and 'ringing' = 5 (/ɹ/ /ɪ/ /ŋ/ /ɪ/ /ŋ/). Tricky because you must count SOUNDS, not letters - 'gh' is one sound, and 'ng' is the single sound /ŋ/.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Which brackets do you use for phonemes vs. allophones?
flashcards.back: / / = phonological/broad transcription, used for PHONEMES. [ ] = phonetic/narrow transcription, used for ALLOPHONES and actual phonetic detail.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: List the six steps for solving a phonology problem.
flashcards.back: 1) Identify the sounds you are investigating. 2) Identify any minimal pairs (if none, move on). 3) List the environments for each sound - do any overlap? 4) Make generalizations using natural classes. 5) Determine which is the underlying sound (wider distribution). 6) Write a rule for the data.
flashcards.source: [Language Files, Ch. 3, Exercise 25: Standard Italian - instructor walkthrough & answer key]

flashcards.front: In the Standard Italian data, which minimal pairs appear and what do they prove?
flashcards.back: [tiŋgo] 'I dye' vs. [tɛŋgo] 'I keep' → /i/ and /ɛ/ are separate phonemes. [fuŋgo] 'mushroom' vs. [faŋgo] 'mud' → /u/ and /a/ are separate phonemes. Each pair is identical except the middle vowel, so those vowels are in contrastive distribution.
flashcards.source: [Language Files, Ch. 3, Exercise 25: Standard Italian - instructor walkthrough & answer key]

flashcards.front: Are [n] and [ŋ] in complementary or contrastive distribution in Standard Italian? How do you know?
flashcards.back: COMPLEMENTARY. There are no minimal pairs for [n] and [ŋ], and when you list their environments none overlap - [ŋ] appears only before [g] and [k], while [n] appears elsewhere.
flashcards.source: [Language Files, Ch. 3, Exercise 25: Standard Italian - instructor walkthrough & answer key]

flashcards.front: What natural class conditions [ŋ] in Standard Italian?
flashcards.back: VELAR STOPS. [ŋ] appears only before [g] (voiced velar stop) and [k] (voiceless velar stop). [n] appears before [t], [d], and the vowel [e].
flashcards.source: [Language Files, Ch. 3, Exercise 25: Standard Italian - instructor walkthrough & answer key]

flashcards.front: Which sound is the underlying phoneme in the Italian data, and why?
flashcards.back: /n/. It has the WIDER DISTRIBUTION - [n] occurs in three environments (before [t], [d], and [e]) while [ŋ] occurs in only one (before velar stops). So Italian has one phoneme /n/ realized as either [n] or [ŋ] depending on environment.
flashcards.source: [Language Files, Ch. 3, Exercise 25: Standard Italian - instructor walkthrough & answer key]

flashcards.front: Write the rule for the Italian nasal data and name the process.
flashcards.back: /n/ → [ŋ] / ___ velar stops. This is PLACE OF ARTICULATION ASSIMILATION - the alveolar nasal becomes a velar nasal when it precedes a velar stop.
flashcards.source: [Language Files, Ch. 3, Exercise 25: Standard Italian - instructor walkthrough & answer key]

flashcards.front: In the Farsi data, do [r], [ɾ], and [r̥] belong to one, two, or three phonemes?
flashcards.back: ONE. There are no minimal pairs among them and none of their environments overlap, so they are in complementary distribution — three allophones of a single phoneme.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

flashcards.front: State the environments for [r], [ɾ], and [r̥] in the Farsi data.
flashcards.back: [r]: word-initially (#_a rah, #_i ris, #_u ruz), after a consonant (d_i qædri), and before a consonant (æ_n hærntowr̥). [ɾ]: only between vowels (e_i beɾid, i_æ biɾæŋg, e_a tʃeɾa, a_i daɾid). [r̥]: only word-finally (tʃar̥, tʃedʒur̥, ʃir̥, hærntowr̥).
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

flashcards.front: Which Farsi sound is the underlying phoneme, and why?
flashcards.back: /r/. It has the WIDEST distribution — word-initial, post-consonantal, and pre-consonantal — and is the ELSEWHERE case, appearing wherever the two more specific rules don't apply. The restricted allophones each need a stated condition; [r] does not.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

flashcards.front: Write the three rules for the Farsi data.
flashcards.back:
/r/ → [r̥] / ___ #  (word-final devoicing)
/r/ → [ɾ] / V ___ V  (intervocalic tapping)
/r/ → [r] elsewhere
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

flashcards.front: Why is 'intervocalic' a better generalization than 'before a front vowel' for the Farsi tap?
flashcards.back: Because every environment in the data has a vowel on BOTH sides: e_i, i_æ, e_a, a_i. Stating only the following vowel ignores half the pattern and wrongly predicts a tap after a consonant. V___V is the stronger, more economical claim.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

flashcards.front: What two phonological processes are at work in the Farsi data?
flashcards.back: FINAL DEVOICING — the voiced trill loses voicing word-finally ([r̥]). LENITION (tapping) — the trill weakens to a single tap between vowels ([ɾ]), the same kind of weakening as English /t/ → [ɾ].
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

flashcards.front: Do the Farsi tapping and devoicing rules conflict?
flashcards.back: No. Intervocalic tapping requires a vowel AFTER the rhotic; word-final devoicing requires a word boundary after it. Those conditions can never both be met, so the rules never compete and no ordering is needed.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

flashcards.front: Compare the Farsi and Standard Italian problems.
flashcards.back: ITALIAN: one phoneme /n/, TWO allophones, conditioned by a FOLLOWING natural class (velar stops), process = place assimilation. FARSI: one phoneme /r/, THREE allophones, conditioned by POSITION (word-final vs. intervocalic vs. elsewhere), processes = devoicing and lenition. Both are solved with the same six-step method.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

flashcards.front: Why can't you describe a vowel as 'alveolar'?
flashcards.back: Place-of-articulation labels (bilabial, alveolar, velar...) describe where a consonant constriction is formed. Vowels involve little or no constriction, so they're described instead by tongue HEIGHT, tongue BACKNESS, and lip ROUNDING — e.g. /i/ is high front unrounded, /æ/ is low front.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

flashcards.front: What is morphology, and what is the lexicon?
flashcards.back: Morphology is the study of how morphemes combine to form new words. The lexicon is the 'mental dictionary' — the store of words and word parts a language's users can draw on.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: How do we know where word boundaries are?
flashcards.back: Speaker intuitions give the best indication. Words can be pronounced alone while individual morphemes often cannot; pauses fall between words, not morphemes; and speakers don't normally produce words morpheme-by-morpheme.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Show that words are not the smallest units of meaning.
flashcards.back: antidisestablishmentarianism = anti-dis-establish-ment-ari-an-ism. Words are made up of morphemes; a morpheme is the smallest unit of meaning and cannot be broken down further and still mean something.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What does the Mohawk example show about cross-linguistic variation?
flashcards.back: Teninonhsihsákha = te-ni-nonhs-ihsak-ha ('you.&.I-two-house-seek-go.and') means 'Let's go look for the house.' A single morphologically complex word in Mohawk corresponds to a whole phrase in English — languages differ enormously in how they build words.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: How many morphemes are in 'walking' and 'retypes'?
flashcards.back: walking = 2 (walk + -ing). retypes = 3 (re- + type + -s).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What is the method of morphological analysis?
flashcards.back: Compare similar words. Find pairs where one has a particular sequence of sounds and the other does not, then hypothesize that the extra sounds carry the extra meaning. Analyze in chunks — group similar forms with similar meanings, pull out what's shared, then link the leftovers.
