flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Isthmus Zapotec: zigi 'chin' / kazigi 'chins'. What's the plural morpheme?
flashcards.back: /ka-/ is the plural marker, a prefix. Confirmed across diaga/kadiaga 'ear(s)' and zike/kazike 'shoulder(s)'.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Dolakha Newar: chẽ 'house' / chẽku 'at the house'. What's the morpheme?
flashcards.back: /-ku/ is a locative suffix marking location. Note it covers 'at', 'in', and 'on' — one morpheme in this language corresponds to several in English.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: How many free and bound morphemes are in 'retypes' and 'workers'?
flashcards.back: retypes = 1 free (type) and 2 bound (re-, -s). workers = 1 free (work) and 2 bound (-er, -s).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Root vs. stem?
flashcards.back: ROOT is the central morpheme at the core of a complex word — every word has one. STEM is anything a morpheme can attach to. All roots can be stems, but stems are not always roots: in un-tru-th-ful-ly the root is 'tru', while 'truth' and 'truthful' serve as stems.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Name the four affix types with an English example of each.
flashcards.back: PREFIX before the stem (un-wise). SUFFIX after the stem (truth-ful). INFIX inside the stem (abso-bloody-lutely). CIRCUMFIX around the stem (a-fish-in' in some American English varieties).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Give the Ilocano example of each affix type.
flashcards.back: PREFIX taga-: amianan 'north' → taga-amianan 'Northerner'. SUFFIX -an: giling 'grind' → giling-an 'grinder'. INFIX -in-: kuton 'ant' → k-in-uton 'ant-infested'. CIRCUMFIX pag-...-en: ragsak 'happy' → pag-ragsak-en 'make happy'.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What two mistakes do people make identifying infixes and circumfixes?
flashcards.back: (1) If two prefixes precede a root, the inner one is NOT an infix — same for suffixes (art-ful-ness). (2) A prefix and suffix surrounding a root do NOT make a circumfix (in-put-s, un-forget-able). When in doubt assume a combination of prefixes and suffixes — circumfixes are rare.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Tagalog: bili 'buy' → binili 'bought'. What affix type?
flashcards.back: An INFIX. The past-tense marker /-in-/ is inserted inside the stem: b-in-ili, s-in-ulat.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: German: lieb 'love' → geliebt 'loved'. What affix type, and inflectional or derivational?
flashcards.back: A CIRCUMFIX /ge-...-t/ marking past tense. It is INFLECTIONAL because it does not change the meaning or word class of the stem — it only conveys tense.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Inflectional vs. derivational morphology — the four contrasts.
flashcards.back: INFLECTIONAL: does not create a new lexeme, never changes word class, highly productive, predictable meaning; codes relationships between constituents. DERIVATIONAL: creates new lexical items, can change word class, meanings not necessarily predictable, often productively limited.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: List the English inflectional affixes from the lecture.
flashcards.back: -s plural (Plums are delicious); -s 3rd singular present (Sharon changes her car's oil); -ed past tense (Voters rejected the measure); -ing progressive (Sarah is riding her bike).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Cree: /tʃi:ma:n/ 'canoe' vs. /nitʃi:ma:n/ 'my canoe'. What's the morpheme?
flashcards.back: /ni-/ is an inflectional prefix signaling first person possessive. Confirmed by /so:niya/ 'money' → /niso:niya/ 'my money' and /wiya:ʃ/ 'meat' → /niwiya:ʃ/ 'my meat'.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Bontoc: /fikas/ 'strong' → /fumikas/ 'he is becoming strong'. What's the morpheme?
flashcards.back: /-um-/, a derivational infix meaning 'to become'. Also kilad/kumilad 'red', bato/bumato 'rock', fusul/fumusul 'enemy'.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Farsi: dana 'wise' → danai 'wisdom'. What affix type and class?
flashcards.back: A SUFFIX /-i/, and it is DERIVATIONAL — it creates nouns from adjectives, changing the category of the stem. Also xub/xubi, darošt/darošti, bozorg/bozorgi, širin/širini.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Why is derivation 'productively limited'? Give examples.
flashcards.back: Derivational affixes are selective about which stems they attach to: un-happy but *un-blue; re-paint but *re-eat, *re-die; neighbor-hood but *friend-hood. The asterisk marks a form speakers of the language can't say.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Lexical vs. grammatical morphemes, and how do they map to open/closed class?
flashcards.back: LEXICAL (content) morphemes carry core meaning — nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs — and form the OPEN class, which readily gains new members. GRAMMATICAL (functional) morphemes serve a function — prepositions, determiners, conjunctions, pronouns, auxiliaries — and form the CLOSED class, which rarely changes.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: How are lexical categories identified?
flashcards.back: By their PATTERNS — which affixes they take (cats, books, pens but *olds) — and by which words and categories can occur together in phrases (a monkey, the pen but *a tall, *a she).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What does Jabberwocky demonstrate about lexical categories?
flashcards.back: In "'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves", you can identify categories without knowing meanings: the derivational suffix -y suggests 'slithy' is an adjective, the inflectional -s suggests 'toves' is a plural noun, and the determiner 'the' signals a noun phrase in which the first word modifies the second.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Are lexical categories universal?
flashcards.back: No. Korean and Japanese lack definite and indefinite articles. Some categories are common cross-linguistically (nouns) and others much less so (definite articles).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Name the six major ways to form new words, plus two others.
flashcards.back: COMPOUNDING, ACRONYM, BACK-FORMATION, ABBREVIATION, EPONYM, BLENDING. Also NEOLOGISM (novel coinage) and LOANWORDS from other languages.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Distinguish acronym, initialism, clipping, and back-formation.
flashcards.back: ACRONYM — initials pronounced as a word (scuba, NASA, fomo). INITIALISM/ABBREVIATION — initials said letter by letter (fyi, FBI, DC). CLIPPING — a longer word shortened (phone, gym, app). BACK-FORMATION — removing what is wrongly taken to be an affix (whelmed, tamale).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Name the four types of morphological systems.
flashcards.back: ISOLATING (analytic) — mainly free morphemes, one morpheme per word (Mandarin). AGGLUTINATING — bound morphemes attach with clear boundaries (Hungarian). FUSIONAL — one morpheme carries several meanings at once and boundaries blur (Russian). POLYSYNTHETIC — many stems and affixes form one word, often a whole sentence (Sora).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Why is Russian /tʃita-yet/ fusional rather than agglutinating?
flashcards.back: Because /-yet/ simultaneously carries BOTH 3rd person AND present tense, and /-l/ carries both 3rd person and past. One morpheme fuses multiple meanings, so you can't segment them apart — unlike agglutinating languages where boundaries are clean.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Are languages pure types?
flashcards.back: No. Languages are rarely pure examples of one type. A language may be mostly one type while containing elements of another — the classifications form a continuous spectrum.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What is allomorphy? Give an affix and a root example.
flashcards.back: A morpheme taking different forms depending on phonological context. AFFIX: the prefix in- is usually [ɪn], but [ɪŋ] in 'incomplete' and [ɪm] in 'imperfect'. ROOT: leaf [lif] vs. leaves [livz].
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Why can't [grapho] 'I write' be analyzed on its own?
flashcards.back: In isolation there's no way to tell which part means 'I' and which means 'write'. Only by comparing it to another form — [graphe] 'he writes' — can you isolate /graph-/ 'write', /-o/ 'I', and /-e/ 'he'.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Chickasaw: what are the root morphemes for 'to be tall' and 'to be hungry'?
flashcards.back: chaaha = 'to be tall' (it appears in Sachaaha, Chaaha, Chichaaha, Hoochaaha). hopoba = 'to be hungry' (Hopobatok, Hoohopobatok, Sahopoba).
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Morphology walkthrough: Chickasaw problem (adapted from Fromkin et al., An Introduction to Language, 8e) - instructor answer key]

flashcards.front: Chickasaw: give the morphemes for past tense, 'I', 'you', and 'he/she'.
flashcards.back: Past tense = -tok (suffix). 'I' = sa- (prefix). 'You' = chi- (prefix). 'He/she' = ∅, the NULL morpheme — there is no prefix at all.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Morphology walkthrough: Chickasaw problem (adapted from Fromkin et al., An Introduction to Language, 8e) - instructor answer key]

flashcards.front: How do we know 'he/she' is a null morpheme in Chickasaw?
flashcards.back: Because 'Chaaha' with NO prefix means 'He/she is tall', while sa-, chi-, and hoo- mark 'I', 'you', and 'they'. The default, unmarked form carries the he/she meaning, so that meaning is realized with no overt morpheme.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Morphology walkthrough: Chickasaw problem (adapted from Fromkin et al., An Introduction to Language, 8e) - instructor answer key]

flashcards.front: If the Chickasaw root for 'to be old' is sipokni, how do you say 'You are old', 'He was old', and 'They are old'?
flashcards.back: 'You are old' = Chisipokni (add chi- 'you'). 'He was old' = Sipoknitok (no subject prefix because he/she is null, plus -tok for past). 'They are old' = hoosipokni (add hoo- 'they', no -tok because it's present).
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Morphology walkthrough: Chickasaw problem (adapted from Fromkin et al., An Introduction to Language, 8e) - instructor answer key]

flashcards.front: What extra morphemes can be recovered from the Chickasaw data beyond what the question asks?
flashcards.back: tikahbi = 'to be tired' (Satikahbi, Chitikahbitok) and chchokwa = 'to be cold' (Chichchokwa). The question doesn't ask for them, but the data supports them.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Morphology walkthrough: Chickasaw problem (adapted from Fromkin et al., An Introduction to Language, 8e) - instructor answer key]

flashcards.front: Finnish classwork: is the morphology in töllö/töllöni/töllöltä/töllöltäni inflectional or derivational?
flashcards.back: INFLECTIONAL. Nothing changes word class — all forms stay nouns — and the added meanings ('my', 'from') are predictable and productive.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Morphology classwork: word-formation and Finnish vowel-harmony problems]

flashcards.front: List all the morphemes in the Finnish data, with meanings and bound/free status.
flashcards.back: töllö 'TV' — FREE root. sisko 'sister' — FREE root. -ni 'my' (1st person possessive) — BOUND. -ltä / -lta 'from' (ablative case) — BOUND. ⚠ Note: 'tani' is NOT a single morpheme — siskoltani segments as sisko-lta-ni, two separate suffixes.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Morphology classwork: word-formation and Finnish vowel-harmony problems]

flashcards.front: What causes the -ltä / -lta alternation in Finnish?
flashcards.back: VOWEL HARMONY, an assimilation process in which vowels in a word become more similar. Finnish suffix vowels agree in BACKNESS with the stem: töllö has front vowels ([ø]) so it takes the front form -ltä ([æ]); sisko has back vowels so it takes the back form -lta ([ɑ]).
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Morphology classwork: word-formation and Finnish vowel-harmony problems]

flashcards.front: Finnish for 'dog' is koira. How do you say 'from my dog'?
flashcards.back: koiraltani. koira contains BACK vowels, so vowel harmony selects the back form -lta (not -ltä), then the possessive -ni attaches: koira + lta + ni.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Morphology classwork: word-formation and Finnish vowel-harmony problems]

flashcards.front: Identify the word-formation process: fridge, playdate, NASA, cardigan, spork.
flashcards.back: fridge = CLIPPING (shortened from refrigerator). playdate = COMPOUNDING. NASA = ACRONYM. cardigan = EPONYM (after the 7th Earl of Cardigan). spork = BLENDING.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Morphology classwork: word-formation and Finnish vowel-harmony problems]

flashcards.front: Why is 'fridge' a clipping rather than an abbreviation?
flashcards.back: A clipping shortens a longer word while keeping its meaning and word class — fridge from refrigerator, like gym, app, exam. An abbreviation/initialism is formed from INITIAL LETTERS said one by one (fyi, FBI, DC). Fridge keeps a chunk of the original word, not its initials.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Morphology classwork: word-formation and Finnish vowel-harmony problems]

flashcards.front: What is syntax, and what two things does word order affect?
flashcards.back: The study of the rules, principles, and processes that combine words to construct sentences. Word order affects our INTERPRETATION ('The dog chased the cat' vs. 'The cat chased the dog') and the AVAILABLE interpretations ('Old women and men were invited' — are the men old too?).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Define grammaticality, interpretability, felicity, and acceptability.
flashcards.back: GRAMMATICALITY — whether a sentence is built according to the grammatical rules of the language; judgments reflect a speaker's mental, implicitly learned knowledge. INTERPRETABILITY — whether it can receive a coherent interpretation. FELICITY — whether it is appropriate to its context. ACCEPTABILITY — a broad term covering any ill- or well-formedness.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Show that grammaticality and interpretability are independent.
flashcards.back: GRAMMATICAL BUT NOT INTERPRETABLE: 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously' (while *'Furiously sleep ideas green colorless' is neither). UNGRAMMATICAL BUT INTERPRETABLE: “Chomsky's idea are exciting” — you know exactly what it means despite the agreement error.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What is basic word order, and what are the six logical possibilities?
flashcards.back: A language's ordering of verb, subject, and object. SVO (The squirrel ate the almond), OVS, SOV, OSV, VSO, VOS — illustrated in lecture with squirrel/almond permutations.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: How does grammatical gender differ from sociocultural gender?
flashcards.back: Grammatical gender is a noun classification system. It can correlate with sociocultural gender for people, but not always: German has three genders and Mädchen ('girl') is NEUTER — das/ein Mädchen — because German syntax requires the suffix -chen to pattern as neuter.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Besides meaning, what factors affect gender assignment?
flashcards.back: Phonetics and phonology, the morphosyntactic properties of the language, semantic features like human/animate/object type, and processing and psycholinguistic factors.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Name the four constituency tests.
flashcards.back: Pronominal substitution, answer fragments, movement, and coordination.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Give an example of each constituency test.
flashcards.back: SUBSTITUTION: 'A man with dark glasses (He) is following us.' ANSWER FRAGMENT: 'The keys are on the table' → Where are the keys? 'On the table.' MOVEMENT: 'We had a lot of fun over the weekend' → 'Over the weekend, we had a lot of fun.' COORDINATION: 'Her friends (and Mary) were playing tennis.'
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What is the crucial caution about using constituency tests?
flashcards.back: Failing a single test does NOT mean the string isn't a constituent, and passing a single test does NOT prove that it is. Apply as many tests as possible before concluding either way.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: How are syntactic categories defined?
flashcards.back: By DISTRIBUTION. Words and constituents in the same category can substitute for one another without loss of grammaticality, and show similar distributional patterns in sentences.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Give the English phrase structure rules for S, NP, VP, and PP.
flashcards.back: S → NP VP. NP → (Det) (Adj) N (PP). VP → V (NP) (PP). PP → PREP (NP). The arrow means 'is made up of'; parentheses mark optional elements.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: How does the NP rule account for Bobbi, the dog, and that scary spider on my leg?
flashcards.back: NP → (Det) (Adj) N (PP). Bobbi = N alone. the dog = Det + N. our wonderful pet = Det + Adj + N. that scary spider on my leg = Det + Adj + N + PP. All fit the one rule because the bracketed elements are optional.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Why are 'the apple' and '*apple the' different in English?
flashcards.back: Phrase structure rules are language-specific. English has NP → Det N, so 'the apple' and 'a beautiful house' are well-formed while *'apple the' and *'house beautiful a' are not.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What does 'more intelligent leaders' show about structure and meaning?
flashcards.back: That a change in meaning is a change in CONSTITUENCY. Grouping [more [intelligent leaders]] gives 'more leaders who are intelligent'; grouping [[more intelligent] leaders] gives 'leaders who are more intelligent'. Same words, different hierarchical structure.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What does the Navajo data show about cross-linguistic variation?
flashcards.back: All languages have constituency and hierarchical phrase structure, but the phrase structure RULES vary. Navajo 'ashkii ateed yiyiiltsá' ('boy girl saw') places the verb last, so its VP rule is VP → NP V rather than English's VP → V NP.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Name the three grammatical roles an NP can play, plus the fourth category.
flashcards.back: Subject (Subj), Direct Object (DO), and Indirect Object (IO) — plus OBLIQUE for any argument that is none of these.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: How do you tell an indirect object from an oblique in English?
flashcards.back: By the double object construction. Indirect objects can SHIFT to sit right after the verb: 'I taught French to three students' → 'I taught three students French.' Obliques cannot: 'She drove her car to Portland' → *'She drove Portland her car.' Both follow 'to', so the shift test is what separates them.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Name the four ways languages code grammatical relations.
flashcards.back: (1) Linear order. (2) Inflectional marking on the NP — case. (3) Inflectional marking on the verb — agreement. (4) Adpositions — prepositions or postpositions.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: How does Latin code grammatical roles?
flashcards.back: Through case endings on nouns rather than word order. 'Canis fêlem vîdit' (dog-NOM cat-ACC saw) = 'the dog saw the cat'; 'Canem fêlis vîdit' (dog-ACC cat-NOM saw) = 'the cat saw the dog'. The word order is identical — only the endings change.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: How do Standard Arabic and Spanish code grammatical roles?
flashcards.back: ARABIC — inflection on the VERB: fataħnaahu = fataħ 'opened' + -naa '1PL.NOM' + -hu '3SG.ACC' = 'We opened it'. When arguments are purely pronominal, Arabic codes relations on the verb. SPANISH — verb inflection (como 'I eat', comes 'you eat') AND word order together: 'el perro mordió el gato'.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: How does Korean code grammatical roles?
flashcards.back: Through case markers on nouns: -i marks nominative, -ul marks accusative. 'ku swunkyeng-i totwuk-ul capasseyo' and 'totwuk-ul ku swunkyeng-i capasseyo' both mean 'That policeman caught a thief' — scrambling the order doesn't change roles because case carries them.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Define transitivity and the three verb types with lecture examples.
flashcards.back: Transitivity is how many arguments a verb requires. INTRANSITIVE — subject only ('John slept'). TRANSITIVE — subject and object ('She ate the bread'). DITRANSITIVE — subject, object, and indirect object ('I threw the ball to Sophie').
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What is a grammar in the formal sense, and what types exist?
flashcards.back: A formal, theoretical model determining what is structurally allowed in a language and what is not. Types include generative grammars, constraint-based grammars, functional grammars, and dependency grammars.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What makes a grammar 'generative'?
flashcards.back: A language L can be defined as a SET of sentences. A generative grammar for L is a system of rules that generates the sentences of L — and ONLY L. It must produce everything in the set and nothing outside it.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Give three equivalent ways to represent syntactic grouping.
flashcards.back: Trees, brackets, and boxes. [S [NP [N Alice]] [VP [V eats] [NP [N cake]]]] encodes exactly the same structure as the corresponding tree.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Write the rule set that generates the tree for 'Alice eats cake'.
flashcards.back: S → NP VP; NP → N; VP → V NP; N → Alice, cake; V → eats.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What is syntactic ambiguity? Give two lecture examples.
flashcards.back: When the grammar can assign at least two structures to one sentence, sometimes corresponding to different interpretations. 'black coffee drinkers' — [black coffee] drinkers vs. black [coffee drinkers]. 'I saw the man in my car' — the PP can attach to the VP (I was in my car) or to the NP (the man was in my car).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: In the tree for 'the dog bit the cat on the nose', what does a node tell you?
flashcards.back: The elements under a node form a CONSTITUENT. That's the whole interpretive content of the diagram — everything dominated by a single node hangs together as a unit.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

flashcards.front: In 'The smart girl gave her friend a generous present for his birthday', what role does each NP play?
flashcards.back: 'The smart girl' = SUBJECT. 'her friend' = INDIRECT OBJECT (it sits right after the verb in the double object construction). 'a generous present' = DIRECT OBJECT. 'for his birthday' = OBLIQUE — a PP that is none of the three core roles.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Syntax classwork: constituency, transitivity, ambiguity, and grammatical-role coding]

flashcards.front: Is 'cut' ditransitive in 'They cut the paper in many shapes'?
flashcards.back: No. 'in many shapes' is an OBLIQUE prepositional phrase, not an indirect object. Ditransitive requires a recipient-type indirect object — 'I threw the ball to Sophie' or 'I gave John a book'. So 'cut' is intransitive and transitive only.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Syntax classwork: constituency, transitivity, ambiguity, and grammatical-role coding]

flashcards.front: What is the transitivity of 'arrive'?
flashcards.back: INTRANSITIVE. 'I will arrive' takes a subject and no object, and you cannot *'arrive something'. Any following PP ('arrive at the station') is an oblique, not an object.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Syntax classwork: constituency, transitivity, ambiguity, and grammatical-role coding]

flashcards.front: What is the transitivity of 'send'?
flashcards.back: TRANSITIVE and DITRANSITIVE. 'I send a package' takes a direct object; 'I send her a package' / 'I sent a package to her' adds an indirect object, which is the ditransitive pattern.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Syntax classwork: constituency, transitivity, ambiguity, and grammatical-role coding]

flashcards.front: How do you tell whether a post-verbal PP makes a verb ditransitive?
flashcards.back: Apply the double-object shift. If the phrase can move to sit directly after the verb as a bare NP ('I sent a package to her' → 'I sent her a package'), it is an indirect object and the verb is ditransitive. If it cannot ('They cut the paper in many shapes' → *'They cut many shapes the paper'), it is an oblique.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Syntax classwork: constituency, transitivity, ambiguity, and grammatical-role coding]

flashcards.front: Explain the two readings of 'I once saw a stranger with my binoculars.'
flashcards.back: READING 1 — 'with my binoculars' attaches to the VP, modifying how I saw: I used my binoculars to see the stranger. READING 2 — it attaches to the NP 'a stranger', modifying the stranger: the stranger had my binoculars. Same words, two attachment sites, two meanings.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Syntax classwork: constituency, transitivity, ambiguity, and grammatical-role coding]

flashcards.front: In the constructed language (Cal-ea gal-ap van), how are grammatical roles marked?
flashcards.back: By CASE, through inflectional endings on the nouns: -ea marks the subject and -ap marks the object. Word order does not carry the roles — 'Cal-ea gal-ap van' and 'Cal-ap gal-ea van' keep the same order but swap who chases whom.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Syntax classwork: constituency, transitivity, ambiguity, and grammatical-role coding]

flashcards.front: In the constructed language, how would you say 'the bird saw the dog'? (hab = bird, cal = dog, tam = saw)
flashcards.back: Hab-ea cal-ap tam. hab 'bird' + -ea (subject marker), cal 'dog' + -ap (object marker), then the verb tam 'saw' — the data is verb-final.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Syntax classwork: constituency, transitivity, ambiguity, and grammatical-role coding]

flashcards.front: What is semantics?
flashcards.back: The study of meaning — specifically the systematic ways languages structure meaning, especially in words and phrases; how meaning is represented and transmitted; and how meaning depends on structure.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What does the mug/cup/bowl/glass exercise demonstrate?
flashcards.back: That word meanings are NOT clear-cut. Boundaries are fuzzy, with clear cases and unclear cases. Meaning depends on context — the same vessel is a 'bowl' with rice in it and a 'cup' with a hot drink; large = 'bowl', small = 'cup'. Meanings are tied to human uses and social/cultural norms, like whether something has a saucer.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Name the three theories of how word meaning is mentally represented, and the conclusion.
flashcards.back: DICTIONARY-STYLE (defined using other words), MENTAL IMAGE (stored as a prototype), and USAGE-BASED (stored with the contexts of use). The conclusion: mental representations are probably composed of ALL THREE aspects.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Give the pro and con of dictionary-style definitions.
flashcards.back: PRO: useful, and can genuinely help people learn word meanings. CON: it's a paraphrase rather than anything basic — if words are defined in terms of other words, how is any meaning ever learned? Nothing connects to anything more fundamental. (Think of children, or people who can't read.)
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Give the pro and con of mental image definitions.
flashcards.back: PRO: mental images really are used when we conceptualize things. CON: different people have different experiences and images — think of 'mom' — so how do we share meanings? The images are prototypical, and some concepts (reciprocity, 'from') are hard to visualize at all.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Define synonymy and give examples. Are synonyms ever identical?
flashcards.back: Words or expressions with the same meaning in some or all contexts: vacation/holiday, youth/adolescent, automobile/car, remember/recall, purchase/buy, big/large. They usually have slightly different meanings — overlapping but not identical senses (film/movie/flick; eat/consume/ingest/wolf down).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Define hyponymy, hypernym, and hyponym.
flashcards.back: A relation between a more general and a more specific word. X is a HYPONYM of Y if X is a subset of Y; Y is the HYPERNYM (superset). dog = hypernym, poodle = hyponym. Multi-layered hyponymic relationships create TAXONOMIES: cook → fry/boil/roast → stir-fry/sauté/blanch/simmer.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Name and define the three types of antonymy.
flashcards.back: CONTRARY — opposite regions of a scale with intermediate values (young/old, thin/thick). COMPLEMENTARY — when one is true the other is false (dead/alive, pass/fail, off/on). REVERSIVE — movement in opposite directions (come/go) or change between reversible states (melt/freeze).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Homophony vs. polysemy — what's the test?
flashcards.back: HOMOPHONY: identical in form, NO relation in meaning — the identity is coincidence (ail~ale, bank~bank). POLYSEMY: one word, multiple meanings that are distinct but RELATED (eye as body part and verb; head as body part and organization leader). The test is whether the meanings are historically/conceptually connected.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Give examples of polysemy as a shift between semantic frames.
flashcards.back: surf (ocean → Internet), attack (war/fighting → problems), foot (body part → landscape, 'foot of a hill'), head (body part → organization), tail (body part → following behind).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Classify: 'Selena hit the ball with the wooden bat' / 'The bat flew away'.
flashcards.back: HOMOPHONY. The two 'bat' meanings have no relation — the identical form is coincidence.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Classify: 'I purchased a couch' / 'I bought the matching tables'.
flashcards.back: SYNONYMY. Purchase and buy are different words with the same meaning.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Classify: 'my hair looking funny' / 'a funny joke'.
flashcards.back: POLYSEMY. One word with two distinct but related senses (odd/strange versus amusing).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What is deixis, and why is it both symbolic and indexical?
flashcards.back: The marking of orientation or position of entities and events relative to points of reference — words needing CONTEXT to be understood. SYMBOLIC because conventional; INDEXICAL because dependent on context. They are 'pointing words' (here, now, I, you) whose referents change with the situation.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Name the three types of deixis with examples.
flashcards.back: PERSON — I, she, he, they. SPATIAL — here, there, this, that. TEMPORAL — yesterday, tomorrow, before, after.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What distinctions can person deixis encode beyond 1st/2nd/3rd?
flashcards.back: FORMAL vs. INFORMAL (you vs. thou). INCLUSIVE vs. EXCLUSIVE first person plural 'we' ('we including you' vs. 'we not including you'). And number beyond singular/plural — DUAL (exactly two), TRIAL (exactly three), PAUCAL (a few but not many).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Describe the Fijian and Malagasy spatial deixis systems.
flashcards.back: FIJIAN has a three-term system: oŋgo 'this (near me)', oŋgori 'this (near you)', oya 'that (away from you and me)'. MALAGASY has a rich remoteness system with three degrees of nearness: eo / eto / ety — 'here / right here / right next to me'.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Compare the English, Kusaiean, and Lithuanian tense systems.
flashcards.back: ENGLISH — two-term, past vs. non-past ('I walk' / 'I walked'). KUSAIEAN — two-term, future vs. non-future (Sepe el mas ekweyah/ingena 'was/is sick'; Sepe el ac misac 'will die'). LITHUANIAN — three-term: skait-o PRES, skait-ỹs FUT, skait-ė PAST.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What is lexicalization, and what does it NOT prove?
flashcards.back: The encoding of concepts in the words of a language. Different languages lexicalize different concepts (Inuktitut aput/qana/piqsirpoq; Pennsylvania German fedderschei; French flâner). ⚠ It does NOT prove language relativism — a missing word doesn't mean speakers can't understand the concept; it only means they haven't coined a term for it.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What are classifiers, and what determines the choice?
flashcards.back: Obligatory grammatical elements used with nouns when counting in many languages — like English 'five ears of corn'. The choice is based on SEMANTIC PROPERTIES of the noun. Indonesian: orang (people), ekor (animals), biji (small round objects — eggs, bullets, jewels, grapes), helai (thin flat objects — paper, cloth, leaves, feathers, handkerchiefs).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What is the key point about semantic roles vs. grammatical roles?
flashcards.back: THEY ARE INDEPENDENT. Not all agents are subjects, and not all patients are objects. Syntactic role is the grammatical position in the sentence; semantic role is the part an NP plays in the actual event.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Analyze 'The dog bit the cat' and 'The cat was bitten by the dog' for both role types.
flashcards.back: ACTIVE: 'the dog' = Subject (syntactic) and Agent (semantic); 'the cat' = Object and Patient. PASSIVE: 'the cat' = Subject but PATIENT; 'the dog' = oblique but AGENT. The passive dissociates the two systems.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: How are syntactic and semantic roles encoded in English?
flashcards.back: SYNTACTIC roles are determined by linear order, sometimes verb agreement, sometimes morphological form. SEMANTIC roles are NOT coded overtly in English — there is no morphology marking them; we interpret them.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: List the nine semantic roles from the lecture.
flashcards.back: Agent, Patient, Experiencer, Instrument, Cause, Recipient, Benefactive, Locative, Temporal.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Distinguish Agent, Experiencer, and Cause.
flashcards.back: AGENT — the responsible initiator/doer, connected with volition, will, or intentionality ([Tammy] drove the car). EXPERIENCER — receives sensory input, NOT connected with volition ([Fatima] likes blueberry pancakes). CAUSE — a natural force bringing about a change of state, no intention or volition ([The snow] caved in the roof).
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Distinguish Recipient from Benefactive.
flashcards.back: RECIPIENT receives a physical object: Ivan gave a banana to [Amanda]. BENEFACTIVE is the one FOR WHOM an action is performed: I baked a cake for [my brother].
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: 'Hilda gave Carlos a present' vs. 'The storm gave Carlos the chills' — analyze Carlos.
flashcards.back: SAME grammatical role, DIFFERENT semantic role. In both, Carlos is the INDIRECT OBJECT. But in the first he is the RECIPIENT; in the second he is the EXPERIENCER.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: 'Marcus opened the door' vs. 'The key opened the door' — what does this show?
flashcards.back: Both subjects have the same SYNTACTIC role but different SEMANTIC roles: Marcus = Agent, the key = Instrument. English subjects can carry different semantic roles depending on the verb and situation.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What does the Haida data show?
flashcards.back: That some languages mark SEMANTIC roles morphologically, where English marks grammatical ones. Haida uses a different pronoun for agent and experiencer: 'skuts hl guntl'aats'' ('I swallowed a bone') marks 'I' as 1.SG.AGNT, while 'dang dii kuyaadaang' ('I love you') marks both as experiencers. English pronouns mark SUBJ/OBJ instead ('I see him' / 'He sees me').
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Define referent and sense.
flashcards.back: REFERENT — the entity in the external world that a linguistic expression relates to; the real-world thing an utterance refers to. SENSE — the meaning of an expression in the mind; the mental conception of the thing referred to. They are somewhat independent.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Can an expression have sense without reference? Give the lecture example.
flashcards.back: Yes. 'The current king of France' makes perfect sense — it has mental associations — but has no referent, since there is no such person. 'The current president of France' has both. 'A unicorn' is another sense-without-reference case.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Do referents have to be real?
flashcards.back: No. The lecture uses 'Garfield' as a referent for 'cat' — but Garfield isn't anywhere in the world. Referents can be ideas, concepts, or historical/fictional figures shared by a community of speakers.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: What do 'Clark Kent' and 'Superman' demonstrate?
flashcards.back: That two expressions can share a single REFERENT while differing in SENSE. People can use both terms without realizing they point to the same person.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: Why do we need both sense and reference?
flashcards.back: SENSE lets us discuss how one object can be referred to in many different ways. REFERENCE lets us talk about meaning being fundamentally related to experience and to things that exist in the world. Also, senses do not have to be 'correct' to make a reference — speaker and listener just need shared knowledge enough for a similar understanding.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

flashcards.front: How many roles are in the reference table vs. the lecture, and what's added?
flashcards.back: The TABLE lists 14 roles; the LECTURE lists 9. The table adds THEME, STIMULUS, SOURCE, GOAL, and PATH, and renames the lecture's CAUSE as FORCE/CAUSER.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 semantic roles reference table - Inventory of Standard Semantic Roles]

flashcards.front: Theme vs. Patient — what's the deciding question?
flashcards.back: WAS IT CHANGED? PATIENT undergoes a change of state or is directly affected (The frost melted [the ice]). THEME is moved, located, or described WITHOUT being fundamentally changed (He placed [the textbook] on the desk).
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 semantic roles reference table - Inventory of Standard Semantic Roles]

flashcards.front: How do the textbook, the table, and the lecture define theme and patient?
flashcards.back: TEXTBOOK (Anderson): a patient is a theme that is ALSO changed — so patient is a subtype of theme. TABLE: theme and patient are separate; theme is explicitly NOT changed. LECTURE: has no theme; patient covers anything affected. All three agree the deciding test is whether the entity is changed.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 semantic roles reference table - Inventory of Standard Semantic Roles]

flashcards.front: What is the Stimulus, and what role does it always pair with?
flashcards.back: The entity, event, or concept that TRIGGERS a mental or sensory response. It pairs with the EXPERIENCER: in 'The loud alarm startled the horse', the alarm is the Stimulus and the horse is the Experiencer.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 semantic roles reference table - Inventory of Standard Semantic Roles]

flashcards.front: Name the three motion roles with an example of each.
flashcards.back: SOURCE — where movement starts (from Oakland). GOAL — the endpoint or targeted state (to the campus library). PATH — the route covered along the way (along the gravel track).
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 semantic roles reference table - Inventory of Standard Semantic Roles]

flashcards.front: Recipient vs. Benefactive under the reference table?
flashcards.back: RECIPIENT comes into PHYSICAL POSSESSION of an object (I sent my classmate a copy of the notes). BENEFACTIVE profits from — or is disadvantaged by — the action WITHOUT necessarily possessing anything (She proofread the paper for her friend).
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 semantic roles reference table - Inventory of Standard Semantic Roles]

flashcards.front: Force/Causer vs. Agent vs. Instrument?
flashcards.back: AGENT acts intentionally and volitionally (The student drafted the syntax tree). FORCE/CAUSER is inanimate or natural and has NO intent (The heavy gale shattered the window panes). INSTRUMENT is the inanimate tool an agent uses (He split the logs with an axe).
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 semantic roles reference table - Inventory of Standard Semantic Roles]

flashcards.front: Can Goal apply to an abstract state, not just a place?
flashcards.back: Yes. The table defines Goal as the endpoint, final destination, OR TARGETED STATE. So 'for relaxation' in 'We were playing a game of Monopoly for relaxation' is a defensible Goal — relaxation is the state the activity aims at.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 semantic roles reference table - Inventory of Standard Semantic Roles]

flashcards.front: Is 'rose' (the flower) and 'rose' (past tense of rise) polysemy or homophony?
flashcards.back: HOMOPHONY. The two senses have no meaning relation — one is a noun for a plant, the other an irregular past-tense verb form. Polysemy requires distinct but RELATED meanings, as with 'head' (body part → leader of an organization).
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Semantics & Pragmatics classwork - Parts 1-2: word meanings and semantic roles]

flashcards.front: How do you decide between homophony and polysemy on an exam?
flashcards.back: Ask whether the two senses are CONNECTED. If you can trace a conceptual or historical link — mouth of a body → mouth of a cave; bright light → bright person — it's POLYSEMY. If the link is pure coincidence — tail/tale, rose/rose, bank/bank — it's HOMOPHONY.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Semantics & Pragmatics classwork - Parts 1-2: word meanings and semantic roles]

flashcards.front: What is the semantic role of 'a game of Monopoly' in 'We were playing a game of Monopoly for relaxation'?
flashcards.back: THEME. The game is what the activity is about, and it isn't changed, so it's Theme rather than Patient. It is NOT a Path — Path requires motion through space (along the gravel track). 'For relaxation' is a defensible GOAL, since Goal covers a targeted state.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Semantics & Pragmatics classwork - Parts 1-2: word meanings and semantic roles]

flashcards.front: Analyze 'Angela was reading stories to the children this morning' for semantic roles.
flashcards.back: Angela = AGENT. stories = THEME (read, but not changed). this morning = TEMPORAL. the children = RECIPIENT is the common answer, though strictly the table's Recipient requires physical possession — since hearing a story transfers nothing physical, GOAL or BENEFACTIVE is arguably a tighter fit. Know both arguments.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Semantics & Pragmatics classwork - Parts 1-2: word meanings and semantic roles]

flashcards.front: Analyze 'He supplied the reporters with information' for semantic roles.
flashcards.back: He = AGENT. the reporters = RECIPIENT. information = THEME — the thing transferred, which isn't itself changed.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Semantics & Pragmatics classwork - Parts 1-2: word meanings and semantic roles]

flashcards.front: Analyze 'Earle has been earning money through his poetry' for semantic roles.
flashcards.back: Earle = AGENT. money = THEME. his poetry = INSTRUMENT — the means by which the earning is carried out.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Semantics & Pragmatics classwork - Parts 1-2: word meanings and semantic roles]

flashcards.front: What hypernym works best for 'fish', and why is 'marine life' imprecise?
flashcards.back: ANIMAL (or vertebrate). 'Marine life' means sea-dwelling organisms, which excludes freshwater fish like trout and catfish — so it isn't a true superset of 'fish'. A hypernym must properly contain every member of the hyponym.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Semantics & Pragmatics classwork - Parts 1-2: word meanings and semantic roles]

flashcards.front: What is pragmatics, and how does it differ from semantics?
flashcards.back: Pragmatics is MEANING IN CONTEXT. Semantics is meaning at the level of structural form; pragmatics relies on sociocultural and interactional contexts.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

flashcards.front: Why does pragmatics rely on inference?
flashcards.back: Because you must determine the possible meanings and interpret based on context. 'It's 100 degrees outside.' — 'Really?' Is that doubt or surprise? There's no structural cue, so miscommunications can occur.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

flashcards.front: Name and define the four Gricean conversational maxims.
flashcards.back: QUANTITY — be informative, not too much or too little. QUALITY — be truthful and well-supported. RELEVANCE — be relevant to the situation. MANNER — be concise, clear, and orderly. To understand one another, interlocutors must cooperate and follow these.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

flashcards.front: Implicature vs. entailment — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: IMPLICATURE: a possible inference the speaker INTENDS the listener to understand — they imply it. ENTAILMENT: a logically NECESSARY inference. 'I just really love waking up so early' ENTAILS that I wake up early, but IMPLIES that I'm being facetious. Pragmatics dictates implicature, not entailment.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

flashcards.front: Why would a speaker break a maxim on purpose?
flashcards.back: To create an IMPLICATURE. We interpret meaning on the assumption that others are following the maxims, so a deliberate violation signals that something beyond the literal content is intended — sarcasm, humour, evasion.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

flashcards.front: Give an example of how semantics can arise from pragmatics.
flashcards.back: SEMANTICIZATION. 'Since' originally referred only to time; it was then used pragmatically to indicate causality; now it can be used like 'because'. The pragmatic inference became part of the word's semantic meaning.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

flashcards.front: What is pragmatic competence, and why does it matter for non-native speakers?
flashcards.back: Language- and culture-dependent knowledge of appropriate use — how to greet, thank, say goodbye, compliment, flirt. 'How are you?' is an Anglophone greeting where the asker doesn't literally want to know, which can trip up non-native speakers.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

flashcards.front: Explain Brown and Levinson's politeness theory.
flashcards.back: From the 1970s. Two types of politeness, negative and positive, both based on FACE. NEGATIVE FACE = not being burdened or inconvenienced. POSITIVE FACE = being praised or complimented. A FACE-THREATENING ACT challenges face: a NEGATIVE FTA imposes, a POSITIVE FTA insults. Politeness seeks to MITIGATE FTAs.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

flashcards.front: Classify: 'Would you mind shutting the window?' vs. 'Shut the window.'
flashcards.back: The first is NEGATIVE POLITENESS — it minimizes the imposition on the hearer's negative face. The second is a bald imperative with no mitigation.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

flashcards.front: Classify: 'You're doing so well in this class, you're a brilliant student.'
flashcards.back: POSITIVE POLITENESS — it attends to the hearer's positive face by praising and complimenting.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

flashcards.front: What does the Stacy dinner scenario illustrate?
flashcards.back: Politeness norms around paying. Stacy offers to cover the meal, friends protest and offer their share, she insists, they ask if she's sure, she confirms, they put wallets away and thank her. The ritual protest-and-insist sequence is itself the politeness norm — accepting instantly, or continuing to protest past the confirmation, would violate it.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

flashcards.front: Give two cross-cultural examples of differing politeness norms.
flashcards.back: ISRAELIS are stereotyped as rude because Israeli politeness rules emphasize DIRECTNESS. In NORTHERN EUROPE, smiling at strangers and talking to strangers on public transit are considered impolite — and to Americans, Northern Europeans can seem rude for not engaging with a friendly stranger.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

flashcards.front: Write a turn that violates the maxim of QUALITY.
flashcards.back: Quality requires truthfulness. Example: 'How did you do on that Linguistics assignment?' — 'I did so well that the professor is going to ask me to lecture next week.' The claim is an exaggeration that isn't well-supported.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Semantics & Pragmatics classwork - Part 3: Gricean maxims and politeness]

flashcards.front: Write a turn that violates the maxim of QUANTITY.
flashcards.back: Quantity requires the right amount of information. Example: 'What did you do this weekend?' — 'Lots of stuff.' Far too little information for the question asked.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Semantics & Pragmatics classwork - Part 3: Gricean maxims and politeness]

flashcards.front: Write a turn that violates the maxim of RELEVANCE.
flashcards.back: Relevance requires staying on topic. Example: 'Did you take the trash out before the truck came this morning?' — a long answer about waste-management providers struggling to meet demand in expanding urban areas. It never addresses the question.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Semantics & Pragmatics classwork - Part 3: Gricean maxims and politeness]

flashcards.front: Write a turn that violates the maxim of MANNER.
flashcards.back: Manner requires being concise, clear, and orderly. Example: 'Where are you going out tonight?' — 'To a community gathering where commercial vendors dispense libations to the harmony of synchronized acoustic vibrations.' Obscure and needlessly long for 'a bar with live music'.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Semantics & Pragmatics classwork - Part 3: Gricean maxims and politeness]

flashcards.front: Give a negative FTA and a negative politeness strategy to mitigate it.
flashcards.back: NEGATIVE FTA (an imposition): 'Can you read my 20-page linguistics final right now?' MITIGATION: 'I'm sorry to bother you, I know you're swamped with finals of your own. But if you have a few spare minutes over the weekend, do you think you could briefly scan my linguistics final? No worries if you can't — I know this is last minute.' It apologizes, minimizes the imposition, and offers an easy out.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Semantics & Pragmatics classwork - Part 3: Gricean maxims and politeness]

flashcards.front: Give a positive FTA and a positive politeness strategy to mitigate it.
flashcards.back: POSITIVE FTA (an insult): 'Your part of the group project was entirely wrong, now the rest of us have to fix your incorrect work.' MITIGATION: 'You did a great job with the formatting and design of your slides. I think we just need a few minor tweaks and it'll align perfectly with the rest of the project. What do you think?' It affirms the person's worth and invites collaboration.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Semantics & Pragmatics classwork - Part 3: Gricean maxims and politeness]

flashcards.front: What three moves make a negative politeness mitigation work?
flashcards.back: (1) Acknowledge and apologize for the imposition. (2) Minimize the size of the request — 'a few spare minutes', 'briefly scan'. (3) Offer an easy way out — 'no worries if you can't'. All three reduce the threat to the hearer's negative face.
flashcards.source: [ANTH 4 Semantics & Pragmatics classwork - Part 3: Gricean maxims and politeness]

flashcards.front: Define settler colonialism.
flashcards.back: The arrival of politically and militarily powerful new inhabitants in an area where they intend to STAY, and where displacing the original inhabitants is essential to their goals — usually farming.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

flashcards.front: How does the lecture connect English's global spread to settler colonialism?
flashcards.back: British settler colonialism in the eastern US, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand — and US settler colonialism in California — brought large numbers of English speakers. Indigenous people lost their land and often their languages, and since contact they have been killed or forced to assimilate. The loss has been particularly severe in California.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

flashcards.front: What happened to the Patwin people, and how is the language being reclaimed?
flashcards.back: The Patwin lived along Putah Creek until the 1830s, when Mexican soldiers took them to the Solano mission (now Sonoma). Today the Yocha Dehe nation funds reclamation with Cache Creek casino profits: community language classes, a school with a bilingual website, a keyboard-friendly spelling system developed with UC Davis linguists, and road signs with original place names along Highway 16.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

flashcards.front: Who was the last speaker of Mutsun, and how was the language preserved?
flashcards.back: Ascención Solórzano (1855–1929), the last first-language speaker, bilingual in Spanish. She worked as a traditional healer in Santa Barbara, and in the last year of her life shared her language with linguist J.P. Harrington, whose audio recordings made later reclamation possible.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

flashcards.front: How did the Mutsun language (almost) get lost?
flashcards.back: The Mutsun were missionized at San Juan Bautista. Cultural and linguistic repression began in the missions and continued with genocide by Anglo-American settlers in the 1800s.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

flashcards.front: Summarize the effect of the Spanish missions on Indigenous languages.
flashcards.back: Mission era 1769–1834. Language loss in the missions came from POPULATION LOSS and REPRESSION of language and culture. But outside the missions, Indigenous people fought back and contained Spanish to the mission areas by 1845 — a containment that could have become the status quo but for the influx of Anglo-American settlers.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

flashcards.front: Why did Gold Rush settlement cause far greater loss than the missions?
flashcards.back: Missionaries and Spanish soldiers occupied only lands around the missions. Gold Rush settlers (1848–1855, about 300,000 arriving) occupied much larger areas already inhabited by Indigenous people and saw them as an obstacle to be eliminated. Many were killed, others relocated to reservations, others enslaved on ranches.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

flashcards.front: What state policy does the lecture identify as genocidal?
flashcards.back: In January 1851, Governor Peter H. Burnett told the state legislature that a war of extermination would continue until the Indian race became extinct. The state then issued a treasury bond to pay bounty hunters and state militias to seek out and kill Indigenous people.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

flashcards.front: What population figures does the lecture give for Indigenous Californians?
flashcards.back: Approximately 1 million in the late 1700s; about 30,000 by around 1860; fewer than 20,000 by 1900. All known Native Americans were under U.S. government protection by 1870. (Pre-contact estimates vary widely between scholars; use the lecture's figures on the exam.)
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

flashcards.front: How are Valentin Lopez and Lajos Szoboszlai connected to Mutsun reclamation?
flashcards.back: Valentin Lopez, Mutsun tribal chair, and Lajos Szoboszlai, a former UC Davis linguistics graduate student, collaborated to learn Mutsun together using the 1930 documentation by Ascención Solórzano and J.P. Harrington. Szoboszlai's 2017 dissertation chronicles the collaboration.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

flashcards.front: Give the Mutsun phrases from Val Lopez's greeting.
flashcards.back: miSmin Tuuhis = good afternoon; eene = and; Tumsanak kannis = thank you; saanaypu = coming / today's gathering; kanraakat = my name is. For 'chairperson' he used a word for leader.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

flashcards.front: What does 'English as a killer language' refer to in the lecture?
flashcards.back: The boarding school experience: thousands of Indigenous children across North America, from about 1870 to 1970, were sent to schools where English was imposed and their languages suppressed. Andy Windyboy describes his 1960s–70s experience in 'Our Spirits Don't Speak English'.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

flashcards.front: Why does the lecture say the spread of English is not neutral?
flashcards.back: Because it is the DIRECT RESULT of colonization, and it continues to put many Indigenous and minoritized languages at risk. Global English is not coincidental.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

flashcards.front: Name the reasons languages become extinct.
flashcards.back: GRADUAL LOSS — newer generations prefer a language of higher prestige. FORCED cultural/linguistic ASSIMILATION. LINGUICIDE — when all or nearly all speakers die from natural disasters, wars, etc. Many Indigenous languages are now endangered because of colonization.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

flashcards.front: Bottom-up vs. top-down revitalization, with examples.
flashcards.back: BOTTOM-UP is grassroots, at the community level: daycares in the endangered language, study groups, family language policies. TOP-DOWN is institutional, from government or institutions: language policies, standardization, compulsory education, bilingual education. Both often happen at once.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

flashcards.front: Summarize the revival of Hebrew.
flashcards.back: Hebrew, a northwest Semitic language (Afroasiatic family, related to Aramaic and Arabic), ceased to be spoken around 200 CE and was used only for liturgical and poetic purposes. Eliezer Ben-Yehuda (1858–1922), a lexicographer, worked to revive it and raised his son Itamar Ben-Avi as the first native Hebrew speaker in modern times. Hebrew is now spoken by many as a first language.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

flashcards.front: What resistance did Hebrew revival face?
flashcards.back: Strong resistance within the Jewish community, since many saw Hebrew as a language reserved for RELIGIOUS spaces rather than everyday life.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

flashcards.front: Give the Celtic language speaker figures from the lecture.
flashcards.back: Scottish Gaelic: less than 2% of Scots. Irish: about 40% in Ireland. Welsh: about 30%. Breton: less than 20%. Cornish: about 500 speakers. Manx: about 1,800 speakers.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

flashcards.front: Which Celtic languages went extinct and were revived, and which never stopped being spoken?
flashcards.back: CORNISH and MANX went extinct and have since been REVIVED. Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Welsh, and Breton have been CONTINUOUSLY spoken. All lost status and speakers due to English imperialism over millennia.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

flashcards.front: Why is Cherokee the most published Indigenous language in the US?
flashcards.back: Because Sequoyah created a writing system for Cherokee in the early 19th century, letting people read and write it and leading to extensive documentation.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

flashcards.front: What happened with Cherokee in 2019?
flashcards.back: Tribal governments declared a STATE OF EMERGENCY for the Cherokee language and pledged to redouble revitalization efforts — showing that even a heavily documented language can be endangered.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

flashcards.front: How does the Master-Apprentice program work?
flashcards.back: It links young people with older fluent speakers, outside a classroom, and is adaptable to each community. It began through a collaboration between California tribes and UC Berkeley linguists, and has spread to Indigenous communities worldwide. One version runs 300+ hours over three years, using only the heritage language.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

flashcards.front: What ethical concerns surround language documentation?
flashcards.back: Linguists are often OUTSIDERS to the community. They can be EXPLOITATIVE and fail to give back. Research carries inherent POWER DIFFERENTIALS. WHITE SAVIOR narratives arise. The lecture cites Bronisław Malinowski as an example. One counter: people studying their OWN communities.
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

flashcards.front: What discussion questions accompany the Manx video?
flashcards.back: How could the Manx further spread the use of their heritage language? And do you agree with the last speaker that a heritage language should NOT be compulsory in schools — why or why not?
flashcards.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Language Loss, Reclamation & Revitalization
notes.body:
★ SETTLER COLONIALISM = powerful newcomers who intend to STAY and must DISPLACE the original inhabitants (usually for farming). This is what spread Inner Circle English.
★ GLOBAL ENGLISH IS NOT NEUTRAL — it is the direct result of colonization and still endangers Indigenous and minoritized languages.
★ THREE CAUSES OF LANGUAGE DEATH: GRADUAL LOSS (prestige), FORCED ASSIMILATION, LINGUICIDE (speakers die).
★ CALIFORNIA TIMELINE: Mission era 1769–1834 → Spanish contained to missions by 1845 → gold found 1848 → Gold Rush 1848–1855 (~300,000 settlers) → Burnett's extermination address January 1851 → fewer than 20,000 Native Americans by 1900.
★ MISSIONS vs. GOLD RUSH: missions occupied only mission lands; settlers took far larger areas and sought to ELIMINATE Indigenous people. That difference drove the scale of loss.
★ KNOW THE PEOPLE: ISHI (last Yahi speaker, d. 1916); ASCENCIÓN SOLÓRZANO (last Mutsun first-language speaker, d. 1929); J.P. HARRINGTON (recorded her); VALENTIN LOPEZ + LAJOS SZOBOSZLAI (reclaiming Mutsun); SEQUOYAH (Cherokee writing system); ELIEZER BEN-YEHUDA (Hebrew revival).
★ PATWIN / YOCHA DEHE: casino-funded classes, a bilingual school website, a keyboard-friendly spelling system, Highway 16 place-name signs.
★ BOARDING SCHOOLS (~1870–1970) = 'English as a killer language'.
★ BOTTOM-UP (grassroots: daycares, family policy) vs. TOP-DOWN (institutional: policy, standardization, compulsory education). Often both at once.
★ HEBREW: stopped being spoken ~200 CE, liturgical only, revived by Ben-Yehuda, whose son Itamar Ben-Avi was the first modern native speaker. Faced religious resistance.
★ CELTIC: Cornish and Manx went EXTINCT and were REVIVED; Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Welsh, and Breton were CONTINUOUSLY spoken. Know the percentages.
★ CHEROKEE: most published Indigenous language in the US thanks to Sequoyah — yet still declared a language emergency in 2019. Documentation alone doesn't guarantee survival.
★ MASTER-APPRENTICE: CA tribes + UC Berkeley; young learners paired with older speakers; outside the classroom; adopted worldwide.
★ DOCUMENTATION ETHICS: outsider status, exploitation, power differentials, white savior narratives (Malinowski). Counter: communities studying themselves.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

notes.title: Master-Apprentice, Fieldwork, and the Ethics of Documentation
notes.body:
MASTER-APPRENTICE LANGUAGE LEARNING PROGRAM:
• Started with a collaboration between several Native tribes in California and linguists from UC BERKELEY.
• Meant to be ADAPTABLE for communities, OUTSIDE of a classroom.
• LINKS YOUNG PEOPLE WITH OLDER SPEAKERS of a language.
• Has been used by other Indigenous communities across the world.
• Video example: the First Peoples' Heritage, Language and Culture Council pairs a fluent First Nations speaker with a committed learner for over 300 hours across three years, speaking only the First Nations language.

FIELDWORK:
• Some linguists and linguistic anthropologists specialize in LANGUAGE DOCUMENTATION.
• They go to an often remote community to document a language that has not been documented.
• Intentions: to PRESERVE the language and to ADD TO LINGUISTIC KNOWLEDGE.
• J.P. Harrington, discussed in the language loss lecture, documented California Indigenous languages.

ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS OF LANGUAGE DOCUMENTATION:
• Linguists are often OUTSIDERS to a community.
• They can be EXPLOITATIVE of the community and not give back.
• Inherent POWER DIFFERENTIALS in research.
• WHITE SAVIOR narratives.
• Example cited: Bronisław Malinowski.
• ONE COUNTER: people studying their OWN communities.

RESOURCE: CoLang (Institute on Collaborative Language Research).
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

notes.title: Case Studies: Hebrew, Celtic Languages, and Cherokee
notes.body:
THE CASE OF HEBREW:
• A northwest Semitic language of the Afroasiatic family (a relative of Aramaic and Arabic).
• Originally spoken by ancient Israelites and their descendants, but CEASED to be a spoken language around 200 CE.
• Used only for LITURGICAL and POETIC purposes.
• ELIEZER BEN-YEHUDA (1858–1922), a lexicographer, worked on reviving Hebrew.
• He raised his son, ITAMAR BEN-AVI, as the FIRST NATIVE HEBREW SPEAKER in modern times.
• Met with STRONG RESISTANCE in the Jewish community, as many saw Hebrew as a language reserved for religious spaces.

MODERN HEBREW:
• Now a revived language spoken by many as a FIRST language, mostly in Israel/Palestine but also in Jewish communities worldwide.
• The lecture's sign photo is written in Hebrew, Palestinian Arabic, and — notably — English.

ONGOING EFFORTS:
• Hebrew is just one case. Many endangered languages, mostly Indigenous, continue to be revived — many competing with English and other colonial languages.

CELTIC LANGUAGES:
• Lost status and speakers due to ENGLISH IMPERIALISM over millennia.
• CONTINUOUSLY SPOKEN: Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Welsh, Breton.
• WENT EXTINCT, SINCE REVIVED: Cornish and Manx.
• FIGURES: Scottish Gaelic <2% of Scots | Irish ~40% in Ireland | Welsh ~30% | Breton <20% | Cornish ~500 speakers | Manx ~1,800 speakers.
• Manx video questions: how could the Manx further spread their heritage language? Should a heritage language be compulsory in schools?

CHEROKEE:
• Indigenous language of the Cherokee people, from what is now the southeastern US.
• The MOST PUBLISHED Indigenous language in the US.
• Because SEQUOYAH, a Cherokee man in the early 19th century, created a writing system for Cherokee — letting people read and write it, which led to extensive documentation.
• In 2019, tribal governments announced a STATE OF EMERGENCY for the Cherokee language and pledged to redouble revitalization efforts.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

notes.title: Global English, Language Death, and Methods of Revitalization
notes.body:
GLOBAL ENGLISH:
• The spread of English across the world is NOT of neutral value or coincidental.
• It is the DIRECT RESULT OF COLONIZATION.
• It directly continues to affect and put many Indigenous and minoritized languages at risk.

LANGUAGE LIFE & DEATH — languages become extinct for many reasons:
• GRADUAL LOSS — newer generations prefer a language of higher prestige.
• FORCED cultural/linguistic ASSIMILATION.
• LINGUICIDE — when all or nearly all speakers die because of natural disasters, wars, etc.
• Many Indigenous languages are now endangered because of colonization.

LANGUAGE REVITALIZATION (or LANGUAGE REVIVAL):
• Attempts to halt or reverse the decline of a language, or to revive a DORMANT one.
• Those involved may be community members, linguists, government parties, etc.
• Some languages have been SUCCESSFULLY revived.

METHODS OF REVITALIZATION:
• BOTTOM-UP — from the grassroots at the community level. Ex: starting a daycare in an endangered language, study groups, family language policies.
• TOP-DOWN — more institutional, from a government or other institution down to people. Language policies, standardization, compulsory education, bilingual education.
• There are OFTEN BOTH methods happening SIMULTANEOUSLY.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Revitalization]

notes.title: Reclaiming Mutsun, and the Boarding School Experience
notes.body:
THE MUTSUN LANGUAGE AND PEOPLE:
• An Ohlone/Costanoan people.
• The last speaker of Mutsun, ASCENCIÓN SOLÓRZANO, died in 1929. She was also a Spanish speaker.
• Most Mutsun today speak only English; some speak Spanish and English.

HOW MUTSUN (ALMOST) GOT LOST:
• The Mutsun were missionized at SAN JUAN BAUTISTA.
• Cultural and linguistic repression started in the missions and continued with genocide by Anglo-American settlers in the 1800s.

RECLAIMING MUTSUN:
• ASCENCIÓN SOLÓRZANO (1855–1929) — last first-language speaker, bilingual in Spanish. Spent most of her life in Santa Barbara working as a traditional healer. In the last year of her life she shared her language with linguist J.P. Harrington.
• J.P. HARRINGTON (1884–1961) — his life's work was audio-recording Indigenous languages of North America. These recordings enable Indigenous people today to RECLAIM their ancestral languages.
• COLLABORATION: Valentin Lopez, Mutsun tribal chair, and Lajos Szoboszlai, a former UCD Linguistics graduate student, collaborated to learn Mutsun together, using documentation compiled by Solórzano and Harrington in 1930.
• Szoboszlai's 2017 dissertation chronicles the process.
• Val's greeting: miSmin Tuuhis 'good afternoon' | eene 'and' | Tumsanak kannis 'thank you' | saanaypu 'coming / today's gathering' | kanraakat 'my name is'. For 'chairperson' he used a word for leader.
• Video: Val Lopez leads his nieces Adelina and Aleya Lopez in singing a women's gathering song in the language of the Amah Mutsun Tribal Band, for Native American Heritage Month at Cleveland Elementary in Oakland.

ENGLISH AS A KILLER LANGUAGE — THE BOARDING SCHOOL EXPERIENCE:
• Andy Windyboy, in 'Our Spirits Don't Speak English', describes his experience of language loss in a boarding school in the 1960s and 1970s.
• This happened to THOUSANDS of children across North America from about 1870 to 1970.

LANGUAGE LOSS IN THE BRITISH ISLES:
• British colonization started by subjugating Celtic populations — Irish, Scottish, and others. (The source deck ends partway through this slide; see the Revitalization lecture for the Celtic language figures.)
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

notes.title: Missions, the Gold Rush, and Genocidal Policy
notes.body:
SPANISH IN THE CALIFORNIA MISSIONS:
• MISSION ERA: 1769–1834.
• Stated goal: to save the 'lost souls' of the people of California; teach the Catholic faith, farming, etc.
• Native Americans were brought to the missions, baptized, then FORCIBLY KEPT there.

SUMMARY OF SPANISH INCURSION:
• Language loss in the missions came from POPULATION LOSS and REPRESSION of language and culture.
