• Outside the missions, Indigenous people FOUGHT against the Spanish and CONTAINED Spanish to the mission areas by 1845.
• That containment could have become the status quo — but for the influx of new settlers, mostly Anglo-Americans from the East.

THE GOLD RUSH & ENGLISH:
• Gold discovered in California in 1848. By then Mexican and Anglo ranchers and agriculturalists had already increased in number.
• Hundreds of settlers became THOUSANDS during the Gold Rush, 1848–1855 — explorers, miners, and farmers. About 300,000 new settlers.

MISSION vs. GOLD RUSH SETTLER EFFECTS:
• Missionaries and Spanish soldiers occupied ONLY lands around the missions.
• Settlers occupied MUCH LARGER areas already inhabited by Indigenous people, and saw them as an obstacle to be ELIMINATED.
• Many were killed, others relocated to reservations, others enslaved to work on ranches.

GENOCIDAL POLICIES:
• January 1851: California Governor Peter H. Burnett, addressing the state legislature, said a war of extermination would continue between the two races until the Indian race became extinct.
• The state then issued a TREASURY BOND to pay for the extermination — used to pay bounty hunters and state militias to seek out and kill Indigenous people.

POPULATION, PER THE LECTURE:
• ~1 million in the late 1700s → ~30,000 by around 1860 → fewer than 20,000 by 1900.
• All known Native Americans were under U.S. government protection by 1870.
(Note: pre-contact population estimates vary widely among scholars. Use the lecture's figures for the exam.)
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

notes.title: Settler Colonialism and Language Loss in California
notes.body:
⚠ CONTENT NOTE: this lecture covers genocide and forced assimilation of Indigenous Californians.

INNER CIRCLE ENGLISH AND SETTLER COLONIALISM:
• SETTLER COLONIALISM = the arrival of politically and militarily powerful new inhabitants in an area where they intend to STAY, and where displacing the original inhabitants is essential to their goals (usually farming).
• Practiced by the British in the eastern US, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand; and by the United States in California. It meant the arrival of LARGE NUMBERS OF ENGLISH SPEAKERS.

INDIGENOUS PEOPLE LOSE THEIR LAND, AND OFTEN THEIR LANGUAGES:
• Since contact, Indigenous people have been killed or forced to assimilate. They are STILL resisting language and culture loss.
• This loss has been particularly SEVERE in California.
• ISHI, a man of the Yahi nation — no one has spoken Yahi since Ishi died in 1916.

WHERE UC DAVIS NOW STANDS:
• Patwin people lived along Putah Creek until the 1830s.
• Mexican soldiers captured them and took them to the Solano mission (in what is now Sonoma).
• The Contemplative Garden in the UCD Arboretum memorializes their names.
• Today many of their descendants live along Cache Creek.

PATWIN LANGUAGE & PEOPLE TODAY:
• Patwin is the language of the YOCHA DEHE nation, which funds reclamation with profits from the Cache Creek casino. Efforts include:
   – Language classes for community members
   – A school for the children with a bilingual website; UCD linguists helped develop a spelling system easy to type on a regular keyboard
   – Road signs with original place names along what is now Highway 16
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Language Loss & Reclamation in California (adapted from a talk by Lajos Szoboszlai)]

notes.title: Pragmatics Classwork — Maxim Violations and Face-Threatening Acts
notes.body:
PART 3, QUESTION 1 — FOUR TURNS VIOLATING OR FLOUTING EACH GRICEAN MAXIM:

QUALITY (be truthful and well-supported):
   P1: 'How did you do on that Linguistics assignment?'
   P2: 'I did so well that the professor is going to ask me to lecture next week.'
   → An unsupported exaggeration.

QUANTITY (right amount of information):
   P1: 'What did you do this weekend?'
   P2: 'Lots of stuff.'
   → Far too little information.

RELEVANCE (stay on topic):
   P1: 'Did you take the trash out before the truck came this morning?'
   P2: 'Local waste management providers are having difficulty meeting the demands of urban areas with high expansion rates, multiplying the amount of trash and stops to collect it.'
   → Never answers the question.

MANNER (concise, clear, orderly):
   P1: 'Where are you going out tonight?'
   P2: 'To a community gathering where commercial vendors dispense libations to the harmony of synchronized acoustic vibrations.'
   → Obscure and needlessly elaborate for 'a bar with live music'.

PART 3, QUESTION 2 — FACE-THREATENING ACTS AND MITIGATION:

NEGATIVE FTA (an imposition on the hearer's freedom from burden):
   'Can you read my 20-page linguistics final right now?'
NEGATIVE POLITENESS MITIGATION:
   'I'm sorry to bother you, I know you are swamped with finals of your own. But if you have a few spare minutes over the weekend, do you think you could briefly scan my Linguistics final? No worries if you can't, I know this is last minute.'
   → THREE MOVES: apologize for the imposition; minimize the request ('a few spare minutes', 'briefly scan'); offer an easy out ('no worries if you can't').

POSITIVE FTA (an insult to the hearer's desire for approval):
   'Your part of the semantics and pragmatics group project was entirely wrong, now the rest of us have to put in extra time to fix your incorrect work.'
POSITIVE POLITENESS MITIGATION:
   'You did a great job with the formatting and design of your slides. I think we just need to make a few minor tweaks, and it will align perfectly with the rest of the project. What do you think?'
   → THREE MOVES: affirm genuine worth; reframe the problem as minor and shared; invite collaboration rather than assigning blame.

★ PATTERN TO REMEMBER: match the mitigation to the face being threatened. An IMPOSITION needs NEGATIVE politeness (hedging, apology, easy out). An INSULT needs POSITIVE politeness (praise, solidarity, shared ownership).
notes.source: [ANTH 4 Semantics & Pragmatics classwork - Part 3: Gricean maxims and politeness]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Pragmatics Lecture
notes.body:
★ PRAGMATICS = MEANING IN CONTEXT. Semantics = meaning on structural form. Pragmatics adds sociocultural and interactional context.
★ PRAGMATICS RELIES ON INFERENCE — 'Really?' can be doubt or surprise; nothing structural disambiguates it.
★ THE FOUR GRICEAN MAXIMS — memorize with one-line definitions: QUANTITY (right amount of info), QUALITY (truthful), RELEVANCE (on topic), MANNER (clear and orderly).
★ COOPERATION is the premise: we interpret on the ASSUMPTION others are following the maxims.
★ IMPLICATURE vs. ENTAILMENT IS THE BIG DISTINCTION. Entailment = logically NECESSARY. Implicature = intended but not necessary. 'I love waking up early' ENTAILS I wake up early; it IMPLIES sarcasm.
★ PRAGMATICS DICTATES IMPLICATURE, NOT ENTAILMENT.
★ DELIBERATELY BREAKING A MAXIM CREATES IMPLICATURE — that's how sarcasm and much humour work.
★ SEMANTICIZATION: a pragmatic inference can become semantic over time — 'since' (time → cause → 'because').
★ PRAGMATIC COMPETENCE is language- and culture-dependent. 'How are you?' is a greeting, not a question — a classic non-native-speaker trap.
★ POLITENESS THEORY = BROWN AND LEVINSON, 1970s. Know the names and the decade.
★ FACE: NEGATIVE face = not being burdened. POSITIVE face = being praised. ⚠ 'Negative' doesn't mean bad — it means freedom FROM imposition.
★ FTAs: NEGATIVE FTA = imposing. POSITIVE FTA = insulting. Politeness MITIGATES them.
★ MATCH THE STRATEGY TO THE FACE: hedging and apologizing for imposing = NEGATIVE politeness. Complimenting and affirming = POSITIVE politeness.
★ POLITENESS IS CULTURE-SPECIFIC: Israeli norms emphasize directness; Northern European norms discourage smiling at or talking to strangers. Neither is 'rude' — the norms simply differ.
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

notes.title: Pragmatic Competence and Politeness
notes.body:
PRAGMATIC COMPETENCE:
• Pragmatic knowledge is LANGUAGE- and CULTURE-DEPENDENT.
• How do you greet someone? Thank them? Say goodbye? Give a compliment? Flirt?
• 'How are you?' is an Anglophone greeting. Pragmatically, English speakers generally know the asker doesn't actually want to know how they're doing.
• This could cause issues for non-native speakers.

POLITENESS:
• What is considered polite relies on PRAGMATIC COMPETENCE.
• When can you accept a gift? Who pays for dinner?
• THE STACY SCENARIO: Stacy and her friends go out to dinner. When the check comes they all pull out their wallets. Stacy says she will cover the meal. Several friends protest, offering to cover their share. She insists, and they ask if she's sure. She says yes, and they put their wallets away and thank her.
   → Discussion question: how might the friends have reacted COUNTER to pragmatic/politeness norms?

POLITENESS THEORY — Brown and Levinson, 1970s:
• TWO TYPES of politeness: NEGATIVE and POSITIVE.
• Both related to the concept of FACE.
• NEGATIVE FACE: not being burdened, inconvenienced.
• POSITIVE FACE: being praised, complimented.
• FACE-THREATENING ACT (FTA): challenging the face.
   – NEGATIVE FTA: imposing on another person.
   – POSITIVE FTA: insulting another person.
• POLITENESS SEEKS TO MITIGATE FTAs.

IDENTIFY THE POLITENESS TYPE (from the deck):
• 'Would you mind shutting the window?' vs. 'Shut the window.' → NEGATIVE politeness (minimizes imposition)
• 'You're doing so well in this class, you're a brilliant student.' → POSITIVE politeness (praise)
• 'If it's not too much trouble, could you get me a glass of water, please?' → NEGATIVE politeness
• Saying 'please' and 'thank you' → politeness mitigating imposition

POLITENESS CROSS-CULTURALLY:
• What is deemed polite in one cultural context could be RUDE in another.
• Israelis are stereotyped as rude because Israeli politeness rules emphasize DIRECTNESS.
• In Northern Europe, smiling at strangers is considered impolite, as is talking to strangers on public transit.
• To Americans, Northern Europeans could seem rude for not engaging with a friendly stranger.
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

notes.title: What Is Pragmatics? Inference and the Gricean Maxims
notes.body:
PRAGMATICS = MEANING IN CONTEXT.
• SEMANTICS is meaning on a structural form.
• PRAGMATICS relies on sociocultural and interactional contexts.
• Opening question from the deck: how can you tell the difference between sarcasm and being genuine?

PRAGMATICS RELIES ON INFERENCES:
• Determine possible meanings, then interpret based on context.
• 'It's 100 degrees outside.' Reply: 'Really?'
• How should 'really' be interpreted — as an expression of doubt, or of surprise?
• MISCOMMUNICATIONS CAN OCCUR.

GRICEAN CONVERSATIONAL MAXIMS:
In order to understand one another, interlocutors must COOPERATE and follow these maxims (rules):
• QUANTITY — should be informative, not too much or too little information
• QUALITY — must be truthful and well-supported
• RELEVANCE — should be relevant to the situation
• MANNER — should be concise, clear, orderly
(Exercise: think of turns that would violate each of these.)

IMPLICATURE AND ENTAILMENT:
• We make interpretations of meaning based on the ASSUMPTION that other speakers are following the maxims.
• IMPLICATURES are possible inferences that the speaker INTENDS the listener to understand — they imply it.
• ENTAILMENT: logically NECESSARY inferences.
• 'I just really love waking up so early in the morning' ENTAILS that I wake up early.
• 'I just really love waking up so early in the morning' IMPLIES that I'm being facetious.
• ★ PRAGMATICS DICTATES IMPLICATURE, NOT ENTAILMENTS.
• People may PURPOSEFULLY BREAK a maxim to create implicature — which can be humorous: 'I don't suffer from insanity. I enjoy every minute of it.'

SEMANTICS VS. PRAGMATICS:
• Some semantic meaning has come from the SEMANTICIZATION of pragmatic inferences over time.
• Example: 'since' used to only refer to time, was used pragmatically to indicate causality, and can now be used like 'because'.
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Pragmatics]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Semantics Classwork & Common Mistakes
notes.body:
★ HOMOPHONY vs. POLYSEMY: ask whether the senses are RELATED. Related = polysemy. Coincidence = homophony.
★ ROSE (flower) / ROSE (past of rise) IS HOMOPHONY. Two unrelated parts of speech sharing a form is a red flag for coincidence.
★ Reliable polysemy signals: body part → landscape or organization (mouth, head, foot); concrete → abstract metaphor (bright).
★ A HYPERNYM MUST CONTAIN EVERY MEMBER. Test it against edge cases — 'marine life' fails for freshwater fish.
★ PATH REQUIRES MOTION THROUGH SPACE. Something being played, read, earned, or supplied is a THEME, not a Path.
★ THEME = involved but UNCHANGED (stories being read, money being earned, information being supplied). PATIENT = CHANGED.
★ GOAL covers TARGETED STATES too — 'for relaxation' is a legitimate Goal.
★ RECIPIENT strictly means PHYSICAL POSSESSION. Watch for 'to'-phrases where nothing physical changes hands.
notes.source: [ANTH 4 Semantics & Pragmatics classwork - Parts 1-2: word meanings and semantic roles]

notes.title: Semantics Classwork — Word Meanings and Semantic Roles
notes.body:
PART I — HOMOPHONY OR POLYSEMY?
• Tail (animal appendage) / Tale (a story) → HOMOPHONY.
• Mouth (oral cavity) / Mouth (an opening or entrance) → POLYSEMY — body-to-landscape frame shift.
• Bright (emitting light) / Bright (intelligent) → POLYSEMY — metaphorical extension.
• Rose (flower) / Rose (past tense of rise) → HOMOPHONY. ⚠ The senses are NOT related: one is a plant noun, the other an irregular past-tense verb. Coincidence of form only.
• Head (upper body) / Head (highest position in an organization) → POLYSEMY — the lecture lists this exact pair as a frame shift.
THE TEST: can you trace a conceptual or historical connection? Connected → polysemy. Coincidence → homophony.

HYPERNYMS:
• Hammer → tool ✓ | T-shirt → clothing ✓ | Pink → color ✓
• Fish → ANIMAL (or vertebrate). ⚠ 'Marine life' excludes freshwater fish, so it isn't a true superset.

HYPONYMS: appliance → refrigerator, washer, dryer, dishwasher ✓ | musical instrument → flute, tuba, drums ✓ | furniture → couch, chair, recliner, table ✓ | fish → shark, flounder, salmon ✓

PART 2 — SEMANTIC ROLES (analyzed with the 14-role reference table, which includes Theme, Goal, and Path):
• 'We persuaded Mary to apply for the job as bus driver.' — We = AGENT; Mary = EXPERIENCER (being persuaded is a psychological effect); the job = GOAL (targeted endpoint).
• 'He supplied the reporters with information.' — He = AGENT; the reporters = RECIPIENT; information = THEME. ✓
• 'Earle has been earning money through his poetry.' — Earle = AGENT; money = THEME; his poetry = INSTRUMENT. ✓
• 'We were playing a game of Monopoly for relaxation.' — We = AGENT; a game of Monopoly = THEME (⚠ NOT Path); for relaxation = GOAL (a targeted state). ✓ for Goal.
• 'Angela was reading stories to the children this morning.' — Angela = AGENT; stories = THEME; the children = RECIPIENT (common answer — see edge case); this morning = TEMPORAL.

EDGE CASE — 'reading stories TO the children': the table's Recipient requires PHYSICAL POSSESSION. Hearing a story transfers nothing physical, so GOAL (the endpoint the reading is directed at) or BENEFACTIVE (they benefit) is arguably tighter. Recipient is still widely accepted for 'to'-phrases with transfer-like verbs. Be ready to argue either way.
notes.source: [ANTH 4 Semantics & Pragmatics classwork - Parts 1-2: word meanings and semantic roles]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Semantic Roles Reference Table
notes.body:
★ 14 ROLES in the table vs. 9 in the lecture. The table ADDS Theme, Stimulus, Source, Goal, Path, and RENAMES Cause → Force/Causer.
★ THEME vs. PATIENT: ask 'was it CHANGED?' Changed = Patient. Moved, located, or described but unchanged = Theme.
★ Textbook says patient is a SUBTYPE of theme; the table says they're SEPARATE. Both use change as the test.
★ STIMULUS triggers the response; EXPERIENCER has it. They come as a pair: [the alarm] startled [the horse].
★ THE MOTION TRIO: SOURCE (from), GOAL (to / toward a targeted state), PATH (along / through).
★ GOAL INCLUDES ABSTRACT TARGETED STATES, not just places — 'for relaxation' qualifies.
★ PATH REQUIRES MOTION THROUGH SPACE. A thing being played, read, or earned is never a Path.
★ RECIPIENT = PHYSICAL POSSESSION. BENEFACTIVE = profits WITHOUT possessing.
★ AGENT (intent) vs. FORCE/CAUSER (no intent, natural) vs. INSTRUMENT (a tool an agent uses).
★ 'Stimulus' also appears in your wk02 notes with a DIFFERENT meaning — the element held constant in a matched-guise study. Don't mix them up.
notes.source: [ANTH 4 semantic roles reference table - Inventory of Standard Semantic Roles]

notes.title: Lecture vs. Reference Table vs. Textbook — Reconciling the Role Lists
notes.body:
THREE SOURCES, THREE INVENTORIES — know where they agree and where they don't.

LECTURE (9 roles): Agent, Patient, Experiencer, Instrument, Cause, Recipient, Benefactive, Locative, Temporal.

REFERENCE TABLE (14 roles): adds THEME, STIMULUS, SOURCE, GOAL, PATH, and renames Cause as FORCE/CAUSER.

TEXTBOOK (Anderson, wk06): lists agent, experiencer, theme/patient, instrument, goal, source, and more.

THE THEME / PATIENT PROBLEM — the most important difference:
• TEXTBOOK: 'a patient is a theme that is also changed by the event' — patient is a SUBTYPE of theme.
• TABLE: theme is 'without being fundamentally changed' — theme and patient are SEPARATE.
• LECTURE: no theme at all; patient covers anything that 'undergoes a change of state, or [is] directly affected'.
★ THE COMMON GROUND: all three use CHANGE as the deciding test.
   Changed → PATIENT.   Not changed (moved, located, described) → THEME.

EQUIVALENCES:
• Lecture CAUSE = Table FORCE/CAUSER (natural force, no intent).
• Table STIMULUS has no lecture equivalent — it's the trigger paired with an Experiencer.
• Table SOURCE / GOAL / PATH have no lecture equivalent — they handle motion events.

⚠ EXAM STRATEGY: if a question uses roles the lecture never taught (Theme, Goal, Path), it is drawing on the table or the textbook. If it offers only the nine lecture roles, choose from those — and an unchanged object then defaults to PATIENT, since the lecture has no Theme.
notes.source: [ANTH 4 semantic roles reference table - Inventory of Standard Semantic Roles]

notes.title: Semantic Roles Reference Table — the 14-Role Inventory
notes.body:
SOURCE: the uploaded 'Inventory of Standard Semantic Roles' reference table — the standard thematic roles (theta-roles) used across major syntactic and semantic frameworks.

PARTICIPANT ROLES:
• AGENT — animate entity that intentionally, volitionally performs or initiates an action. [The student] drafted the syntax tree.
• PATIENT — undergoes a physical action, is directly affected, and CHANGES its state. The frost melted [the ice].
• THEME — undergoes motion, is located, or is described WITHOUT being fundamentally changed. He placed [the textbook] on the desk.
• EXPERIENCER — animate entity that experiences a psychological, mental, or sensory perception. [Mary] understands the structural theory.
• STIMULUS — the entity, event, or concept that TRIGGERS a mental or sensory response in an Experiencer. [The loud alarm] startled the horse.
• RECIPIENT — a specific animate endpoint that comes into PHYSICAL POSSESSION of an object. I sent [my classmate] a copy of the notes.
• BENEFACTIVE — profits from (or is disadvantaged by) an action WITHOUT necessarily possessing anything. She proofread the paper for [her friend].
• INSTRUMENT — the inanimate tool, means, or object used BY AN AGENT. He split the logs with [an axe].
• FORCE / CAUSER — an inanimate entity or natural phenomenon that instigates change WITHOUT INTENT. [The heavy gale] shattered the window panes.

MOTION ROLES:
• SOURCE — the starting point, initial location, or prior state. We traveled all the way from [Oakland].
• GOAL — the endpoint, destination, or TARGETED STATE. They walked over to [the campus library].
• PATH — the trajectory, route, or ground covered during movement. The runner sped along [the gravel track].

SETTING ROLES:
• LOCATIVE — the physical or spatial site where an event occurs or an entity is situated. The vocabulary lists are sitting on [the desk].
• TEMPORAL — the point or duration of time of an event or state. The morning seminar wrapped up at [noon].
notes.source: [ANTH 4 semantic roles reference table - Inventory of Standard Semantic Roles]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Semantics Lecture
notes.body:
★ SEMANTICS = the study of meaning and how it depends on structure. PHRASAL semantics = phrases/sentences; LEXICAL semantics = words.
★ THE MUG/CUP/BOWL EXERCISE: word meanings have FUZZY boundaries, depend on context, contents, size, and social/cultural norms.
★ THREE THEORIES OF MENTAL REPRESENTATION: dictionary-style (circular problem), mental image/prototype (sharing problem, hard to visualize abstracts), usage-based. ANSWER: probably ALL THREE combined.
★ SYNONYMY = same meaning, usually with slight differences and overlapping-not-identical senses.
★ HYPONYMY: hyponym = SUBSET (poodle), hypernym = SUPERSET (dog). Nested layers create TAXONOMIES.
★ THREE ANTONYM TYPES — memorize with examples: CONTRARY (scale with middle: young/old), COMPLEMENTARY (one true = other false: dead/alive), REVERSIVE (opposite directions or reversible states: come/go, melt/freeze).
★ HOMOPHONY vs. POLYSEMY IS THE BIG EXAM TRAP: homophony = identical form, UNRELATED meanings, coincidence (bank/bank, bier/beer). Polysemy = one word, distinct but RELATED meanings (head: body part → organization; foot: body → hill).
★ DEIXIS = words needing context; both SYMBOLIC (conventional) and INDEXICAL (contextual). Three types: PERSON, SPATIAL, TEMPORAL.
★ Know the systems: Fijian THREE-term spatial (near me / near you / far from both); English past/non-past; Kusaiean future/non-future; Lithuanian three-term.
★ LEXICALIZATION = encoding concepts in words (Inuktitut snow, fedderschei, flâner). ⚠ IT DOES NOT PROVE LANGUAGE RELATIVISM.
★ CLASSIFIERS are obligatory in many languages and chosen by SEMANTIC properties: Indonesian orang (people), ekor (animals), biji (small round), helai (thin flat).
★ ★ THE KEY POINT OF THE UNIT: SEMANTIC ROLES AND GRAMMATICAL ROLES ARE INDEPENDENT. Not all agents are subjects; not all patients are objects.
★ ACTIVE: subject = agent, object = patient. PASSIVE: subject = PATIENT, oblique = AGENT. The passive is what dissociates them.
★ THE NINE ROLES: Agent (volition), Patient (undergoes change), Experiencer (sensory, NO volition), Instrument (means, needs an agent), Cause (natural force, NO agent), Recipient (gets a physical object), Benefactive (action done FOR them), Locative, Temporal.
★ AGENT vs. CAUSE vs. INSTRUMENT: agent has volition; cause is a natural force with none; instrument is the means and usually implies an agent.
★ RECIPIENT vs. BENEFACTIVE: recipient RECEIVES an object; benefactive is who it's done FOR.
★ THE CARLOS PAIR: 'Hilda gave Carlos a present' (RECIPIENT) vs. 'The storm gave Carlos the chills' (EXPERIENCER) — same grammatical role (indirect object), different semantic role.
★ ENGLISH has NO overt morphology for semantic roles. HAIDA marks them in pronouns (agent 'I' ≠ experiencer 'I'), where English marks subject/object instead.
★ SENSE = meaning in the mind. REFERENT = the real thing it points to. 'The king of France' has SENSE but NO referent. 'Clark Kent'/'Superman' = one referent, two senses. Referents need not be real (Garfield, Mickey Mouse).
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

notes.title: Reference and Sense
notes.body:
There are two fundamental aspects of linguistic meaning: SENSE and REFERENCE. They are somewhat independent.

REFERENT — the entity in the external world to which a linguistic expression relates; the real-world thing an utterance refers to.
SENSE — the meaning of an expression by virtue of how it is said; the mental conception of the thing the utterance refers to.

FOR GENERAL CONCEPTS this is easy:
• The REFERENTS of 'cat' are all the instances of cat in the world.
• The SENSE of 'cat' is all the mental knowledge associated with 'cat' in the mind of a listener.

REFERENTS DON'T HAVE TO BE REAL:
• The book gives 'Garfield' as a referent for 'cat' — but where is Garfield in the world?
• Referents can be ideas, concepts, or historical/fictional figures shared by a community of speakers.

SENSE WITHOUT REFERENCE:
• 'The current president of France' — makes sense, HAS a referent.
• 'The current king of France' — makes a different sense, has NO referent. It is still a meaningful phrase.
• 'A unicorn' is the same: mental associations, no real referent.

ONE PHRASE, MANY SENSES:
• 'The president of the United States' can mean the head of the executive branch generally, OR a fictional character, OR a specific person.
• The senses of a phrase may also change over time.
• The referent of 'The President of the United States of America' changes with each administration, but the phrase keeps largely the same meaning — which suggests the phrase has meaning INDEPENDENT of its referent.

ONE REFERENT, MANY SENSES:
• 'Clark Kent' and 'Superman' mean different things but refer to a single person. They differ in SENSE. People can use both terms without realizing they point to the same person.

SENSES DO NOT HAVE TO BE 'CORRECT' to make a reference — speaker and listener simply need shared knowledge allowing a similar understanding of the utterance.

WHY WE NEED BOTH:
• SENSE lets us discuss how a single object can be referred to in many different ways.
• REFERENCE lets us talk about meaning being fundamentally related to experience and to things existing in the world.

★ CLICKER ANSWERS:
• 'Mickey Mouse' → makes sense, HAS a referent (we all agree on a mental concept for it).
• 'The queen/king of America' → makes sense, has NO referent (we won't all arrive at a collective understanding of this individual).
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

notes.title: Semantic Roles and Their Independence from Grammatical Roles
notes.body:
GRAMMAR VS. MEANING:
• Different types of GRAMMATICAL (syntactic) roles hold between verbs and NP arguments.
• ALSO, different types of SEMANTIC (meaning-based) roles hold between verbs and arguments.
• ★ THESE ARE SEPARATE AND CAN BE INDEPENDENT. This is flagged as the KEY POINT of the unit.

SEMANTIC ROLE = the way a referent noun contributes to the state/action/situation in a phrase. A fairly small, abstract set.

THE ACTIVE/PASSIVE DEMONSTRATION:
   'The dog bit the cats'
      Syntactic role:  Subject   |  Object
      Semantic role:   Agent     |  Patient
   → In a simple sentence with the verb in unmarked ACTIVE form, the subject is the agent.

   'The cats were bitten by the dog'
      Syntactic role:  Subject   |  [oblique]
      Semantic role:   Patient   |  Agent
   → With the verb morphologically marked as PASSIVE, the subject is the patient and the oblique is the agent.

HOW EACH IS ENCODED:
• SYNTACTIC roles — determined by linear order in English; sometimes verb agreement; sometimes morphological form.
• SEMANTIC roles — NOT coded overtly in English; no overt morphology. We interpret them.

THE NINE SEMANTIC ROLES:
• AGENT — the responsible INITIATOR of an action, the doer. Connected with VOLITION, will, or intentionality. [Tammy] drove the car. [Jorge] gave me flowers. [I] broke the window.
• PATIENT — the entity that undergoes a change of state or is directly affected. I cleaned [the car]. Hyun-ju broke [the glass]. Mike burned [the cake].
• EXPERIENCER — an NP that receives SENSORY INPUT. NOT connected with volition or will. [Fatima] likes blueberry pancakes. [Wei] felt threatened by the lion. [Tom] smelled the flowers.
• INSTRUMENT — the MEANS by which an event is carried out; the intermediary through which an agent acts. Usually requires an agent. Michel cut the bread with [the knife]. The child broke the window with [a hammer].
• CAUSE — any NATURAL FORCE bringing about a change of state. Does NOT require an agent (no intention, no volition). [The snow] caved in the roof.
• RECIPIENT — an NP which receives a PHYSICAL OBJECT. Ivan gave a banana to [Amanda]. Suzanna brought [me] a cake.
• BENEFACTIVE — an NP FOR WHICH an action is performed. I baked a cake for [my brother].
• LOCATIVE — the location of an action or state. [Midwest] is cold in winter. I live in [Europe].
• TEMPORAL — the time at which the action or state occurred. She left home [yesterday]. I graduated in [2002].

★ THE CARLOS EXAMPLE:
   'Hilda gave Carlos a present' / 'The storm gave Carlos the chills'
   • GRAMMATICAL role in both: INDIRECT OBJECT (same)
   • SEMANTIC role: RECIPIENT in the first, EXPERIENCER in the second (different)
   → Same grammatical role, different semantic role.

★ THE SUBJECT EXAMPLES — one syntactic role, many semantic roles:
• Marcus opened the door → AGENT | The key opened the door → INSTRUMENT (both Subject)
• [Miska] opened the door → Agent | [My cake] was eaten by Sarah → Patient | [I] smell smoke → Experiencer (or Agent, depending on the event) — all grammatical SUBJECTS.

CROSS-LINGUISTICALLY — HAIDA (indigenous language of California, ~14 living speakers):
• skuts hl guntl'aats' ('bone 1.SG.AGNT swallowed') = 'I swallowed a bone' → 'I' is marked as AGENT.
• dang dii kuyaadaang ('2.SG.EXP 1.SG.EXP love') = 'I love you' → both are marked as EXPERIENCERS.
• Different pronoun for Agent 'I' and Experiencer 'I'.
★ CONTRAST: in English, pronouns mark GRAMMATICAL roles ('I see him' vs. 'He sees me'). In Haida, pronouns mark SEMANTIC roles.
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

notes.title: Lexicalization and Classifiers
notes.body:
DO ALL LANGUAGES EXPRESS CONCEPTS THE SAME WAY? No — there is evidence that languages differ in how they express particular concepts within a single word.

INUKTITUT — words for snow:
• aput 'snow on the ground' | qana 'falling snow' | piqsirpoq 'drifting snow' | qimuqsuq 'snow drift'

ENGLISH — animals:
• cub 'baby bear' | piglet 'baby pig' | kitten 'baby cat' | puppy 'baby dog' | lamb 'baby sheep' | cow 'female cattle' | bull 'male cattle'

PENNSYLVANIA GERMAN:
• fedderschei 'the condition of being reluctant to write letters'
• aagehaar 'an eyelash hair that grows inwardly and irritates the sclera'

FRENCH:
• flâner 'to wander around aimlessly but enjoyably' | chez X 'at the house/place of X'

LEXICALIZATION = when concepts are encoded in the words of a language. The fact that different languages lexicalize different concepts tells us languages differ in how they express particular concepts.

⚠ IMPORTANT CAVEAT: when a specific lexical item exists for a concept in one language and not another, it just means the speakers of that language have created a term for a specific concept. It is NOT impossible for speakers of another language to understand that concept. In other words, THIS IS NOT NECESSARILY EVIDENCE FOR LANGUAGE RELATIVISM — the idea of your language shaping how you view the world.

CLASSIFIERS:
• In many languages, classifiers after nouns are OBLIGATORY elements of the grammar.
• Similar to English expressions like 'five ears of corn' or 'five pieces of bread'.
• Very often the choice of classifier is based on SEMANTIC PROPERTIES of the noun.
INDONESIAN:
• ORANG — counting people: dua orang laki-laki 'two men'; tiga orang guru 'three teachers'
• EKOR — counting animals: lima ekor burung 'five birds'; sepuluh ekor anjing 'ten dogs'
• BIJI — small round objects: dua belas biji telur 'a dozen eggs'; enam biji peluru 'six bullets'; tiga biji buah anggur 'three grapes'
• HELAI — thin flat objects: enam helai kertas 'six pieces of paper'; dua belas helai duan 'twelve leaves'; enam belas helai bulu 'sixteen feathers'
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

notes.title: Deixis
notes.body:
DEIXIS is the marking of the orientation or position of entities and events with respect to certain points of reference. Deictic words REQUIRE CONTEXT to be understood.
   'Meet me here tomorrow.'  vs.  'Meet John at the library on Tuesday, February 19th.'
• Without deixis our communication system breaks down in funny or frustrating ways (cf. 'Who's on First').

Deixis is BOTH:
• SYMBOLIC — since it is conventional
• INDEXICAL — since it depends on context
• Often called 'POINTING WORDS': here and now, I and you. These words do not always refer to the same set of referents; their meanings change with context.

THREE TYPES:
• PERSON DEIXIS — I, she, he, they
• SPATIAL DEIXIS — here, there, this, that
• TEMPORAL DEIXIS — yesterday, tomorrow, before, after

PERSON DEIXIS:
• The most basic opposition across many languages is SPEAKER ('1st person', I) vs. HEARER ('2nd person', you).
• 3rd person pronouns (he, she, they) are common but NOT universal.
• Other distinctions: FORMAL vs. INFORMAL ('you' vs. 'thou'); INCLUSIVE vs. EXCLUSIVE first person plural 'we' ('we including you' vs. 'we not including you'); and number — SINGULAR, DUAL (exactly two), TRIAL (exactly three), PAUCAL (a few but not too many), PLURAL (many).

SPATIAL DEIXIS:
• HERE → the located object is near the speaker. THERE → away from the speaker.
• Many languages have THREE-TERM systems: near the speaker / near the hearer / far from the speaker.
• FIJIAN: na ŋone oŋgo 'this child (near me)' | na ŋone oŋgori 'this child (near you)' | na ŋone oya 'that child (away from you and me)'
• MALAGASY has a rich remoteness system — three degrees of nearness: eo / eto / ety = 'here / right here / right next to me'.

TEMPORAL DEIXIS:
• Marked by words (yesterday, before, after, now) and in many languages by TENSE AFFIXES on the verb.
• ENGLISH — two-term, past vs. non-past: 'I walk to school everyday' / 'I walked to school everyday'.
• KUSAIEAN — two-term, future vs. non-future: 'Sepe el mas ekweyah/ingena' (was/is sick); 'Sepe el ac misac' (will die).
• LITHUANIAN — three-term: jìs skaĩt-o 'he reads' (PRES), skaĩt-ỹs 'he will read' (FUT), skaĩt-ė 'he read' (PAST).
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

notes.title: Lexical Semantic Relations: the '-nyms'
notes.body:
Words, meanings and concepts do NOT exist in isolation. They can be grouped into sets and may be semantically related to other words.
   Dark vs. Light | Branch vs. Branch | Mammal vs. Dog | Terrier vs. Dog

SYNONYMY — words or expressions with the same meaning in some or all contexts. Synonyms usually have slightly DIFFERENT meanings and frequently have overlapping but not identical senses.
   vacation/holiday | youth/adolescent | automobile/car | remember/recall | purchase/buy | big/large
   Also: film, movie, flick, motion picture | eat, consume, ingest, wolf down | sleep, slumber, catch some z's

HYPONYMY — a relation between two words, one more general (HYPERNYM) and one more specific (HYPONYM).
• Word X is a HYPONYM of Y if X is a SUBSET of Y.
• Word X is a HYPERNYM of Y if Y is a SUBSET of X.
   dog (hypernym) / poodle (hyponym) | shirt ~ tank top | cook ~ fry | child ~ baby
• Multi-layered hyponymic relationships create TAXONOMIES:
     cook → fry, boil, roast → stir-fry, sauté, blanch, simmer

ANTONYMY — words that are opposites with respect to at least one aspect of their meaning.
   young/old | boy/girl | hot/cold | come/go | thin/thick | dark/light | risky/safe | rich/poor
THREE TYPES:
• CONTRARY — opposite regions of a SCALE with intermediate values (young/old, thin/thick)
• COMPLEMENTARY — when one is true, the other is false (dead/alive, pass/fail, off/on)
• REVERSIVE — movement in opposite directions (come/go), or change between reversible states (melt/freeze)

HOMOPHONY — two words identical in FORM but with NO relation in meaning. The formal identity is just COINCIDENCE.
   ail~ale | assent~ascent | bier~beer | dough~doe | past~passed | bank~bank

POLYSEMY — a single word with multiple meanings that are distinct but RELATED. Typical for most lexemes.
   rent (payment) ~ to rent (tenant) ~ to rent (landlord) | eye (body part) ~ eye (verb) | wood (from a tree) ~ wood (place of many trees)
• Often a SHIFT FROM ONE SEMANTIC FRAME TO ANOTHER:
     surf (ocean → Internet) | attack (war → problems) | foot (body → landscape) | head (body → organization) | tail (body → following behind)
• NOT synonymy (same meaning) and NOT homophony (same sound, unrelated).

MENTAL LEXICON: a single sequence of phonemes can have multiple RELATED meanings attached ('bright' — polysemy), or can happen to be identical in two words with nothing else in common ('bank' — homophony).

★ CLICKER ANSWERS FROM THE DECK:
• 'Selena hit the ball with the wooden bat' / 'The bat flew away' → HOMOPHONY
• 'I purchased a couch' / 'I bought the matching tables' → SYNONYMY
• 'my hair looking funny' / 'a funny joke' → POLYSEMY
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

notes.title: Fuzzy Meaning and How Word Meanings Are Represented
notes.body:
THE MUG / CUP / BOWL / GLASS EXERCISE:
• A long series of images, each asking: mug, cup, bowl, glass, or other?
• THE POINT: do these words have clearly defined meanings, or are the boundaries FUZZY? Are there clear cases and unclear cases?

DOES IT MATTER WHAT'S IN THEM?
• Same vessel + rice = 'bowl'
• Same vessel + hot drink = 'cup'

DOES SIZE / RELATION TO US MATTER?
• Large = 'bowl'; small = 'cup'

CONCLUSION: word meanings are NOT clear-cut. They may depend on many factors including features of CONTEXT, and they are related to human uses and social/cultural norms (like having saucers, or what we put inside something).

WHAT IS THE MENTAL REPRESENTATION OF A WORD'S MEANING?

1. DICTIONARY-STYLE DEFINITIONS — stored like dictionary entries, defined using other words plus usage examples.
   • PRO: useful; a paraphrase of meaning; can actually help people learn word meanings.
   • CON: how can we learn the meaning of any word if words are defined in terms of other words? Not connected to anything more basic. (Think of children, or people who can't read, or having a concept with no word attached.)

2. MENTAL IMAGE DEFINITIONS — stored as a mental image, a PROTOTYPE ('DOG').
   • PRO: mental images really are things we use when we conceptualize.
   • CON: different people have different experiences and images — how do we share meanings? (Think of 'mom'.) The images are prototypical, and some things are hard to visualize (e.g. 'reciprocity', 'from').

3. USAGE-BASED DEFINITIONS — stored with the ways and contexts in which we use them (rice = bowl, hot drink = cup).

★ CONCLUSION: mental representations are probably composed of ALL THREE of these aspects.

LEXICAL SEMANTICS AND THE LEXICON:
• CONTENT WORDS: mug, cup, bowl, glass — relations like antonymy, polysemy, homonymy apply here.
• FUNCTION WORDS: she, the, is, will, there — phenomena like deixis and tense/mood apply here.
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

notes.title: Topics to Know — Semantics (roadmap)
notes.body:
The lecture listed these as the concepts to master:
• PHRASAL SEMANTICS: semantic roles
• LEXICAL SEMANTICS: the '-nyms' (synonymy, hyponymy, antonymy, homophony, polysemy)
• DEIXIS
• LEXICALIZATION

WHAT IS SEMANTICS?
• The study of meaning.
• The study of the systematic ways in which languages structure meaning, especially in words and phrases.
• The way meaning is represented and transmitted.
• The way meaning depends on structure.

LEVELS OF GRAMMAR (assembly-line model): Phonology → Morphology → Syntax → Semantics.

PHRASAL SEMANTICS = meaning patterns conveyed in phrases and sentences.
LEXICAL SEMANTICS = meaning patterns in words.
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Semantics (adapted from Dr. G. Zellou)]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Syntax Classwork & Common Mistakes
notes.body:
★ DITRANSITIVE REQUIRES AN INDIRECT OBJECT, NOT JUST A PP. 'They cut the paper in many shapes' is transitive + oblique, not ditransitive. Test it with the double-object shift.
★ THE SHIFT TEST IS THE WHOLE GAME: if it can move to sit right after the verb as a bare NP, it's an indirect object. 'I sent a package to her' → 'I sent her a package' ✓. 'She drove her car to Portland' → *'She drove Portland her car' ✗.
★ ARRIVE IS INTRANSITIVE. A verb with no object is intransitive no matter what PP follows it. Check the example you write actually demonstrates the label you gave.
★ MATCH YOUR EXAMPLE TO YOUR LABEL. If you call a verb transitive, the example sentence must contain a real direct object — not an oblique PP.
★ MANY VERBS TAKE MORE THAN ONE FRAME: send is transitive AND ditransitive; understand is transitive AND usable intransitively. Don't stop at the first frame you think of.
★ PP-ATTACHMENT AMBIGUITY: when a PP can attach to the VP or to the preceding NP, you get two structures and two meanings ('with my binoculars', 'in my car').
★ IF THE WORD ORDER STAYS THE SAME AND THE MEANING FLIPS, THE LANGUAGE IS USING CASE — not linear order. This is the Latin diagnostic, and it's how the constructed-language problem works.
★ -ea = subject/nominative, -ap = object/accusative; the constructed language is verb-final: Hab-ea cal-ap tam.
notes.source: [ANTH 4 Syntax classwork: constituency, transitivity, ambiguity, and grammatical-role coding]

notes.title: Syntax Classwork — Constituency, Transitivity, Ambiguity, Role Coding
notes.body:
PART 1 — Break down the sentences and identify the NP arguments (subject, direct object, indirect object, or oblique):
• 'I drink tea that is not caffeinated in the morning.'
   I = SUBJECT | tea that is not caffeinated = DIRECT OBJECT | in the morning = OBLIQUE
• 'The smart girl gave her friend a generous present for his birthday.'
   The smart girl = SUBJECT | her friend = INDIRECT OBJECT | a generous present = DIRECT OBJECT | for his birthday = OBLIQUE
• 'The cat swatted the cabinets in the kitchens.'
   The cat = SUBJECT | the cabinets = DIRECT OBJECT | in the kitchens = OBLIQUE

PART 2 — TRANSITIVITY. Remember the definitions: INTRANSITIVE = subject only; TRANSITIVE = subject + direct object; DITRANSITIVE = subject + direct object + INDIRECT object.
⚠ THE KEY TEST: a following PP does NOT make a verb ditransitive. Only a true indirect object does — the kind that can shift into the double object construction ('I sent a package to her' → 'I sent her a package').
• cut — intransitive ('They cut') and transitive ('They cut the paper'). NOT ditransitive: in 'They cut the paper in many shapes', 'in many shapes' is an OBLIQUE.
• arrive — INTRANSITIVE. 'I will arrive' has no object; 'arrive at the station' adds an oblique, not an object.
• claim — transitive. 'I claim victory!'
• panic — intransitive ('I panicked'); note 'We panicked at the sound of sirens' is still intransitive, since the PP is oblique. Panic CAN be transitive with a genuine object: 'The news panicked investors.'
• work — intransitive ('She works hard every day') and transitive ('The artist works the clay').
• understand — transitive ('I understand the problem') and can be used intransitively ('I understand').
• send — transitive ('I send a package') AND ditransitive ('I send her a package' / 'I sent a package to her').
• exit — intransitive ('Exit, please') and transitive ('I exited the building').

PART 3 — AMBIGUITY: 'I once saw a stranger with my binoculars.'
• Interpretation 1 — PP attaches to the VP: I used my binoculars to see the stranger.
• Interpretation 2 — PP attaches to the NP 'a stranger': the stranger had my binoculars.
• This is PP-attachment ambiguity, the same structure as the lecture's 'I saw the man in my car'.

PART 4 — CONSTRUCTED LANGUAGE:
   Cal-ea gal-ap van.  (dog-SUBJ cat-OBJ chase) 'The dog chases the cat.'
   Cal-ap gal-ea van.  (dog-OBJ cat-SUBJ chase) 'The cat chases the dog.'
• ANSWER: roles are marked by CASE — inflectional endings on the nouns. -ea makes a root the SUBJECT; -ap makes it the OBJECT.
• The word order is identical in both sentences, so order is NOT doing the work — exactly the Latin pattern.
• The data is verb-final (SOV).
• 'The bird saw the dog' (hab = bird, cal = dog, tam = saw) = HAB-EA CAL-AP TAM.
notes.source: [ANTH 4 Syntax classwork: constituency, transitivity, ambiguity, and grammatical-role coding]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Syntax Lecture
notes.body:
★ SYNTAX = rules/principles/processes combining words into sentences. Word order affects BOTH the interpretation and the set of AVAILABLE interpretations.
★ FOUR JUDGMENT TYPES: GRAMMATICALITY (follows the rules), INTERPRETABILITY (makes coherent sense), FELICITY (fits the context), ACCEPTABILITY (umbrella term).
★ THE TWO CLASSIC EXAMPLES: 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously' = grammatical, NOT interpretable. “Chomsky's idea are exciting” = ungrammatical, IS interpretable. They're independent properties.
★ SIX BASIC WORD ORDERS: SVO, SOV, VSO, VOS, OVS, OSV. English is SVO.
★ GRAMMATICAL GENDER ≠ sociocultural gender. German Mädchen 'girl' is NEUTER because -chen patterns as neuter. Assignment is also driven by phonology, morphosyntax, semantics, and processing.
★ FOUR CONSTITUENCY TESTS: substitution, answer fragments, movement, coordination. ⚠ ONE TEST IS NEVER DECISIVE — neither passing nor failing. Apply as many as possible.
★ SYNTACTIC CATEGORIES are defined DISTRIBUTIONALLY — same category = can substitute without losing grammaticality.
★ MEMORIZE THE RULES: S → NP VP | NP → (Det) (Adj) N (PP) | VP → V (NP) (PP) | PP → PREP (NP). Parentheses = optional. → means 'is made up of'.
★ A CHANGE IN MEANING IS A CHANGE IN CONSTITUENCY — 'more intelligent leaders' has two groupings and two meanings.
★ NAVAJO VP → NP V (verb last), not English's VP → V NP. All languages have hierarchy; the RULES vary.
★ THE OBLIQUE TEST: indirect objects shift into the double object construction ('I taught three students French'); obliques cannot (*'She drove Portland her car'). Both follow 'to', so the shift is what separates them.
★ FOUR WAYS TO CODE GRAMMATICAL RELATIONS: linear order, case (on nouns), agreement (on verbs), adpositions.
★ KNOW THE LANGUAGE EXAMPLES: Latin = case, order unchanged. Arabic = verb inflection. Korean = case particles -i/-ul with flexible order. Spanish = verb inflection AND order. English = order plus prepositions.
★ TRANSITIVITY: intransitive (John slept), transitive (She ate the bread), ditransitive (I threw the ball to Sophie).
★ GENERATIVE GRAMMAR generates the sentences of L — AND ONLY L. That 'only' is the whole point.
★ TREES, BRACKETS, BOXES are EQUIVALENT notations. In a tree, everything under a node is a CONSTITUENT.
★ SYNTACTIC AMBIGUITY = one sentence, two structures. 'black coffee drinkers'; 'I saw the man in my car' (PP attaches to VP or NP).
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Grammars, Trees, and Syntactic Ambiguity
notes.body:
DEFINITION OF A GRAMMAR: formal and theoretical models determining what is structurally allowed/included in a language and what is not.
TYPES: Generative Grammars, Constraint-based Grammars, Functional Grammars, Dependency Grammars.

FORMAL LANGUAGES & GENERATIVE GRAMMAR:
• A language L can be defined as a SET of sentences.
   Eng = {They are happy, Bob is in the room, The cat ran, ...}
   Not-Eng = {*is happy he, *cat the ran, *in is Bob the room, ...}
• A GENERATIVE GRAMMAR for L is a system of rules that generates (the sentences of) L — AND ONLY L.

PHRASE STRUCTURE GRAMMARS: group words into phrases and assign structure in a tree-like format.

TREES, BRACKETS, OR BOXES — three equivalent notations:
• [S [NP [N Alice]] [VP [V eats] [NP [N cake]]]]

TREES AND DERIVATIONS — trees can be described by a rule set that generates them:
   S → NP VP
   NP → N
   VP → V NP
   N → Alice, cake
   V → eats

SYNTACTIC AMBIGUITY:
• Sometimes the same sentence can receive different syntactic analyses — the grammar assigns at least two structures to it.
• Sometimes those two structures correspond to different interpretations.
• 'black coffee drinkers': [black coffee] drinkers vs. black [coffee drinkers]
• 'I saw the man in my car': the PP 'in my car' can attach to the VP (I was in the car) or to the NP (the man was in the car)

EXERCISE FROM THE DECK:
• Diagram 'Abe bought the book about the man with the money' into its constituents, and draw TWO trees capturing the structural ambiguity.
• Grammar given: S → NP VP; NP → (D) N (PP); VP → V (NP) (PP); PP → P NP
   N → Abe, man, money, book | D → the | V → saw, chased | P → about, with
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Grammatical Roles, Obliques, and How Languages Code Them
notes.body:
GRAMMATICAL ROLES indicate the syntactic role an NP plays in an utterance:
• Subject (Subj), Direct Object (DO), Indirect Object (IO)

INDIRECT OBJECTS IN ENGLISH:
• Marked by the preposition 'to'; direct objects take no case marking.
     Subj      V        DO    IO
     NP                 NP    NP
     Lorraine brought sushi to me.

INDIRECT OBJECTS VS. OBLIQUES — both can follow 'to', so you need a test:
• 'She went to Portland' — 'to Portland' is OBLIQUE.
• EVIDENCE: indirect objects can SHIFT directly after the verb in the DOUBLE OBJECT CONSTRUCTION:
   I taught French to three students. → I taught three students French. ✓
• Oblique arguments CANNOT shift:
   She drove her car to Portland. → *She drove Portland her car. ✗

ENGLISH OBLIQUES:
• Any argument that is not a subject, object, or indirect object.
• Most obliques are NPs inside prepositional phrases: from the bank, under the table.
• Obliques have NO grammatical relation with the verb — no behavior unites them or defines them as a special grammatical class.

FOUR WAYS LANGUAGES CODE GRAMMATICAL RELATIONS:
1. Coding through LINEAR ORDER
2. Coding through inflectional markings on the NP (CASE)
3. Coding through inflectional marking on the VERB (AGREEMENT)
4. Coding through ADPOSITIONS (prepositions or postpositions)

LATIN — case on nouns, word order unchanged:
• Canis fêlem vîdit (dog-NOM cat-ACC saw) = 'the dog saw the cat'
• Canem fêlis vîdit (dog-ACC cat-NOM saw) = 'the cat saw the dog'
• Latin changes the roles WITHOUT changing the word order, by modifying the case endings.

ENGLISH — linear order and prepositions:
• I gave John a book. / I gave a book to John.
• I baked John a cake. / I baked a cake to John.

STANDARD ARABIC — inflection on the verb:
• fataħnaahu = fataħ 'opened' + -naa '1PL.NOM' + -hu '3SG.ACC' = 'We opened it'
• When there are only pronominal arguments, Arabic codes relations on the verb.

SPANISH — both verb inflection and word order:
• como 'I eat' / comes 'you eat'
• el perro mordió el gato ('the dog bite-3sg.PT the cat') = 'the dog bit the cat'

KOREAN — case markers on nouns:
• ku swunkyeng-i totwuk-ul capasseyo (policeman-NOM thief-ACC caught)
• totwuk-ul ku swunkyeng-i capasseyo (thief-ACC policeman-NOM caught)
• Both = 'That policeman caught a thief.' Order varies; case carries the roles.

AGREEMENT: the form of the verb may depend on properties of the subject or object — number (singular, plural, dual), person (1st, 2nd, 3rd), gender.
• English 'be' (person and number): I am happy / we, you, they are happy / she, he, it is happy.
• Arabic agrees for number, person, AND gender.

TRANSITIVITY — verbs require different numbers of arguments:
• INTRANSITIVE: subject only — John slept.
• TRANSITIVE: subject and object — She ate the bread.
• DITRANSITIVE: subject, object, and indirect object — I threw the ball to Sophie.
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Cross-Linguistic Variation: Navajo
notes.body:
ALL languages have constituency and hierarchical phrase structure.
BUT there is variation in phrase structure RULES cross-linguistically.

NAVAJO DATA:
• ashkii ateed yiyiiltsá  ('boy girl saw') = 'The boy saw the girl'
• ateed ashkii yichi yalti ('girl boy to talks') = 'The girl talks to the boy'

In the second sentence the structure is: S → NP VP, where the VP contains PP then V — the verb comes LAST and the postpositional element precedes it.

★ EXAM QUESTION FROM THE DECK: What is the phrase structure rule for the Navajo verb phrase in 'ashkii ateed yiyiiltsá'?
   Answer: VP → NP V  (not VP → V NP, which is the English pattern)
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Syntactic Categories and Phrase Structure Rules
notes.body:
SYNTACTIC CATEGORY — each word/constituent belongs to one.
• Words/constituents in the same category can SUBSTITUTE for one another without loss of grammaticality.
• Categories are defined in terms of their DISTRIBUTIONAL properties in a sentence; same category = similar distribution.

LEXICAL CATEGORIES: Noun (book, Jill, giraffe, liberty), Verb (run, eat, swim), Adjective (red, happy, afraid, big, fake), Preposition (for, at, in, on, about), Adverb (again, always, often, slowly).

PHRASAL CATEGORIES:
• Noun Phrase: the book, Jill, a giraffe with a very long neck
• Verb Phrase: run, eat a carrot, swim fast, give money to charity
• Adjective Phrase: red, happy and excited, afraid of snakes
• Preposition Phrase: for the sake of argument, about the issue, on the table
• Adverbial Phrase: slowly, more slowly, more slowly than me

HIERARCHICAL STRUCTURE: words are organized into constituents (phrases). A PHRASE is a word or words functioning as a unit according to phrase structure rules.

SENTENCES HAVE TWO PRINCIPAL CONSTITUENTS — NP and VP:
   S = NP + VP     (the dog) (bites)
   S → NP VP       → means 'is made up of'
   'A sentence is made up of a noun phrase followed by a verb phrase.'

A CHANGE IN MEANING IS A CHANGE IN CONSTITUENCY:
• [more [intelligent leaders]] = 'more leaders who are intelligent'
• [[more intelligent] leaders] = 'leaders who are more intelligent'

NOUN PHRASE — all behave the same in 'I love to look at ______ everyday':
   Bobbi | them | the dog | our wonderful pet | that scary spider on my leg
        (Det)   (Adj)      N        (PP)
         —       —        Bob       —
         —       —        them      —
        the      —        dog       —
        our   wonderful   pet       —
        that   scary     spider   on my leg
   NP → (Det) (Adj) N (PP)

PREPOSITIONAL PHRASE — all behave the same in 'Noah drove ______':
   around | under the bridge | from Ohio | by the rowdy stadium parking lot
   PP → PREP (NP)

VERB PHRASE — all behave the same in 'Rosa ______':
   ran | played the piano | watched the big game on Saturday
   VP → V (NP) (PP)

PHRASE STRUCTURE RULES ARE LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC:
• English: the apple (NP → Det N) but *apple the; a beautiful house (NP → Det Adj N) but *house beautiful a.

TREE DIAGRAMS: THE ELEMENTS UNDER A NODE FORM A CONSTITUENT. Worked example in lecture: 'the dog bit the cat on the nose'.
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Constituency and the Four Constituency Tests
notes.body:
CONSTITUENCY: in a sentence, some words hang together more closely than others and form a unit called a CONSTITUENT. We detect constituents by running constituency tests.

THE FOUR TESTS:

1. PRONOMINAL SUBSTITUTION — constituents can be replaced by pronouns like s/he, they, it, that, them, then, there, do that, that way.
   • A man with dark glasses (He) is following us.
   • I bought a few good looking mangos (them).
   • We watched a movie about cheese-making (did that) last week.
   • Annette went to Brazil (there).

2. ANSWER FRAGMENTS — questions formed with wh-words (who, what, where, when) can be answered by constituents.
   • That is my brother. → Who is that? My brother.
   • He is making a mess. → What's he doing? Making a mess.
   • The keys are on the table. → Where are the keys? On the table.

3. MOVEMENT — constituents can be moved as a group.
   • We had a lot of fun over the weekend. → Over the weekend, we had a lot of fun.
   • I've always enjoyed playing soccer. → Playing soccer, I've always enjoyed.

4. COORDINATION — constituents can be joined with and, or, but.
   • Her friends (and Mary) were playing tennis.
   • We peeled the onion (and poured them in the pot).
   • The car could go over the bridge (or through the tunnel).

⚠ HOW TO USE THE TESTS:
• Failing to pass a single test does NOT mean the test string is not a constituent.
• Passing a single test does NOT necessarily mean the test string IS a constituent.
• Apply as MANY tests as possible to show or rule out constituent status.

PRACTICE SENTENCES FROM LECTURE:
• Martha found a lovely pillow for the couch.
• The light in this room is terrible.
• I wonder whether Bonnie has finished packing her books.
• Melissa slept in her class.
• Pete and Max are fighting over the bone.
• I gave a bone to Pete and to Max yesterday.
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Word Order and Grammatical Gender
notes.body:
WORD ORDER:
• Linguistic units are typically produced and processed LINEARLY, so the order of units can matter.
• Word order refers to how a language requires the ordering of its words or phrases, especially the verb and its nominal arguments.
   The squirrel bit the man. / The man bit the squirrel.

BASIC WORD ORDER — the ordering of verb, subject, and object. All six logical options, with the squirrel/almond example:
• SVO: The squirrel ate the almond.
• OVS: The almond ate the squirrel.
• SOV: The squirrel the almond ate.
• OSV: The almond the squirrel ate.
• VSO: Ate the squirrel the almond.
• VOS: Ate the almond the squirrel.

GRAMMATICAL GENDER:
• Related to but NOT the same as sociocultural gender.
• It is a CLASSIFICATION SYSTEM FOR NOUNS which, when it comes to people, CAN correlate with sociocultural gender — but not always.
• German has three genders (feminine, masculine, neuter). The noun Mädchen ('girl') is NEUTER, not feminine:
   der/ein Mann | die/eine Frau | das/ein Mädchen
• The syntactic rules of German require the suffix '-chen' to pattern as neuter.

OTHER FACTORS AFFECTING GENDER CLASSIFICATION:
• Phonetics and phonology
• Morphosyntactic properties of the language
• Semantic features such as human, animate, type of object
• Processing and psycholinguistics
(Reference charts cited in lecture: WALS features 30A number of genders, 31A sex-based vs. non-sex-based systems, 32A systems of gender assignment.)
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: What Is Syntax? Well-formedness and Linguistic Judgments
notes.body:
SYNTAX: the study of rules, principles, and processes that combine words to construct sentences.
• The way words are put together affects our INTERPRETATIONS:
   The dog chased the cat. / The cat chased the dog.
• It can also affect the AVAILABLE interpretations of a sentence:
   'Old women and men were invited.' — are the men old too, or only the women?

WELL-FORMEDNESS — a cline, not a switch:
• The dog is sleeping under the blanket. ✓
• The dogs are sleeping under the blanket. ✓
• The dog is sleeping below the blanket. ✓
• The dog are sleeping under the blanket. ✗ (agreement)
• Are sleeping the dog under the blanket. ✗ (order)
• Dog blanket is the the sleeping under. ✗✗
• Is the the under sleeping Dog blanket. ✗✗✗

BASIC CONCEPTS:
• GRAMMATICALITY — whether a sentence is constructed according to the grammatical rules of a language. Grammaticality judgments reflect a speaker's MENTAL and IMPLICITLY LEARNED knowledge of the language.
• INTERPRETABILITY — whether a sentence can receive a coherent interpretation.
• FELICITY — whether a sentence is appropriate for the context it was used in.
• ACCEPTABILITY — a broad term covering any linguistic ill/well-formedness.

GRAMMATICALITY VS. INTERPRETABILITY ARE INDEPENDENT:
• Grammatical but NOT interpretable: 'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously.' (Compare *'Furiously sleep ideas green colorless' — neither grammatical nor interpretable.)
• Ungrammatical but interpretable: “Chomsky's idea are exciting.”
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Syntax (adapted from Dr. Masoud Jasbi & Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS - Morphology Classwork & Common Mistakes
notes.body:
★ CLIPPING vs. ABBREVIATION: clipping shortens a word and keeps a chunk of it (fridge, gym, app, exam). An abbreviation/initialism uses INITIAL LETTERS said one at a time (fyi, FBI, DC). An ACRONYM uses initials but is said as a word (NASA, scuba).
★ WHEN LISTING MORPHEMES, INCLUDE THE ROOTS. They are morphemes, and they are the FREE ones in the set.
★ DON'T INVENT MORPHEMES THAT SPAN A BOUNDARY. 'tani' in siskoltani is just -lta + -ni. Segment from the known pieces outward.
★ VOWEL HARMONY is an ASSIMILATION process: vowels within a word become more similar. In Finnish, suffix vowels agree in BACKNESS with the stem vowels.
★ Finnish front vowels include ö [ø] and ä [æ]; a [ɑ] is BACK. Front stem → -ltä; back stem → -lta.
★ The conditioning is PHONOLOGICAL, not semantic — nothing to do with gender, animacy, or object vs. person. Finnish has no grammatical gender at all.
★ 'From my dog' = KOIRALTANI (koira is a back-vowel stem, so -lta, then -ni).
★ THE ORDER MATTERS: case suffix first, then possessive — stem + lta/ltä + ni.
notes.source: [ANTH 4 Morphology classwork: word-formation and Finnish vowel-harmony problems]

notes.title: Morphology Classwork - Word Formation & Finnish Vowel Harmony
notes.body:
PROBLEM 1 — identify the method of word creation:
• Fridge → CLIPPING (shortened from 'refrigerator'). ⚠ Not an abbreviation — abbreviations/initialisms are built from initial letters said one by one (fyi, FBI).
• Playdate → COMPOUNDING (two free morphemes).
• NASA → ACRONYM (initials pronounced as a word).
• Cardigan → EPONYM (from James Thomas Brudenell, 7th Earl of Cardigan).
• Spork → BLENDING (spoon + fork).

PROBLEM 2 — Finnish data:
   töllö 'TV'            sisko 'sister'
   töllöni 'my TV'       siskoni 'my sister'
   töllöltä 'from TV'    siskolta 'from sister'
   töllöltäni 'from my TV'  siskoltani 'from my sister'

(1) INFLECTIONAL OR DERIVATIONAL?
• Inflectional — word class never changes and the meanings contributed are predictable and productive.

(2) THE MORPHEMES:
• töllö 'TV' — FREE root
• sisko 'sister' — FREE root
• -ni 'my' (1st person possessive) — BOUND
• -ltä / -lta 'from' (ablative case) — BOUND
⚠ 'tani' is NOT a morpheme. siskoltani segments as sisko-lta-ni — two separate suffixes in sequence. Don't let a string that spans a boundary look like a unit.
⚠ Don't forget the ROOTS. The question asks for the morphemes present, and töllö and sisko are morphemes too — and they're the free ones.

(3) THE CAUSE OF THE ALLOMORPHIC VARIATION:
• VOWEL HARMONY. Finnish suffix vowels assimilate in BACKNESS to the vowels of the stem.
• ö = [ø] rounded mid FRONT vowel; ä = [æ] unrounded open FRONT vowel; a = [ɑ] unrounded open BACK vowel.
• töllö contains FRONT vowels → takes the FRONT suffix -ltä.
• sisko contains BACK vowels → takes the BACK suffix -lta.
• The conditioning is purely PHONOLOGICAL — it has nothing to do with animacy, gender, or whether the noun is an object or a person.

(4) 'FROM MY DOG' (koira):
• koira contains BACK vowels → harmony selects -lta, not -ltä.
• koira + lta + ni = KOIRALTANI.
notes.source: [ANTH 4 Morphology classwork: word-formation and Finnish vowel-harmony problems]

notes.title: Chickasaw Walkthrough - Worked Analysis
notes.body:
THE STRATEGY: analyze the data in CHUNKS. Take groups of similar forms with similar meanings; find what is shared across all the forms and all the meanings in that chunk; link the leftovers.

CHUNK 1 — the 'tall' group:
Sachaaha 'I am tall' | Chaaha 'He/she is tall' | Chichaaha 'You are tall' | Hoochaaha 'They are tall'
• chaaha occurs in ALL the forms, and 'be tall' occurs in ALL the meanings → chaaha = 'to be tall'. (answer a1)
• What REMAINS of the forms (sa-, chi-, hoo-) links to what REMAINS of the meanings → sa- = 'I', chi- = 'you', hoo- = 'they'.
• ★ Notice: if there is NO prefix on chaaha, the default meaning is 'he/she'. So 'he/she' is realized with NO morpheme — a NULL morpheme, ∅. (answer b4)

CHUNK 2 — the 'hungry' group:
Hopobatok 'He was hungry' | Hoohopobatok 'They were hungry' | Sahopoba 'I am hungry'
• hopoba appears in all the forms and 'be hungry' in all the meanings → hopoba = 'to be hungry'. (answer a2)
• We already know hoo- = 'they' and sa- = 'I' from chunk 1.
• The first two forms carry an extra -tok suffix. What differs in their meanings? The first two are PAST tense, the last is present → -tok = past tense. (answer b1)

CHUNK 3 — confirmation:
Satikahbi 'I am tired' | Chitikahbitok 'You were tired' | Chichchokwa 'You are cold'
• sa- appears again with 'I', chi- again with 'you', and -tok again with past tense. Everything checks out.
• Bonus: this data also gives tikahbi = 'to be tired' and chchokwa = 'to be cold' — the question just doesn't ask.

ANSWERS:
a1 chaaha | a2 hopoba
b1 -tok | b2 sa- | b3 chi- | b4 ∅ (the null morpheme)
c1 'You are old' = Chisipokni (add chi- 'you')
c2 'He was old' = Sipoknitok (NO subject prefix, since he/she is null; add -tok for past)
c3 'They are old' = hoosipokni (add hoo- 'they'; no -tok because it's present)
notes.source: [ANTH 4 Morphology walkthrough: Chickasaw problem (adapted from Fromkin et al., An Introduction to Language, 8e) - instructor answer key]

notes.title: Chickasaw Walkthrough - Data and Questions
notes.body:
SOURCE: adapted from Fromkin et al., An Introduction to Language, 8th edition. Chickasaw is a Muskogean language spoken in southcentral Oklahoma.

DATA:
Sachaaha 'I am tall.'            Chaaha 'He/she is tall.'
Chichaaha 'You are tall.'        Hoochaaha 'They are tall.'
Satikahbi 'I am tired.'          Chitikahbitok 'You were tired.'
Chichchokwa 'You are cold.'      Hopobatok 'He was hungry.'
Hoohopobatok 'They were hungry.' Sahopoba 'I am hungry.'

QUESTIONS:
a. What is the root morpheme for (1) 'to be tall' and (2) 'to be hungry'?
b. What is the morpheme meaning (1) past tense, (2) 'I', (3) 'You', (4) 'He/she'?
c. If the Chickasaw root for 'to be old' is sipokni, how would you say (1) 'You are old', (2) 'He was old', (3) 'They are old'?
notes.source: [ANTH 4 Morphology walkthrough: Chickasaw problem (adapted from Fromkin et al., An Introduction to Language, 8e) - instructor answer key]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS - Morphology Lecture
notes.body:
★ MORPHOLOGY = how morphemes combine to form words. LEXICON = the mental dictionary.
★ MORPHEME = smallest unit of meaning; can't be broken down further and still mean something. antidisestablishmentarianism = 7 morphemes.
★ MORPHEMES HAVE CONSISTENT SOUND AND MEANING (un- = 'not' everywhere; -ity = 'state of being').
★ COUNT MORPHEMES, NOT SYLLABLES: walking = 2, retypes = 3. In retypes: 1 free + 2 bound. In workers: 1 free + 2 bound.
★ METHOD OF ANALYSIS: compare similar forms with minimally different meanings; what's shared in form maps to what's shared in meaning; link the leftovers. A single form in isolation cannot be analyzed.
★ FREE morpheme stands alone; BOUND must attach. ROOT = core of the word; STEM = anything an affix attaches to. All roots can be stems, not all stems are roots.
★ FOUR AFFIX TYPES with Ilocano examples: PREFIX taga-, SUFFIX -an, INFIX -in-, CIRCUMFIX pag-...-en.
★ TRAPS: two prefixes ≠ an infix (art-ful-ness); prefix + suffix ≠ a circumfix (un-forget-able). CIRCUMFIXES ARE RARE — when in doubt, say prefix + suffix.
★ INFLECTION: no new lexeme, never changes word class, productive, predictable. English set: -s plural, -s 3sg, -ed past, -ing progressive.
★ DERIVATION: creates new lexemes, CAN change word class, meaning not always predictable, productively LIMITED (*un-blue, *re-die, *friend-hood).
★ THE -ING / -ER TRAP: 'They are walking' = inflectional; 'This is a building' = derivational; 'She is a runner' = derivational; 'I wrote a letter' = NOT a morpheme at all.
★ GERMAN ge-...-t = CIRCUMFIX and INFLECTIONAL (tense only). TAGALOG -in- = INFIX. FARSI -i = SUFFIX and DERIVATIONAL (adjective → noun). BONTOC -um- = derivational infix. CREE ni- = inflectional prefix.
★ LEXICAL/CONTENT = open class (N, V, Adj, Adv). GRAMMATICAL/FUNCTIONAL = closed class (Prep, Det, Conj, Pron, Aux).
★ JABBERWOCKY: you identify categories by PATTERNS (-y → adjective, -s → plural noun) and by CO-OCCURRENCE ('the' signals a noun phrase).
★ CASE marks noun-verb relationships: nominative, accusative, dative, locative, instrumental.
★ SIX WORD-FORMATION METHODS: compounding, acronym, back-formation, abbreviation, eponym, blending — plus clipping, neologism, loanwords. KNOW THE DIFFERENCE between acronym (NASA, said as a word), initialism (FBI, spelled out), and clipping (gym).
★ FOUR SYSTEM TYPES: isolating (Mandarin), agglutinating (Hungarian), fusional (Russian), polysynthetic (Sora). Languages sit on a SPECTRUM, not in boxes.
★ ALLOMORPHY: one morpheme, different forms by phonological context. in- → [ɪn]/[ɪŋ]/[ɪm]; leaf/leaves.
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Types of Morphological Systems and Allomorphy
notes.body:
Languages can be classified according to how they put morphemes together. FOUR TYPES:

1. ISOLATING (ANALYTIC) — mainly FREE morphemes; each word consists of a single morpheme.
   Mandarin Chinese: wo men tan tɕin le ('I plural play piano past') = 'We played the piano'
2. AGGLUTINATING — bound morphemes attach to other morphemes; boundaries between morphemes are EASY to determine.
   Hungarian: o haaz-unk feheer ('the house-our white') = 'Our house is white'
3. FUSIONAL — bound morphemes attach to the stem, but it is DIFFICULT to tell where one morpheme ends and another begins. One morpheme combines multiple aspects of meaning.
   Russian: tʃita-yet 'he is reading' / tʃita-l 'he was reading'. /-yet/ means BOTH 3rd person AND present tense; /-l/ means BOTH 3rd person AND past tense, simultaneously.
4. POLYSYNTHETIC — several stem forms and affixes combine into one word, often a whole sentence.
   Sora (India): nen-adʒ-dʒa-dar-si-em ('I not receive cooked.rice hand you(sg)') = 'I will not receive cooked rice from your hands'

⚠ LANGUAGES ARE RARELY 'PURE' TYPES. A language may be more like one type while also containing elements of another. These classifications are a CONTINUOUS SPECTRUM, not boxes.

ALLOMORPHY: a morpheme can take different FORMS depending on phonological context.
• AFFIX example — the English prefix in- is usually pronounced [ɪn], but [ɪŋ] in <incomplete> and [ɪm] in <imperfect>.
• ROOT example — roots can have allomorphs too: leaf [lif] vs. leaves [livz].

HUNGARIAN PRACTICE — identify all the morphemes:
• [hɔz] 'house' | [ɛjhɔz] 'a house' | [hɔzɔ] 'his/her house'
• [boɾ] 'wine' | [ɛjboɾ] 'a wine' | [boɾɔ] 'his/her wine'
→ /hɔz/ 'house'; /boɾ/ 'wine'; /ɛj-/ 'a' (indefinite article); /-ɔ/ 'his/her' (3rd person possessive)
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Word Formation: Six Major Ways (plus two more)
notes.body:
Words can be added to the lexicon all the time. SIX MAJOR WAYS to form new words from old:

1. COMPOUNDING — a combination of FREE morphemes:
   hotdog, speed-date, binge-watch, buzzword, hotspot, cyberbully, meet-cute
2. ACRONYMS — derived from the initials of words, pronounced as a word:
   scuba, fomo, NASA
3. ABBREVIATIONS or INITIALISMS — said letter by letter:
   lol, fyi, diy, IRS, CIA, FBI, DC
4. BACK-FORMATION — created by removing what is MISTAKENLY considered to be an affix:
   cran-apple, whelmed (< 'underwhelmed'), tamale (< tamales, Sp. tamal)
5. EPONYMS — created from proper nouns (names):
   achilles, freudian, scrooge, xerox, kleenex
6. BLENDING — combining PARTS of words into one:
   smog, blog, podcast, brexit, mocktail, affluenza, bashtag, cronut, dramedy, chillax, jeggings

ALSO COVERED:
• CLIPPINGS — shortening longer words: phone (< telephone), gym, fax, ad, exam, totes, mos def, app, obvs
• NEOLOGISM — creating a completely novel word: zany and grovel (Shakespeare), scrumptdittilyumptious (Roald Dahl), boo, fleek, poggers
• LOANWORDS from other languages: pizza, blitz, czar, bagel, taco

⚠ EASY CONFUSION: an ACRONYM is pronounced as a word (NASA, scuba); an INITIALISM is spelled out (FBI, fyi); a CLIPPING keeps part of one word (gym, app); a BACK-FORMATION strips off a wrongly-perceived affix (whelmed).
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Grammatical vs. Lexical Morphemes, Open/Closed Class, and Lexical Categories
notes.body:
LEXICAL (CONTENT) morphemes have a core meaning:
• 'Bill watches all his favorite shows on Mondays' — Bill, watch, favorite, shows, Mondays

GRAMMATICAL (FUNCTIONAL) morphemes serve a function in the utterance:
• 'John is going to the store for the third time' — is, to, the, for

OPEN CLASS (lexical morphemes): words can be added all the time.
• 'I googled the totally hip ipod on my computer' — googled, totally, hip, ipod, computer

CLOSED CLASS (grammatical morphemes): rarely gain or change members.
• 'I googled the totally hip ipod on my computer' — I, the, on, my

LEXICAL CATEGORIES:
   LEXICAL (content) / OPEN         GRAMMATICAL (functional) / CLOSED
   Noun                             Preposition
   Verb                             Determiner
   Adjective                        Conjunction
   Adverb                           Pronoun
                                    Auxiliary Verb

HOW ARE LEXICAL CATEGORIES IDENTIFIED?
• By their PATTERNS: cats, books, cups, pens, monkeys — but *olds ('*these books are olds').
• By which words and categories CO-OCCUR in phrases: a monkey, the pen — but *a tall, *a she.

JABBERWOCKY (Lewis Carroll):
• "'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves / Did gyre and gimble in the wabe; / All mimsy were the borogoves, / And the mome raths outgrabe."
• The derivational suffix -y tells us 'slithy' could be an adjective.
• The inflectional suffix -s tells us 'toves' could be a plural noun.
• The determiner 'the' tells us there is a noun phrase; with two phrases inside a noun phrase, the first modifies the second.

LEXICAL CATEGORIES ARE NOT UNIVERSAL:
• Korean and Japanese do not have definite and indefinite articles.
• Some categories are common (nouns), others less so (definite articles).

STRUCTURAL CHARACTERISTICS:
• VERB — 3rd person singular -s; past tense -ed; progressive -ing; can be preceded by can or will. Subcategories: TRANSITIVE (subject + object: John ate five hamburgers), INTRANSITIVE (subject only: John walked), DITRANSITIVE (subject + direct + indirect object: I gave her the gift).
• NOUN — number distinction (cat/cats, child/children); can be preceded by a determiner.
• ADJECTIVE — inherent modifiers of nouns; -er and -est endings; can follow very or too.
• ADVERB — modifies verbs (talk loudly), adjectives (truly splendid), or other adverbs (unbelievably quickly).
• DETERMINER — occurs before nouns: articles (a book, the book), demonstratives (these books), possessives (my book).
• ADPOSITIONS — English has PREPOSITIONS (to school, on the table); Turkish has POSTPOSITIONS (evim de = 'house-my at' = 'at my house'). Some languages have both.
• CONJUNCTIONS — connect words or clauses: you and me; English or French.

PRONOUN SUBCATEGORIES:
• PERSONAL — 1st (I/we/us), 2nd (you/yours), 3rd (she/he/they/it)
• DEMONSTRATIVE — point to an entity: this, that, these, those
• INTERROGATIVE — ask questions: who, what, which
• RELATIVE — mark relative clauses: 'the boy WHO ate my cake'; 'a joke THAT we had heard'
• INDEFINITE — non-specific referents: someone, anyone, everyone, somebody
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Inflection vs. Derivation
notes.body:
INFLECTION: morphology that does NOT create a new lexeme.
• Inflectional affixes NEVER change the word class of the word they attach to.
• They tend to be highly PRODUCTIVE.
• They tend to contribute PREDICTABLE meanings.
• They code the relationship between constituents in a phrase and do not change the meaning of the stem:
   - The dog bites the cat (subject-verb agreement)
   - Faisal walked to the store (tense, aspect markers)
   - Mia's hat (possessive relationship)

ENGLISH INFLECTIONAL AFFIXES:
• -s plural — Plums are delicious
• -s 3rd singular subject present — Sharon changes her car's oil herself
• -ed past tense — Voters rejected the measure on the ballot
• -ing progressive — Sarah is riding her bike today

CREE (Algonquian, ~96,000 speakers): /ni-/ is an inflectional prefix signaling first person possessive.
• /tʃi:ma:n/ 'canoe' → /ni-tʃi:ma:n/ 'my canoe'; /so:niya/ 'money' → /ni-so:niya/; /wiya:ʃ/ 'meat' → /ni-wiya:ʃ/

CASE: inflectional morphology marking grammatical relationships between nouns and verbs.
• NOMINATIVE (grammatical subjects), ACCUSATIVE (grammatical objects), DATIVE (indirect objects), LOCATIVE, INSTRUMENTAL.
• Latvian example: Laukā dzīvo tārps 'A worm lives in the field'; Vīrs ēd putnu 'A man is eating the bird'; Putns ēd tārpu 'A bird is eating the worm'; Putnā tagad dzīvo tārps 'The worm now lives in the bird'. Note how putns/putnu/putnā change by case role.

DERIVATION: morphology that CREATES new lexical items.
• Derivational affixes do NOT necessarily add predictable meaning.
• They CAN change the word class of a lexical item.

CHANGING CATEGORY:
• /-er/ verb→noun (write→writer); /-tion/ verb→noun (inform→information); /-ly/ adjective→adverb (quick→quickly)
• Also: -en adjective→verb (blacken), -able verb→adjective (understandable), -ment verb→noun (management), -less noun→adjective (hopeless), en- noun/adj→verb (enable), -ing verb→noun (smoking)

CHANGING CENTRAL MEANING (same category):
• happy → un-happy ('not happy'); paint → re-paint ('paint again'); neighbor → neighbor-hood
• Also: re- 'do again' (reunite), pre- 'before' (prenatal), in-/un- 'not' (intolerable, unassuming), -ish 'sort of' (reddish)

PRODUCTIVELY LIMITED — derivation is selective about stems:
• un-happy but *un-blue | re-paint but *re-eat, *re-die | neighbor-hood but *friend-hood
• The * means 'not grammatical' / 'speakers of this language can't say this'.

BONTOC (Austronesian, Philippines, ~41,000 speakers): /-um-/ is a derivational morpheme meaning 'to become'.
• /fikas/ 'strong' → /f-um-ikas/ 'he is becoming strong'; kilad→kumilad; bato→bumato; fusul→fumusul

FARSI: suffix /-i/ creates nouns from adjectives — DERIVATIONAL because it changes the category of the stem.
• dana 'wise' → dana-i 'wisdom'; xub→xubi; darošt→darošti; bozorg→bozorgi; širin→širini
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Classifying Morphemes: Free/Bound, Root/Stem/Affix, Affix Types
notes.body:
Each morpheme can be classified in multiple ways depending on structure and use: bound/free, root vs. stem vs. affix, affix type, derivational/inflectional, grammatical/lexical, open/closed class.

FREE VS. BOUND:
• FREE morpheme — may occur as an independent word: Fred, book, two, like, not, of, go, run.
• BOUND morpheme — must be attached to some other morpheme: un-, -able, -s. (scared, houses, badly, unsure)

ROOT:
