• The central morpheme to which other morphemes are added; the central part of a complex word. EVERY word has a root at its core.

STEM:
• Anything that a morpheme can attach to. ALL ROOTS CAN BE STEMS, BUT STEMS ARE NOT ALWAYS ROOTS.
• Shared paradigm: true | tru-th | tru-est | tru-ly | tru-th-ful | tru-th-ful-ly | un-true | un-tru-th-ful-ly | un-tru-th-ful-ness

AFFIX:
• Morphemes that attach to roots and stems and modify their meaning. Bound morphemes are also known as affixes.

FOUR AFFIX TYPES (defined by position relative to the stem):
• PREFIX — attaches before: un-wise, un-like. Ilocano taga-: amianan 'north' → taga-amianan 'Northerner'; taga-ili 'from town'; taga-amerika 'American'.
• SUFFIX — attaches after: truth-ful, danc-ing. Ilocano -an: giling 'grind' → giling-an 'grinder'; sagat-an 'strainer'; balkot-an 'wrapper'.
• INFIX — inserted inside another morpheme: abso-bloody-lutely, alli-freaking-gator. Ilocano -in-: kuton 'ant' → k-in-uton 'ant-infested'; ng-in-ilaw 'fly-infested'; k-in-uto 'lice-infested'.
• CIRCUMFIX — part of the morpheme on each side: a-fish-in' (some American English varieties). Ilocano pag-...-en: ragsak 'happy' → pag-ragsak-en 'make happy'; pag-leddaang-en 'make sad'; pag-uray-en 'make wait'; pag-awid-en 'make go home'.

⚠ TWO IMPORTANT CAUTIONS:
• If TWO PREFIXES precede a root, the inner one is NOT an infix — same with suffixes (art-ful-ness).
• If a prefix AND suffix surround a root, that does NOT make them a circumfix (in-put-s, un-forget-able).
• Mohawk niahatitakhenóntie' = n-i-a-ha-ti-takhe-n-ontie' contains NO infixes or circumfixes.
• WHEN IN DOUBT, assume a complex word breaks into a combination of prefixes and suffixes. CIRCUMFIXES ARE RARE.
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Morphological Analysis - Method and Worked Data
notes.body:
THE METHOD:
• Compare similar words — one with a particular sequence of sounds and one without it.
• Hypothesize that the additional sounds add the additional meaning.
• Look for matches of similar sounds with similar meanings.
• Analyze in CHUNKS: take groups of similar forms with similar meanings, find what is shared across all forms and all meanings, then link the leftovers.

WHY ISOLATION FAILS:
• [grapho] 'I write' — alone, there is no way to tell which part means 'I' and which means 'write'.
• Add [graphe] 'he writes' and the analysis falls out: /graph-/ 'write', /-o/ 'I', /-e/ 'he'.

KARO (Omotic, Ethiopia, ~1,500 speakers):
• oya'wan 'I left' | omãmnoy 'I saw myself' | owakán 'I am angry' | okət 'I walked'

ISTHMUS ZAPOTEC (Oaxaca, Mexico, ~80,000 speakers):
• zigi 'chin' / ka-zigi 'chins'; diaga 'ear' / ka-diaga 'ears'; zike 'shoulder' / ka-zike 'shoulders'
• → /ka-/ is the PLURAL morpheme (marker).

DOLAKHA NEWAR (Sino-Tibetan, Nepal, ~5,600 speakers):
• chẽ 'house' / chẽ-ku 'at the house'; lokhu 'water' / lokhu-ku 'at/in the water'; sara 'horse' / sara-ku 'on the horse'; sĩ 'wood' / sĩ-ku 'on the wood'
• → /-ku/ is a LOCATIVE morpheme (marks location).
• NOTE: one morpheme here covers English 'at', 'in', and 'on' — morphemes in one language may correspond to many in another.

ILOKANO — full segmentation practice:
• buneng 'machete'
• agtagi-buneng-ka 'you carry a machete' | man-agtagi-buneng-ka 'you always carry a machete'
• agtagi-buneng-ka-nto 'you will carry a machete' | agtagi-buneng-da 'they carry a machete'
• n-agtagi-buneng-da 'they carried a machete' | n-agtagi-buneng-ak 'I carried a machete'
• agtagi-buneng-ak-to 'I will carry a machete'
• → -ka 'you', -da 'they', -ak 'I', n- past, -to future, man- 'always'
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Morphemes, Words, and Cross-Linguistic Variation
notes.body:
MORPHOLOGY: the study of how morphemes are combined to form new words.
• Every language has a large number of words and word parts available — this 'mental dictionary' is the LEXICON.

WHAT IS A WORD?
• Speaker intuitions provide the best indication of word boundaries.
• Words can be pronounced alone, but individual morphemes sometimes cannot.
• Pauses can fall between words, not morphemes.
• Words are not usually produced morpheme-by-morpheme as speakers talk.

WORDS ARE NOT THE SMALLEST UNITS OF MEANING:
• antidisestablishmentarianism = anti-dis-establish-ment-ari-an-ism

MORPHEME: a meaningful part of a word; the SMALLEST unit of meaning. It cannot be broken down further and still have meaning.
• unbelievable: believe + -able ('able to be believed'); un- + believable ('not able to be believed'). Each of believe, -able, un- is a morpheme.
• the | small-est | dog | sing-s

MORPHEMES HAVE CONSISTENT SOUND AND MEANING:
• un-happy, un-ethical, un-certain, un-lockable, un-appetizing — all 'not X'
• san-ity, musical-ity, pervers-ity, legal-ity, divin-ity — all 'state of being X'

CROSS-LINGUISTIC VARIATION — MOHAWK:
• Teninonhsihsákha = te-ni-nonhs-ihsak-ha ('you.&.I - two - house - seek - go.and') = 'Let's go look for the house.'
• An Iroquoian language spoken by about 3,500 people in Ontario, Quebec and upstate New York.
• A single morphologically complex word equates to what English needs a multi-word phrase to say.
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Concepts to Know - Morphology (roadmap)
notes.body:
The lecture listed these as the concepts to master:
• Lexicon & Morpheme
• Morphological Analysis
• Classifying Morphemes
• Bound/Free morphemes
• Root vs. stem vs. affix
• Affix types
• Derivational/inflectional morphemes
• Grammatical/Lexical morphemes
• Open/Closed class
• Ways of making new words
• Allomorphs

COURSE OUTLINE FOR THE UNIT:
What are Morphemes? → Ways to Categorize Morphemes → Lexical Categories → Types of Morphological Systems → Allomorphy → How to Solve Morphology Exercises
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 001 / ANTH 4 Lecture: Morphology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Farsi Problem & Common Mistakes
notes.body:
★ ANSWER: ONE phoneme /r/ with THREE allophones — [r] elsewhere, [ɾ] intervocalic, [r̥] word-final.
★ No minimal pairs + no overlapping environments = COMPLEMENTARY DISTRIBUTION. Say both parts.
★ The underlying phoneme is the ELSEWHERE case — widest distribution AND no stated condition needed.
★ RULES: /r/ → [r̥] / ___ # ; /r/ → [ɾ] / V ___ V ; /r/ → [r] elsewhere.
★ MISTAKE TO AVOID #1: calling vowels 'alveolar'. Place of articulation describes CONSONANT constrictions. Vowels take tongue HEIGHT, BACKNESS, and ROUNDING — /i/ high front, /æ/ low front, /a/ low.
★ MISTAKE TO AVOID #2: stating only the FOLLOWING segment. If the data shows a vowel on both sides, the generalization is INTERVOCALIC — the stronger and more economical claim.
★ MISTAKE TO AVOID #3: naming only some of the allophones in your conclusion. With three allophones, all three must appear in the final statement.
★ SPELLING: it is COMPLEMENTARY distribution (completing each other), not 'complimentary'.
★ PROCESSES: final devoicing + lenition (trill → tap). Compare Italian, which was place ASSIMILATION.
★ CONTRAST THE TWO PROBLEMS: Italian = 2 allophones conditioned by a FOLLOWING NATURAL CLASS; Farsi = 3 allophones conditioned by POSITION in the word.
notes.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

notes.title: Farsi Classwork — Worked Analysis (six-step method)
notes.body:
STEP 1 — IDENTIFY THE SOUNDS: [r], [ɾ], [r̥].

STEP 2 — MINIMAL PAIRS?
• None. The closest near-pair is [beɾid] 'go' and [daɾid] 'you have', but these differ in TWO places (b/d and e/a), so they are not a minimal pair — and in any case both contain [ɾ].
• No minimal pairs → not contrastive → expect complementary distribution.

STEP 3 — LIST THE ENVIRONMENTS:
   [r]            [ɾ]            [r̥]
   #__a (rah)     e__i (beɾid)   w__# (hærntowr̥)
   #__i (ris)     i__æ (biɾæŋg) a__# (tʃar̥)
   #__u (ruz)     e__a (tʃeɾa)   u__# (tʃedʒur̥)
   d__i (qædri)   a__i (daɾid)   i__# (ʃir̥)
   æ__n (hærntowr̥)
• No environments overlap → COMPLEMENTARY DISTRIBUTION confirmed.

STEP 4 — GENERALIZE WITH NATURAL CLASSES:
• [ɾ] always has a VOWEL ON BOTH SIDES → INTERVOCALIC (V__V). ⚠ Note: it is NOT enough to say '[ɾ] appears before front vowels' — that ignores the preceding vowel and would wrongly predict a tap after a consonant.
• [r̥] always sits at the END OF A WORD → __#. (Note it is preceded by a vowel three times and by a consonant once, so the preceding segment is irrelevant.)
• [r] appears word-initially, after a consonant, and before a consonant — no single positive condition unites these. It is the ELSEWHERE case.

STEP 5 — DETERMINE THE UNDERLYING SOUND:
• [r] has the widest distribution (5 environments vs. 4 each) AND is the only one requiring no stated condition.
• → /r/ is the PHONEME; [r], [ɾ], [r̥] are its allophones.

STEP 6 — WRITE THE RULES:
   /r/ → [r̥] / ___ #        (word-final devoicing)
   /r/ → [ɾ]  / V ___ V      (intervocalic tapping — lenition)
   /r/ → [r]  elsewhere

RULE INTERACTION: the two conditioned rules never compete. Tapping requires a vowel AFTER the rhotic; devoicing requires a word boundary after it. Both can never be satisfied at once, so no ordering is required.

WHY THE RULES MAKE SENSE:
• Final devoicing is extremely common cross-linguistically — voicing is hard to sustain at the end of an utterance.
• Trill → tap between vowels is LENITION, the same weakening seen in English /t/ → [ɾ].
notes.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

notes.title: Farsi Classwork — Data and the Problem
notes.body:
SOURCE: ANTH 4 phonology classwork, question 3. Farsi is an Indo-Iranian language widely spoken in Iran.
FOCUS SOUNDS: [r] (voiced alveolar trill), [ɾ] (alveolar tap/flap), [r̥] (voiceless alveolar trill).

DATA:
[qædri] 'a little bit'      [hærntowr̥] 'however'     [beɾid] 'go'
[rah] 'road'               [tʃar̥] 'four'            [biɾæŋg] 'pale'
[ris] 'beard'              [tʃedʒur̥] 'what kind'     [tʃeɾa] 'why'
[ruz] 'day'                [ʃir̥] 'lion'             [daɾid] 'you have'

THE QUESTION:
Do [r], [ɾ], and [r̥] belong to one, two, or three different phonemes?
• If they belong to different phonemes, give the minimal pairs that show this.
• If they are allophones of one (or two) phonemes, state the rule for their distribution. Which one would you choose to represent the phonemic form, and why?
notes.source: [ANTH 4 Phonology classwork: Farsi [r]/[ɾ]/[r̥] problem]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS - Phonological Analysis Practice
notes.body:
★ MEMORIZE THE 6 STEPS: identify sounds → look for minimal pairs → list environments (overlap?) → generalize with natural classes → pick the wider-distribution sound as the phoneme → write the rule.
★ No minimal pairs + no overlapping environments = COMPLEMENTARY DISTRIBUTION = allophones of ONE phoneme.
★ Minimal pair found = CONTRASTIVE DISTRIBUTION = separate phonemes. In the Italian data the minimal pairs are vowel contrasts: /i/~/ɛ/ and /u/~/a/.
★ The environment list is the whole game - write each sound's environment as _preceding__following_ and compare columns.
★ Generalize with NATURAL CLASSES, not individual segments: [g] and [k] → 'velar stops'.
★ The UNDERLYING phoneme is the one with the WIDER distribution; the restricted allophone is the one your rule derives.
★ Rule format: /underlying/ → [allophone] / ____ environment. Here: /n/ → [ŋ] / ____ velar stops.
★ Name the process when you can - this one is PLACE OF ARTICULATION ASSIMILATION (alveolar nasal → velar nasal before a velar stop).
★ Watch the rule's direction: the environment goes on the side where the trigger actually sits (here, AFTER the nasal).
notes.source: [Language Files, Ch. 3, Exercise 25: Standard Italian - instructor walkthrough & answer key]

notes.title: Standard Italian Exercise - Part 2 Walkthrough ([n] vs. [ŋ])
notes.body:
STEP 1 - IDENTIFY THE SOUNDS: [n] and [ŋ].

STEP 2 - MINIMAL PAIRS?
• With [n] and [ŋ] there are NO minimal pairs. They are therefore not in contrastive distribution, so we can assume complementary distribution - confirmed in Step 3.

STEP 3 - LIST THE ENVIRONMENTS:
   [n]              [ŋ]
   i__t             i__g
   ɛ__d             ɛ__g
   a__t             u__g
   #__e             a__k
   ɛ__t             a__k
   o__e             a__g
• None of these environments overlap, so they are indeed in COMPLEMENTARY DISTRIBUTION (as predicted from Step 2).

STEP 4 - GENERALIZE WITH NATURAL CLASSES:
• Nothing jumps out at first. Both can follow vowels (or a word boundary, for [n]); both can be followed by consonants (and [n] by vowels too).
• But looking at WHICH consonants follow each: only [g] and [k] follow [ŋ]. [n] can be followed by [t], [d], or the vowel [e].
• [g] and [k] are both VELAR STOPS ([g] voiced, [k] voiceless). So:
     [n]: __t, __d, __e        [ŋ]: __ (velar stops)
• Note: even if you collapse [t] and [d] into 'alveolar stops', you still have to stipulate the __e environment, so [n] still has more environments.

STEP 5 - DETERMINE THE UNDERLYING SOUND:
• [n] appears in 3 environments (or 2 if you collapse [t]/[d]); [ŋ] appears in only 1.
• [n] has the WIDER DISTRIBUTION and is therefore the underlying sound (phoneme).
     /n/ = phoneme;  [n] and [ŋ] = allophones
• Standard Italian has one phoneme /n/ realized phonetically as either [n] or [ŋ] depending on environment.

STEP 6 - WRITE THE RULE:
     /n/ → [ŋ] / ____ velar stops
• This makes sense: the alveolar nasal /n/ is realized as the velar nasal [ŋ] when it precedes a velar stop ([g] and [k]). This is an instance of PLACE OF ARTICULATION ASSIMILATION.

ANSWERS TO THE STATED QUESTIONS:
i. [ŋ] appears before [g] and [k], both velar stops - a natural class. [n] appears everywhere else.
ii. These sounds are in COMPLEMENTARY distribution; none of the environments overlap.
notes.source: [Language Files, Ch. 3, Exercise 25: Standard Italian - instructor walkthrough & answer key]

notes.title: Standard Italian Exercise - Data and Part 1 (Minimal Pairs)
notes.body:
SOURCE: Language Files, Ch. 3, Exercise 25. Standard Italian, an Indo-European language of the Romance family.

DATA:
a. [tinta] 'dye'          e. [ʤɛnte] 'people'     i. [fuŋgo] 'mushroom'
b. [tɛnda] 'tent'         f. [sapone] 'soap'       j. [bjaŋka] 'white'
c. [dantsa] 'dance'       g. [tiŋgo] 'I dye'       k. [aŋke] 'also'
d. [neɾo] 'black'         h. [tɛŋgo] 'I keep'      l. [faŋgo] 'mud'

PART 1 - ARE THERE ANY MINIMAL PAIRS?
• Yes. Looking at the data without focusing on any particular sound, (g) and (h) form a minimal pair, and (i) and (l) do also.
• Both pairs are exactly identical EXCEPT for the middle vowel sound.
• This tells us those vowels are in CONTRASTIVE distribution and are allophones of DIFFERENT phonemes.
• From (g) and (h): /i/ and /ɛ/
• From (i) and (l): /u/ and /a/
notes.source: [Language Files, Ch. 3, Exercise 25: Standard Italian - instructor walkthrough & answer key]

notes.title: Steps for Solving Phonology Problems
notes.body:
Step 1: Identify the sounds you are investigating.
Step 2: Identify any minimal pairs. (If there are some, what are they? If there are none, move to Step 3.)
Step 3: List the environments for each sound. Do any environments overlap? If not, they are in complementary distribution.
Step 4: Make generalizations (using natural classes) about the environments in which each sound appears.
Step 5: Determine which is the underlying sound (the phoneme) - that is, which has the wider distribution?
Step 6: Write a rule for the data.
notes.source: [Language Files, Ch. 3, Exercise 25: Standard Italian - instructor walkthrough & answer key]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS - Phonology Lecture
notes.body:
★ PHONETICS = physical properties of speech sounds. PHONOLOGY = psychological/mental properties - how sounds are stored, categorized, and structured in the mind.
★ MINIMAL PAIR = one sound different, meaning changes (pat/bat) → proves the sounds are CONTRASTIVE → they are separate PHONEMES.
★ PHONEME = abstract, psychological, LEARNED category. ALLOPHONE = the actual physical realization of that phoneme.
★ Babies perceive ALL human speech sounds, then narrow to the ambient language; this narrowing is why foreign accents happen and why new sounds get harder with age.
★ pie [pʰaɪ] vs. spy [spaɪ]: phonetically DIFFERENT, phonologically the SAME. sty vs. spy: different on BOTH counts.
★ ASPIRATION IS NOT DISTINCTIVE IN ENGLISH - it never changes meaning. A feature is 'distinctive' only if changing it can change meaning.
★ English aspiration rule: [pʰ]/[tʰ] word-initially; [p]/[t] after [s]. Mutually exclusive → COMPLEMENTARY DISTRIBUTION → PREDICTABLE.
★ CONTRASTIVE = minimal pairs / identical environments → different phonemes → NOT predictable, must be memorized.
★ FREE VARIATION = same environment, either variant, no meaning change (leap [lip] ~ [lip̚]). Only conclude this when you SEE the ~ and two same-meaning variants.
★ BRACKETS: / / = broad/phonemic (phonemes); [ ] = narrow/phonetic (allophones). Expect a question on this.
★ SIX PROCESSES: assimilation (more similar), dissimilation (more different: surprise, February), lenition (weaker: /t/→[ɾ]), metathesis (swap: Wednesday), elision (delete: laboratory), epenthesis (add: Chlowe).
★ PHONOTACTIC CONSTRAINTS = language-specific limits on sound combinations (English *bming; Persian inserts a vowel: berim, kilid, felan).
★ SYLLABLE = ONSET + NUCLEUS + CODA; know how to parse patterns from V up to CCCVCCC.
★ Count SOUNDS, not letters: cough = 3 phonemes, ringing = 5.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Phonotactics and Syllable Structure
notes.body:
WHAT ARE PHONOTACTIC CONSTRAINTS?
• Phonotactic constraints are restrictions on possible combinations of sounds.
• In English you can't use just any two consonants at word onset:
   bring vs. *bming | clean vs. *cgean | fly vs. *fvy
• In Persian, on the other hand, you need a vowel between those consonants:
   berim 'let's go' | kilid 'key' | felan 'something/somebody'

COMMON SYLLABLE PATTERNS IN ENGLISH:
• V - a /ə/
• VC - add /æd/
• VCC - ask /æsk/
• VCCC - asked /æskt/
• CV - go /goʊ/
• CVC - bot /bɑt/
• CVCC - camp /kæmp/
• CVCCC - camps /kæmps/
• CCV - flew /flu/
• CCVC - flute /flut/
• CCVCC - flutes /fluts/
• CCVCCC - crafts /kɹæfts/
• CCCV - spree /spɹi/
• CCCVC - scream /skɹim/
• CCCVCC - screams /skɹimz/
• CCCVCCC - strengths /stɹɛŋθs/

SYLLABLE STRUCTURE:
• Words are composed of one or more syllables.
• A syllable is a phonological unit composed of an ONSET, a NUCLEUS, and a CODA.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Phonological Processes
notes.body:
• ASSIMILATION: sounds next to each other become more similar.
   - ex: English nasal place assimilation
   - ex: voicing assimilation
• DISSIMILATION: sounds close together become more different.
   - ex: surprise, February
• LENITION: a sound becomes “weaker” over time.
   - ex: /t/ → /ɾ/
• METATHESIS: swapping two phonemes.
   - ex: Wednesday
• ELISION: deletion of a sound.
   - ex: laboratory
• EPENTHESIS: adding a sound.
   - ex: Chlowe
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Phonological Data Analysis
notes.body:
Looking at the distribution of physically different sounds in a data set, we can reach an analysis about the phonemic status of those sounds in that language.

ENGLISH SAMPLE DATA:
• [pʰaɪ] “pie”
• [spaɪ] “spy”
• [tʰaɪ] “tie”

CONTRASTIVE DISTRIBUTION:
• You can find minimal pairs of those sounds, OR the two sounds occur in identical environments (word position, adjacent sounds).
• This means the sounds are DIFFERENT PHONEMES.

COMPLEMENTARY DISTRIBUTION:
• Two sounds occur in mutually exclusive (non-overlapping) environments.
• This means the sounds are ALLOPHONES (variants) of one sound.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Complementary vs. Contrastive Distribution, and Free Variation
notes.body:
ALLOPHONES ARE NOT DISTINCTIVE - THEY OCCUR IN COMPLEMENTARY DISTRIBUTION:
• [pʰɪn] 'pin' / [spɪn] 'spin'; [tʰɪn] 'thin' / [stɪŋ] 'sting'.
• [pʰ] and [tʰ] occur word-initially, while [p] and [t] only occur after [s].
• This is COMPLEMENTARY DISTRIBUTION - each sound occurs in its own environment.

COMPLEMENTARY DISTRIBUTION = mutually exclusive positions in words:
• [pʰ]: pat [pʰæt], pool [pʰul], peak [pʰik] → WORD-INITIAL
• [p]: spat [spæt], spool [spul], speak [spik] → AFTER [s]

PREDICTABILITY:
• Allophones in complementary distribution are PREDICTABLE.
• We can predict [pʰ] (and never [p]) at the beginning of words in English.
• We can predict [p] (and never [pʰ]) after [s].

CONTRASTIVE DISTRIBUTION:
• Phonemes occur in contrastive distribution - a change in phoneme creates a word-meaning contrast (/pil/ 'peel' vs. /dil/ 'deal').
• Phonemes are NOT predictable - you have to memorize which phonemes occur in which words (the sound-meaning connection).

FREE VARIATION:
• In some environments, more than one allophone is possible.
• The final /p/ in “lip” can be unreleased (lips stay closed) or released.
• These different sounds do not change the meaning, but they are also NOT predictable.
• i.e. [p] and [p̚]: leap [lip] ~ [lip̚]; soap [sop] ~ [sop̚].
• They are in free variation and NOT separate phonemes, because word meaning does not change.
• ⚠ Free variation is usually indicated with a ~ meaning both variants occur. WHEN IN DOUBT, do not assume this is the solution unless you see that symbol and two variants meaning the same thing.

NOTE ON BRACKETS:
• / / are used for phonological/broad transcription and for PHONEMES.
• [ ] are used for phonetic/narrow transcription and ALLOPHONES.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Phonemes vs. Allophones, Aspiration, and Distinctiveness
notes.body:
PHONEMES VS. ALLOPHONES:
• Phonemes are abstract, psychological sound CATEGORIES.
• Allophones are the different REALIZATIONS of phonemes.
• In phonology we analyze a set of words in a language to discover how physically different sounds are organized into phonemes for that language.

THE PIE / SPY EXAMPLE:
• pie /paɪ/ - there is a puff of air when the bilabial stop is released. This is ASPIRATION (an aspirated stop), written with a superscript h: [pʰaɪ].
• spy /spaɪ/ - there is NO puff of air on release. This is an UNASPIRATED stop, written with no superscript h: [spaɪ].
• So the stops in “pie” and “spy” are phonetically DIFFERENT but phonologically the SAME.
• Contrast: the consonants in “sty” and “spy” are phonetically different AND phonologically different (different phonemes).

DISTINCTIVENESS:
• A phonetic characteristic is DISTINCTIVE when it can cause a change in meaning in the language.
• Aspiration is NOT distinctive in English, because making a stop aspirated or unaspirated does not change the meaning of the word.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Why Phonemes Are 'Psychological' and 'Learned'
notes.body:
BABIES:
• Babies are able to produce and perceive all of the sounds of all human languages.
• But they quickly learn which sounds are important in the language around them.
• They also learn to IGNORE the differences that don't matter in the ambient speech.
• The older we get, the harder it becomes to learn the sounds of a different language - we have learned the phonological patterns of our native language.

FOREIGN ACCENTS:
• Languages each have a unique set of speech sounds.
• A foreign accent occurs when we try to speak a foreign language using the sounds from our NATIVE language.
• When we encounter a speech sound outside our native set, it may be hard to even 'hear' the sound.
• We often hear/produce it by finding the sound in our native set that comes closest.

BIG PICTURE:
• We have trouble with sounds that don't exist in the language(s) we learned as a child.
• Phonology explores how sounds are organized in our brain - which makes speaking our native language efficient and easy, but makes a foreign language much harder.

PHONOLOGICAL KNOWLEDGE:
• Languages differ in the way they group speech sounds into categories.
• That means they differ in which physical details they pay attention to and which they ignore.
• This is language-specific information all speakers of that language share.
• NOTE: foreign accents and second-language perception difficulties are caused in large part by phonological differences between the languages involved.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Minimal Pairs and the Phoneme
notes.body:
SIMPLE ENGLISH EXAMPLE - “pat” vs. “bat”:
• Do these mean different things in English? Yes.
• They are MINIMAL PAIRS - a difference in one sound and the meaning changes.
• Minimal pairs tell us these sounds are CONTRASTIVE - they create meaningful contrast in the language.
• So for speakers of English, /p/ and /b/ are different PHONEMES.

MINIMAL PAIRS AS A DISCOVERY TOOL:
• We can identify the phonemes in a language by locating minimal pairs.
• Minimal pairs are words in which a change in only one sound creates a difference in meaning.
• /pil/ 'peel', /dil/ 'deal', /fil/ 'feel'… thus /p/, /d/, and /f/ are all different phonemes in English.

WHAT IS A PHONEME?
• A phoneme is an ABSTRACT unit of sound that creates meaning in a language.
• Phonemes are PSYCHOLOGICAL - physically different sounds can belong to the same phoneme.
• Phonemes are LEARNED - your brain categorizes all the different sounds into a small set of language-specific phonemes, acquired through experience.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Phonetics vs. Phonology
notes.body:
PHONETICS
• The study of the PHYSICAL properties of speech sounds.

PHONOLOGY
• The study of the PSYCHOLOGICAL properties of speech sounds.
• The study of the representations and systematic structuring of sounds in a language.
• How sounds are represented in the mind.
• Which sounds are significant enough to signal a difference in meaning in a language…
• …versus which sounds might be physically different but do NOT make different words in that language.
• Phonology is the study of speech sounds as mental/psychological objects: how they are categorized, how they are represented, and how they interact when combined.
• Phonological knowledge is a component of GRAMMATICAL knowledge and is shared by all speakers of a language.

NOTE FROM SLIDE: knowing a language means, in part, knowing its phonology.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Concepts to Know - Phonology (roadmap)
notes.body:
The lecture listed these as the concepts to master for this unit:
• Phonology vs. Phonetics
• Minimal pairs
• Phonemes vs. allophones
• Complementary vs. contrastive distribution
• …versus free variation
• Phonological analysis
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: Phonetics Review (lead-in to Phonology)
notes.body:
TRANSCRIPTION:
• The IPA for all American English sounds.

ARTICULATORY DESCRIPTIONS:
• CONSONANTS described by three things: place of articulation, manner of articulation, voicing.
• VOWELS described by three things: tongue height, tongue backness, lip rounding.

WARM-UP CHECKS FROM LECTURE:
• Alveolar example: /z/ (compare /f/ labiodental, /g/ velar, /u/ a vowel).
• Bilabial: /b/, /m/, and /p/ are all bilabial.
• Count PHONEMES not letters: “cough” = 3 (/k/ /ɔ/ /f/); “ringing” = 5 (/ɹ/ /ɪ/ /ŋ/ /ɪ/ /ŋ/).
• Vowel chart practice: high front unrounded = /i/; low back unrounded = /ɑ/; the vowel in “bat” = /æ/; the initial vowel in “about” = /ə/ (schwa).
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonology (adapted from Dr. Georgia Zellou)]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS - Video Lecture 1 (additions beyond the slides)
notes.body:
★ Grammaticality is judged DESCRIPTIVELY - can speakers understand/produce it? - NOT by prescriptive rules; "ain't" is grammatical in its variety.
★ No one "decides" language: rules emerge by community consensus; dictionaries/teachers/linguists DESCRIBE, they don't create.
★ ICON = resembles its meaning (emoji, pictographic road sign); ARBITRARY SIGN = conventional, no inherent link (most words, traffic-light colors, wedding ring).
★ Speech/sign is PRIMARY & ancient (~50k yrs); writing is SECONDARY & recent (~4-5k yrs) and must be taught. No writing system does NOT mean "not a language."
★ Children ACQUIRE a first language implicitly; there's nothing ethnic/inherited about it (being of Danish ancestry doesn't make Danish easier).
★ Register = formality level; STYLE SHIFTING = moving between registers by context.
★ Historical linguistics: PROTO-INDO-EUROPEAN (~5-10k yrs) is the shared ancestor of English, German, Spanish, Italian, Russian, and more.
★ De jure (by law) vs. de facto (in practice) - the lecture's U.S. official-language example.
★ Subfields spotlighted: sociolinguistics (language in social context), computational linguistics/NLP (e.g., Siri), applied linguistics (language teaching), psycholinguistics (acquisition/processing).
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Video Lecture 1 (parts 1-2): What Is Language & Linguistics?]

notes.title: Video Lecture Notes - Language, Identity & Modality (Part 2)
notes.body:
Language is an expression of SOCIAL IDENTITY:
• Regional variation: diaper (US) vs. nappy (UK), elevator vs. lift, "y'all" (US South), the Boston/New England "pahk the cah" pronunciation.
• Registers = levels of formality; moving between them = STYLE SHIFTING (lecture voice vs. friends).
• Regional dialects (California vs. New York vs. Australia) vs. SOCIAL dialects (African American English, Chicano English) - social dialects track social group more than geography.

Modality - spoken/signed is PRIMARY:
• Sign languages are just as valid as spoken languages.
• Speech/sign ~50,000 years old; WRITING only ~4,000-5,000 years old. Many languages have no writing system and are still full languages.
• Children ACQUIRE speech/sign implicitly (no explicit teaching); writing must be explicitly taught (holding a pencil, sound-symbol mapping).

Other points:
• Icons vs. arbitrary signs: an icon resembles its meaning (emoji, road signs); most words + traffic-light colors + wedding rings are arbitrary conventions.
• De jure vs. de facto: the lecture noted the U.S. has historically had no federal de jure official language, with English used de facto.
• Historical linguistics example: Proto-Indo-European (~5-10k yrs ago) diverged into English, German, Spanish, Italian, Russian, etc.
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Video Lecture 1 (parts 1-2): What Is Language & Linguistics?]

notes.title: Video Lecture Notes - Empiricism, Objectivity & Grammaticality (Part 1)
notes.body:
• Linguistics is a SOCIAL SCIENCE built on empiricism: conclusions derive from OBSERVATION of real-world language, treated as data to be analyzed.
• "Objectivity" is the goal (setting aside personal bias), but the instructor stressed it's a touchy ideal that can itself be a FALLACY - revisited later in the course.
• Grammar (linguistic sense) = language STRUCTURE + language USE, not a set of do's and don'ts.
• How linguists judge grammaticality: DESCRIPTIVELY. If speakers of a variety understand/produce a form, it's grammatical. "Ain't" is grammatical in varieties that use it; "me drive the car" is ungrammatical. Linguists avoid "incorrect" because it carries judgment.
• Who decides the rules? NO ONE. Rules emerge through interaction and consensus in a community over time. Dictionary writers and teachers REFLECT rules; they don't invent them. Individuals can encourage change (e.g., using "themselves" as a generic) but can't unilaterally change the shared code.
• Prescriptive rules aren't needed for communication and are easily forgotten; descriptive rules ARE how we communicate and (in a first language) aren't forgotten.
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Video Lecture 1 (parts 1-2): What Is Language & Linguistics?]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Phonetics Lecture
notes.body:
★ PHONETICS = the scientific study of speech sounds/gestures; the minimal units of language. THREE SUBFIELDS: articulatory (production), acoustic (transmission), auditory/perceptual (reception).
★ ~600 vowels + ~200 consonants exist worldwide (Ladefoged 2004); each language uses only a small subset.
★ SEGMENTS (vowels, consonants) vs. SUPRASEGMENTALS (stress, tone, intonation, length).
★ ORTHOGRAPHY IS UNRELIABLE — know an example of each failure: many spellings for one sound (18 for 'he'), one spelling many sounds (car/cell/cello), silent letters (debt, Wednesday), letterless sounds (colonel, soldier). GHOTI = fish (enouGH, wOmen, naTIon).
★ IPA created in 1888 to represent the sounds of all languages — write and read any language.
★ CONSONANTS = airstream mechanism + place + manner (plus voicing and nasality).
★ MEMORIZE PLACES front→back: bilabial, labiodental, interdental, alveolar, (alveolar-)palatal, velar, uvular, glottal — with their example sounds.
★ MEMORIZE MANNERS: stop, fricative, affricate (stop released as fricative), approximant (rhotic/lateral), liquid, glide, trill, nasal.
★ VOICELESS [p t s k] vs. VOICED [b d z g]. NASAL [m n] = velum open.
★ WEIRD SYMBOLS: /j/ yellow, /θ/ thigh, /ð/ thy, /ʒ/ rouge, /ʃ/ shy, /dʒ/ judge, /tʃ/ chair, /ŋ/ long.
★ VOWELS: little/no airflow restriction; classified by TONGUE POSITION (front/back, high/low) and LIP ROUNDING. FORMANTS = frequency peaks.
★ ROUNDED /u o ʊ ɔ/; LAX /ɪ ɛ æ ə ʌ ʊ/. DIPHTHONGS: /aʊ/ ow, /aɪ/ eye, /ɔɪ/ oy — bate, bite, boat, boy.
★ LENGTH is contrastive in Finnish (/muta/ 'mud' vs. /muːta/ 'some other').
★ PHRASE TONE = end of phrase (falling = statement, rising = question). PITCH ACCENT = mid-utterance; 'I never said she stole my money' × 7.
★ TONE types: LEVEL (H, M, L) and CONTOUR (HL, LH); relative to speaker and context.
★ STRESS is a syllable property and is contrastive in English: OBject (n) vs. obJECT (v), PROduce vs. proDUCE, PRESent vs. preSENT.
★ FIVE SIGNED PARAMETERS: location, movement, handshape, orientation, non-manual markers — know one minimal pair for each (apple/onion; tough/physics; orange/color; meet/I-meet-you; hot/very hot).
★ DIACRITICS mark aspiration, length, and unreleased stops.
★ BE READY TO TRANSCRIBE BOTH WAYS — the practice list (heat, hit, fruit, thanks, scream, international, phonetic, alphabet, porcupine, ceremony, February, conscientious) is fair game.
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

notes.title: Phonetics of Signed Languages — Five Parameters
notes.body:
Signed languages have their own articulatory parameters. Minimal pairs differ in exactly one parameter.

1. PLACE / LOCATION
   • apple vs. onion
   • lucky vs. clever
2. MOVEMENT
   • tough vs. physics
   • can vs. shoes
3. HANDSHAPE
   • orange vs. color vs. wrong
   • like vs. white
4. HAND ORIENTATION
   • meet vs. I-meet-you
5. NON-MANUAL MARKERS — facial expressions or head movement
   • late vs. not yet
   • hot vs. very hot

RESOURCES USED IN LECTURE: spreadthesign.com, signingsavvy.com, handspeak.com

DIACRITICS (spoken-language detail marks covered alongside):
• Aspiration
• Length
• Unreleased
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

notes.title: Suprasegmentals: Length, Intonation, Tone, and Stress
notes.body:
LENGTH:
• Speech sounds can differ in length; best understood RELATIVE to speech rate in a particular context.
• In some languages a difference in length creates a difference in meaning. FINNISH:
   'mud' /muta/ vs. 'some other' /muːta/
   'come!' /tule/ vs. 'comes' /tuleː/ vs. 'is windy' /tuːleː/

INTONATION:
• The pattern of pitch movement across an utterance.
• PHRASE TONE — a change in fundamental frequency at the END of a phrase.
• PITCH ACCENT — a MID-utterance change in fundamental frequency.

PHRASE TONE:
• 'You want black coffee or black tea' — read with different intonations.
• Statements typically get a FALLING phrase tone at the end.
• Questions typically get a RISING phrase tone at the end.
• Phrase tone also marks phrasal boundaries.

PITCH ACCENT — seven readings, seven meanings:
• I never said she stole my money.
• I NEVER said she stole my money.
• I never SAID she stole my money.
• I never said SHE stole my money.
• I never said she STOLE my money.
• I never said she stole MY money.
• I never said she stole my MONEY.

TONE:
• The pitch of a single word that creates a meaning distinction.
• LEVEL TONE: High, Mid, Low.
• CONTOUR TONE: High-Low, Low-High, etc.
• Tones are relative to the pitch of the speaker and the linguistic context. (Cantonese six-tone example shown in class.)

STRESS:
• Mostly a property of SYLLABLES.
• Stressed syllables can be longer, louder, and have fuller vowels.
• In many languages including English, stress creates SEMANTIC distinctions:
   object /ˈɒbʤɛkt/ (noun) vs. object /əbˈʤɛkt/ (verb)
   produce /ˈproʊdus/ vs. produce /prəˈdus/
   present /ˈprɛzənt/ vs. present /priˈzɛnt/
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

notes.body:
From the lecture's practice slides — cover one column and work the other direction.

notes.title: Vowels
notes.body:
• Vowels are produced with little to no restriction of the airflow.
• The QUALITY of a vowel depends on the shape of the vocal tract.
• Vowels are made up of a wide range of frequencies. Where frequencies peak, we have FORMANTS.

CLASSIFICATION — TWO FEATURES:
• POSITION OF THE TONGUE: back vs. front; open vs. close (low vs. high)
• LIP SHAPE: rounded vs. unrounded

ENGLISH VOWEL FACTS FROM THE DECK:
• ROUNDED: /u/, /o/, /ʊ/, /ɔ/. Unrounded: all the rest.
• LAX: /ɪ/, /ɛ/, /æ/, /ə/, /ʌ/, /ʊ/
• Chart axes: front — central — back; high — mid — low

DIPHTHONGS:
• The vowels seen so far were MONOPHTHONGS (single vowels).
• A DIPHTHONG is a sequence of two vowels together — 'two vowels for the price of one':
   bate [beɪt] | bite [baɪt] | boat [boʊt] | boy [bɔɪt]
• Quick keys: /aʊ/ = ow, /aɪ/ = eye, /ɔɪ/ = oy
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

notes.title: Articulatory Phonetics and Consonant Classification
notes.body:
THE ART IN ARTICULATION:
• The human vocal tract is like a musical instrument — growing up, we all learned how to play it.
• Producing speech sounds requires complex manipulation of: airflow through the mouth/nose, the shape of the mouth, the lips, the tongue, and more.

CONSONANTS ARE CLASSIFIED BY THREE FEATURES:
1. AIRSTREAM MECHANISM — the airstream may be initiated by the diaphragm/lungs (PULMONIC) or not.
2. PLACE OF ARTICULATION — WHERE the airstream is restricted in the mouth.
3. MANNER OF ARTICULATION — HOW the airstream is manipulated.

PLACES OF ARTICULATION (front → back):
• BILABIAL — both lips together: [p], [b], [m]
• LABIODENTAL — bottom lip to teeth: [f], [v]
• INTERDENTAL — tongue between teeth: [θ], [ð]
• ALVEOLAR — tongue touches the alveolar ridge: [t], [d], [s], [z], [n], [l], [ɹ]
• ALVEOLAR-PALATAL / POST-ALVEOLAR
• PALATAL — front of tongue to the palate: [ʃ], [j]
• VELAR — back of tongue to the velum: [k], [g]
• UVULAR — back of tongue to the uvula: [ʀ], [q], [ɢ] (not in English)
• GLOTTAL — air through an open glottis, or stopped and released there: [h], [ʔ]

VOICING AND NASALITY:
• VOICING — whether the vocal cords vibrate. Voiceless: [p], [t], [s], [k]. Voiced: [b], [d], [z], [g].
• NASAL/ORAL — whether the velum is open and air goes through the nose. Nasal: [m], [n]. Oral: [p], [t].

MANNERS OF ARTICULATION:
• STOP — full closure in the mouth; stopping and releasing the airflow: [p], [b]
• FRICATIVE — small opening creating turbulence/frication: [f], [v]
• AFFRICATE — a stop released as a fricative: [t͡ʃ], [d͡ʒ]
• APPROXIMANT — includes RHOTIC (r-like) and LATERAL (air flows along the sides of the mouth/tongue)
• LIQUID — obstruction, but not as much as a fricative: [l], [ɹ]
• GLIDE — minimal obstruction, very vowel-like; movement from one position to another
• TRILL — rapid vibrations of the articulator
• NASAL — oral closure, air comes out the nasal cavity

WEIRD SYMBOLS TO MEMORIZE:
/j/ = yellow | /θ/ = thigh | /ð/ = thy | /ʒ/ = rouge | /ʃ/ = shy | /dʒ/ = judge | /tʃ/ = chair | /ŋ/ = long
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

notes.title: Orthography and Why We Need the IPA
notes.body:
WRITING SYSTEMS DO NOT REPRESENT SOUNDS ACCURATELY.

THE SAME SOUND CAN HAVE SEVERAL SPELLINGS:
• he, believe, Caesar, see, people, seize, sea, amoeba, machine — 18 ways
• too, true, shoe, flew, through

THE SAME SPELLING MAY CORRESPOND TO DIFFERENT SOUNDS:
• father, want, many, bad, fame
• car, cell, cello, suspicion

SOME LETTERS CORRESPOND TO NO SOUNDS:
• psychology, debt, knot, Wednesday, receipt, thought, foreign, Worcester

SOME SOUNDS CORRESPOND TO NO LETTERS:
• colonel, soldier

DIFFERENT WRITING SYSTEMS MASK SIMILARITIES:
• cake / کیک / ケーキ — same word, three scripts

GHOTI = 'fish':
• GH as in enouGH, O as in wOmen, TI as in naTIon

THE INTERNATIONAL PHONETIC ALPHABET:
• In 1888, linguists set out to create the IPA.
• Developed to represent the (fundamental) sounds of ALL languages.
• Using the IPA, a linguist can write down the words of any language, and can read a word in any language.
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

notes.title: Speech Sounds, Phonetics, and Its Subfields
notes.body:
SPEECH SOUNDS IN WORLD LANGUAGES:
• There are thousands of possible speech sounds.
• Around 600 VOWELS and 200 CONSONANTS across the world's languages (Ladefoged, 2004, p. 179).
• Each language only uses a small SUBSET of these to create its words.

PHONETICS:
• The scientific study of speech sounds or gestures.
• The study of the minimal units that make up language.

THREE MAIN SUBFIELDS:
• ARTICULATORY PHONETICS — speech production
• ACOUSTIC PHONETICS — physical transmission of speech sounds
• AUDITORY PHONETICS — speech reception and perception (textbook label: perceptual phonetics)

TWO BROAD TYPES OF SPEECH SOUNDS:
• SEGMENTS — discrete units of sound appearing one after another (vowels, consonants)
• SUPRASEGMENTALS — sound properties laid on top of and across segments (stress, tone, intonation)
notes.source: [Brotherton, HUM/ANTH 4 Lecture: Phonetics (adapted from Drs. Georgia Zellou & Masoud Jasbi)]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Video Lecture Additions (Week 2)
notes.body:
★ The HAVRE, MONTANA case: Spanish-speaking US citizens ID'd by Border Patrol who cited their Spanish, not race. Linguistic profiling fused with racial profiling; they sued and won a settlement.
★ Baugh's original definition was AUDIO-ONLY; the Montana case extends profiling to face-to-face encounters.
★ English-only ideology is powerful despite Spanish being the second most spoken US language.
★ INCLUSIVE LANGUAGE IDEOLOGY: people choose their own labels and pronouns; includes coming-out narratives, umbrella vs. specific identity terms, and the Latinx debate.
★ REACTIONARY IDEOLOGY: 'I don't have pronouns', objections to singular they, 'Don't Say Gay' laws.
★ SINGULAR THEY is centuries old and uncontroversial in 'a student left their bag' — the objection is ideological.
★ LANGUAGE AS PROXY for race/class discrimination: 'she didn't sound educated' is socially tolerated where naming race is not.
★ PATHOLOGIZING DIALECT: non-standard speakers wrongly referred to speech-language pathology.
★ LINGUISTIC INSECURITY (Preston): Americans doubt their own English because 'we didn't invent English'.
★ MIDLAND is the dialect region Americans broadly call 'normal' / accent-free.
★ Appalachian English is stigmatized via the classist 'white trash' persona — the judgment is social, not linguistic.
★ CREAKY VOICE is near-universal; the Valley Girl association is stereotype. 'Like' is a DISCOURSE MARKER, not a defect.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

notes.title: Video Lecture Additions — Ideologies, Inclusive Language, and Reactionary Response
notes.body:
LANGUAGE IDEOLOGIES VS. ATTITUDES:
• Thinking Italian sounds nice and German sounds harsh is an individual ATTITUDE.
• Ideologies are broader and community-held: 'who/whom', 'only standardized English in the classroom', 'only English in public in the US'.
• For the purposes of this class, language attitudes and language ideologies are treated as the same.

SPANISH IN THE US: Spanish is the second most widely spoken language in the US; the instructor notes the US has among the largest Spanish-speaking populations of any country. Despite this, the English-only ideology drives viral harassment incidents.

INCLUSIVE LANGUAGE (instructor's dissertation area):
• Student activists in LGBTQ and feminist/women's rights communities monitor their own and others' speech.
• Linguistic dimensions: coming-out narratives as a genre (with guides for how to come out to family), pronouns, and identity labels — umbrella terms (gay, queer) versus specific terms (pansexual, demisexual).
• Ongoing debate over whether Latinx is inclusive.

REACTIONARY IDEOLOGIES (reaction against progress):
• 'I don't have pronouns' — nearly everyone prefers particular third-person pronouns; the claim signals disagreement with inclusive ideologies rather than a fact about the speaker. Such speakers are typically still offended if the 'wrong' pronouns are used.
• 'Singular they is grammatically incorrect' — but speakers have used it for hundreds of years, e.g. 'a student left their bag in the classroom', which is uncontroversial. Objection arises because it is associated with LGBTQ rights.

DESCRIPTIVISM REMINDER: linguists describe how people actually use language. The instructor notes finding terms like 'grammar police' / 'grammar Nazis' objectionable.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

notes.title: Video Lecture Additions — Linguistic Profiling in Practice (Havre, Montana)
notes.body:
CASE: Two US citizens in a convenience store in Havre, Montana, buying milk and eggs, were asked for identification by a Border Patrol agent.
• On video, the agent states the reason is that he heard them speaking Spanish, which he claims is unusual there. He explicitly denies it is racial profiling.
• Border Patrol has authority within roughly 100 miles of a border; Montana falls within 100 miles of the Canadian border.
• The women sued the Border Patrol for discrimination and reportedly received a substantial settlement from the federal government.

ANALYSIS POINTS RAISED IN LECTURE:
• The agent connects speaking Spanish in public with assumed legal status, which is in turn associated with ethnicity — basing suspicion of criminality on how someone speaks.
• There are in fact plenty of Spanish speakers in Montana; the premise is also factually weak.
• Baugh originally conceived linguistic profiling as AUDIO-ONLY (e.g. over the phone, where the listener cannot see the speaker). This case shows it also occurs face to face, combining with RACIAL profiling.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS POSED: What language ideology does the agent hold? Is this an example of linguistic profiling?
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Week 2 Video Lecture: Language and Power (parts 1-5)]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Week 2: Language and Power
notes.body:
★ LANGUAGE IDEOLOGY = community-level beliefs about who should speak what, where — always tied to POWER. 'Language attitudes' is treated as equivalent in this course (attitudes skew individual).
★ THE BIG TAKEAWAY: no variety is linguistically better than another. All are complex, logical, rule-governed. Standardized English's status comes from power, not superiority.
★ Language varies by SOUND (British non-rhotic 'flower'), GRAMMAR (double modals 'might could'), and LEXICON ('sigogglin''; soda/pop/Coke).
★ LINGUISTIC PROFILING = denial of goods/services based on how someone sounds. Associated with JOHN BAUGH.
★ BAUGH'S DESIGN: tridialectal (standard/AAVE/Chicano English), same sentence, varied ONLY intonation and prosody — 1988, five Bay Area communities. Standard guise got far more 'available' responses.
★ MATCHED GUISE: same speaker, same neutral passage, two varieties, randomized, Likert ratings; judges never realize it's one speaker. Developed by Giles & Lambert (Canadian French).
★ STATUS variables = educated, intelligent, attractive → lower-status guise rated LOWER. SOLIDARITY variables = friendly, helpful, trustworthy → lower-status guise rated HIGHER. Know this reversal.
★ MENGESHA (2015, UCD): bidialectal African American student, same weather report, grammar and duration identical, only phonology/intonation changed; teachers primed with a KDVS radio employability frame.
★ ACCENT HALLUCINATION (Rubin 1992) = hearing a feature that isn't there, via top-down processing. Examples: 'too many slang words' and 'umms and ahhs' that didn't exist; BX hearing a nonexistent stutter and calling the speaker 'heavy set'.
★ The UCD speaker was a concert pianist and Sociology major — reading was identical across guises, so the judgments measured attitudes toward AAVE, not literacy.
★ CONSEQUENCE TO REMEMBER: non-standard dialects get PATHOLOGIZED — students referred to speech-language pathology for speaking a dialect.
★ SEMANTIC SHIFT: gay (happy → immoral woman → homosexual → 'hopeless'); girl (child of either gender → unmarried girl → sweetheart → sex worker); harlot; hussy; tongzhi ('comrade' → gay community). Terms for women drift toward sexual derogation.
★ RECLAMATION: queer went weird → slur → reclaimed in the 1980s-90s → now academic/activist usage, with a generational split.
★ DESCRIPTIVISM (linguists describe) vs. PRESCRIPTIVISM (telling people how to speak). 'Like' = DISCOURSE MARKER descriptively, 'filler word' prescriptively.
★ CREAKY VOICE is used by nearly everyone, roughly equally across genders — the Valley Girl stereotype is an ideology, not a fact.
★ SINGULAR THEY has centuries of uncontroversial use ('a student left their bag'); objections are ideological reactions, not grammar.
★ PERCEPTUAL DIALECTOLOGY (Dennis Preston): people circle the South and NYC as 'bad' English and the MIDLAND Midwest as 'normal' — even Southerners do.
★ LANGUAGE AS PROXY: criticizing speech is a socially acceptable stand-in for race, class, and regional discrimination.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

notes.title: Perceptual Dialectology, Regional Clips, and Wrap-Up
notes.body:
BAUGH TED TALK — group discussion questions:
• What is the distinction between racial profiling and linguistic profiling?
• Baugh's original study was 1989-90 and Rubin's was around the same time — has the situation changed? Better or worse? What's your evidence?
• Which accents of English enjoy the greatest prestige? Which are considered low prestige in California?
• Have you ever been subject to linguistic profiling? On what occasion?

REGIONAL LISTENING EXCERPTS — rate each speaker: smart? educated? friendly? attractive? helpful?
• Boston accent — a Medford city councilor discussing 'Carr Park'.
• Carolina Brogue — Outer Banks of North Carolina; speakers discuss 'dingbatter' for an outsider.
• Mountain Talk / Appalachian English — western North Carolina; 'poke' for a paper bag, 'over yonder'.
• NOTE: the Outer Banks and Appalachian speakers are both from North Carolina, at opposite ends of one state — variation within a single state.

PERCEPTUAL DIALECTOLOGY EXERCISE: draw a rough map of California, mark where you think people speak differently, and label the areas.

DENNIS PRESTON ON ATTITUDES:
• Describes a long-standing American LINGUISTIC INSECURITY — 'we didn't invent English' — in tension with American populism and a desire not to be stuffy or too correct.
• Asked people to draw on blank US maps where people speak differently, and where the most and least 'correct' English is spoken.
• Nine times out of ten respondents circled the US South or New York City as places where bad English is spoken.
• There is broad agreement that the Ohio/Michigan/Northern Indiana/Wisconsin/Pennsylvania zone is 'normal' English — even Southerners reach up and draw that MIDLAND area. It is treated as the broadcast target.

WHY LANGUAGE IS A PROXY:
• It is still relatively socially acceptable to say 'I didn't hire her because she didn't sound educated' — standing in for race, class, or regional origin.
• Appalachian English is widely perceived as uneducated and lower class, tied to the classist 'white trash' persona.

WRAP-UP:
• Language variation is natural — people use it to create identities.
• NO language variety is better than others. All varieties are complex and logical in different ways.
• There is nothing linguistically superior about standardized American English, Chicano English, Appalachian English, the Carolina Brogue, or African American English — the standard's status comes from POWER.
• Language ideologies can harm speakers interpersonally and institutionally — teachers treating students differently, remedial placement, law enforcement stops.
• They can also UPLIFT marginalized groups, as with inclusive language ideologies in LGBTQ communities.
• If the goal is equity, we must examine language ideologies and how they are used to uplift or marginalize.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

notes.title: Accent Hallucination
notes.body:
ACCENT HALLUCINATION (Rubin, 1992): hearing something that is not there in reality, usually stereotypically attributed; involves TOP-DOWN PROCESSING.
• Rubin's original design: the same lecture recording was played to two groups — one shown a photo of a white woman, one shown a photo of an Asian woman. The group shown the Asian face reported the speaker had an accent, though the recording was identical.

FROM THE UCD STUDY:
• GK claimed the speaker 'used too many slang words' — there were no slang words in the weather report. Slang was stereotypically attributed to AAVE.
• HT believed there were too many 'umms and ahhs' in the AA guise, where there were none.
• MOST SERIOUS — BX, a Caucasian teacher at Canyon: 'He seems to stutter, and be a little slow […] he is not the smartest cookie […] he is not that smart, because he seems stuck on words or thoughts.' BX attributed a speech impediment that did not exist. BX also said the AA guise 'sounded bigger, and heavy set' — traceable to stereotypes of African American males as tough and aggressive. On hearing the standard guise, BX said he sounds 'more intelligent, skinnier', and read the same slow pace as methodical and tactful.

WHY IT MATTERS:
• Teachers' assessments of reading comprehension were undermined simply by identifying the speaker as African American.
• The speaker's reading capability was identical in both guises, so judgments of him as less literate, slow, troubled enunciating, and a struggling reader reflect ATTITUDES TOWARD AAVE, not literacy.
• The speaker was a concert pianist and a Sociology major at UC Davis.
• REAL CONSEQUENCE: students speaking non-standard dialects are often perceived as having speech impediments and referred to speech-language pathologists — their variety is pathologized.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

notes.title: Matched Guise Experiments and the UCD Study
notes.body:
MATCHED GUISE TECHNIQUE:
• Developed by Howard Giles and Wallace Lambert in studies of attitudes toward Canadian French; Baugh's Bay Area tests were a variant.
• Bilingual or bidialectal speakers record the same, relatively neutral material in two languages or dialects believed to have different community status.
• Typically at least 8-10 speakers, randomly presented.
• Participants rank speakers on characteristics using LIKERT SCALES (e.g. 1-5): educated, intelligent, attractive, friendly, helpful, trustworthy.

CONSISTENT RESULTS:
• Lower-status guises are rated LOWER on STATUS variables (educated, intelligent, attractive) — even by judges who speak that same variety.
• Higher-status guises are rated HIGHER on status variables.
• The REVERSE holds for SOLIDARITY variables (friendly, helpful, trustworthy): lower-status guises rate higher.
• Judges are unaware they have been listening to the same speakers.

UCD MATCHED GUISE TEST — Zion Mengesha, 2015 senior honors thesis:
• Recruited a bidialectal African American student to record the same passage — a weather report — twice: once in African American phonology and intonation, once in 'standard' English.
• Grammar did not change and both recordings took exactly the same time.
• Teachers from three school types; half at each heard the AA guise, half the standard guise.

SCHOOL BACKGROUNDS:
• Canyon High School — suburban; average home $998,000; 35% white, 25% Asian, 20% Latino/a, 10% African American; California Distinguished school; 1.1% dropout rate.
• Pinewood High School — urban; average home $500,000; 40% African American, 40% Asian, 21% Latino/a, 1% white; 37% dropout rate.
• Bay Area City College — low-income and first-generation students; 26% white, 19% African American, 15% Asian, 15% Latino/a, 14% multiple, 2% Filipino.

DATA ELICITATION:
• Teachers were primed: told the speaker was interviewing for UC Davis' student-run KDVS radio station and asked to judge his employability.
• Immediately after, they rated speech 1-6 on Likert-scale opposites: educated/not educated, athletic/not athletic, friendly/unfriendly, attractive/unattractive, likely/unlikely to attend college, excitable/calm, employable/unemployable.
• RESULTS: in the AA guise the speaker was rated calmer across the board, low on education and friendliness, slightly higher on athleticism; community college instructors rated him especially low on hireability and likelihood of attending college. In the standard guise he was rated markedly more hireable, more attractive, and more educated.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

notes.title: Linguistic Profiling, Earwitness Testimony, and Baugh's Studies
notes.body:
USE OF STIGMATIZED FORMS — guiding questions:
• Who decides what the 'proper' or 'correct' version of a language is? Who decides what is standardized?
• What are the consequences for speaking a non-standard variety or using a stigmatized form (e.g. 'ain't', or 'queer')?

LINGUISTIC PROFILING: the denial of goods or services based on a person's way of speaking and the assumed characteristics of people who sound a particular way.
• Per Baugh, it has a detrimental impact on the collective quest to advance equal access to fair housing and fair lending.
• The courts are ill equipped to offer adequate legal redress to anyone who falls prey to it at the hands of housing providers, lending institutions, or insurance companies — proving it in court is very difficult.
• US federal law prohibits landlords and sellers from discriminating against tenants based on identity, and prohibits discrimination in lending.

BAUGH'S STUDY DESIGN:
• John Baugh is TRIDIALECTAL: standard American English, AAVE, and Chicano English.
• He answered newspaper ads for apartments, saying: 'Hello, I'm calling about the apartment/house you have advertised in the paper.'
• CRUCIALLY he varied only INTONATION AND PROSODY, not the grammar or the words.
• Early studies: 1988, five Bay Area communities — Palo Alto, East Palo Alto, San Francisco, Oakland, Woodside.
• RESULT: a strong correlation between whether housing was reported available and the intonation of the phrase. The standard American English guise was far more often told units were available.

EARWITNESS TESTIMONY: judging a speaker's identity by voice alone — the same assumption that makes profiling possible.

2002 NEWS SEGMENT (shown in class): Rosa Rice, an African American woman in St. Louis, was treated with hostility when calling about a room; testers from the St. Louis Equal Housing Opportunity Council called the same number — white testers were invited to appointments, African American testers were told nothing was available.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

notes.title: Descriptivism vs. Prescriptivism and Semantic Shift
notes.body:
DESCRIPTIVISM VS. PRESCRIPTIVISM:
• Linguists are (with few exceptions) DESCRIPTIVE — we describe language, we don't tell people how they should use it.
• Prescriptivists tell people how their language should sound (English teachers, self-described 'grammar nerds').
• Most people hold beliefs about how language should or shouldn't be used — these are LANGUAGE ATTITUDES.

SEMANTIC SHIFT: word meanings change over time, and the changes reflect attitudes toward social phenomena.

GAY: 1300 happy → 1825 immoral woman → 1935 homosexual → 1980s 'that's so gay' = hopeless/ridiculous.
GIRL: 1290 child of either gender → 1530 unmarried female child → 1650 sweetheart → 1711 female sex worker.
HARLOT: 1330 low fellow/knave → 1390 male servant → 1450 unchaste woman.
HUSSY: 1530 housewife → 1600s playfully rude term of address → 1700s woman of low behavior.
→ PATTERN: terms for women repeatedly drift toward derogation tied to perceived sexual promiscuity.

QUEER: originally 'weird' → became a slur for non-normative sexuality → reclaimed in the 1980s-90s by the community → now associated with academia (queer studies, queer theory) and activism, and the Q in LGBTQ. Generational difference: some gay people in their 50s-60s still hear it as offensive.

TONGZHI (Chinese, Hong Kong): originally 'comrade' tied to the Communist revolution; taken up in the 1990s to refer to the gay community.

DISCUSSION PROMPT: what other examples of semantic shift can you think of, and how do they relate to language attitudes?
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

notes.title: Language Ideologies
notes.body:
DEFINITION: beliefs/attitudes beyond the individual level concerning what types of languages should be spoken, by whom, and in which contexts. All are related to POWER.
• An individual preference ('Italian sounds nice, German sounds harsh') is an ATTITUDE. Ideologies are broader and community-held. For this class the two terms are treated as equivalent.

CORE EXAMPLES:
• PRESCRIPTIVISM, especially in school — being corrected by a teacher for not speaking 'proper English'; the ideology that standardized American English following prescriptive rules is what belongs in classrooms.
• 'African American English is improper English' — it is not; it is a different variety. This links language ideology to RACE.
• 'Only English should be spoken in public in the US' — visible in viral videos of people harassed for speaking Spanish.

LANGUAGE IDEOLOGIES AND LGBTQ ISSUES:
• Inclusive language ideologies — people should choose the gendered labels and pronouns used for them. Includes coming out as a language genre, pronoun sharing, identity labels (umbrella terms like gay or queer; specific terms like pansexual, demisexual), and debate over Latinx.
• The instructor's dissertation work: how student activists in LGBTQ and feminist communities use language and monitor their own and others' speech.
• REACTIONARY ideologies (reaction against progress): 'I don't have pronouns' (nearly everyone does prefer certain third-person pronouns); the claim that third-person singular they is ungrammatical; 'Don't Say Gay' bills.

'DON'T SAY GAY' BILL:
• Officially the Parental Rights in Education bill (Florida), signed by Gov. Ron DeSantis; the media name is not the official title.
• Bars classroom instruction on sexual orientation or gender identity in K-3, or in a manner not age/developmentally appropriate per state standards — which the law does not define, and for which state standards are near-nonexistent at many grades.
• Consequences noted in lecture: implementation extended by Florida's Dept. of Education; AP Psychology not currently offered in Florida because its curriculum covers these topics; a science teacher resigned under school-board pressure over a Disney film mentioning a gay character; teacher shortages.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

notes.title: Language Varies — Sound, Grammar, Lexicon, Region, Gender
notes.body:
BY SOUND:
• British English speakers don't pronounce /r/ after vowels — 'mother', 'flower'.

BY GRAMMAR:
• African American English and Southern American English allow DOUBLE MODALS ('might could', 'may can'): 'I might could go to the store.' Grammatical there, ungrammatical in California English.

BY LEXICON:
• 'sigogglin'' (Appalachian) = crooked.
• British vs. American: the lift is broken / the elevator is broken; the baby needs their nappy changed / their diaper changed.

BY REGION — the sweetened carbonated beverage map:
• SODA: California and most of the Northeast.
• POP: most of the Midwest; Oregon splits; a patch near the Missouri-Illinois border and around Milwaukee.
• COKE as a generic: the South — a Texas server may ask what kind of Coke you want, and 'Sprite' is a valid answer.

BY GENDER — the Valley Girl persona:
• Associated with young, wealthy white women of the San Fernando Valley (cf. Cher in Clueless).
• Features: frequent 'like', creaky voice, rising intonation.
• 'Like' sentence-medially is prescriptively dismissed as a FILLER WORD; descriptively it is a DISCOURSE MARKER segmenting units of the utterance.
• CREAKY VOICE: stereotyped as young women, but used roughly equally by men and women and by trans and non-binary speakers. It occurs naturally at sentence ends, where English pitch drops to distinguish statements from questions.
• RISING INTONATION: normally marks questions; on declaratives it is stereotyped as Valley Girl speech.

QUICK WRITE: think of someone you interact with (or yourself) — what's distinctive about how they speak, and how does it relate to their identity?
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

notes.title: Agenda & Social Identity (Language and Power)
notes.body:
AGENDA:
• Language varieties and social identity
• Language ideologies / attitudes
• Why this is important in the real world

SOCIAL IDENTITY AND LANGUAGE:
• The way people use language differs based on their identity: gender, region, race/ethnicity, social class.
• Variation shows up in the words used, the sounds, and the grammar.

OPENING CLIP — Appalachian speakers explaining 'sigogglin'' (something crooked, e.g. a wall a carpenter built badly). These speakers are from North Carolina; the Appalachian range also crosses Tennessee and West Virginia.

THE CALIFORNIANS (SNL sketch):
• Parodies Californians, especially the LA area — drawn-out vowels, slurred words, obsessive freeway directions.
• Most Californians don't find it accurate to their own speech; some Bay Area speakers think it's accurate of LA.
• KEY POINT: many Californians assume they have no accent and that their speech is simply normal. It is very noticeable to people outside California.
notes.source: [Brotherton, ANTH/HUM 4 Lecture: Language and Power (deck)]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Lecture 1 (What Is Language & Linguistics)
notes.body:
★ Linguistics = SCIENTIFIC, EMPIRICAL, DESCRIPTIVE study of language — describe what people DO, not what they 'should' do.
★ Descriptive grammar = subconscious, never taught, necessary for communication; Prescriptive grammar = taught, forgettable, decided by 'experts,' not required to communicate.
★ MEMORIZE the eight hallmarks: Arbitrariness, Discreteness, Duality of patterning, Displacement, Productivity, Cultural transmission, Reflexivity, Interchangeability.
★ Match the classic examples to the hallmark: not-present events = DISPLACEMENT; k–æ–t pieces = DISCRETENESS; sounds→meaning at two levels = DUALITY OF PATTERNING; Cat-in-the-Hat / infinite sentences = PRODUCTIVITY; cross-language 'bread' = ARBITRARINESS.
★ Arbitrariness has only PARTIAL exceptions: onomatopoeia & sound symbolism (and the Kiki–Bouba effect) — language stays mostly arbitrary.
★ Animal systems (bees, vervets, apes, dolphins) show SOME features (communication, limited displacement, learned signs, even rudimentary grammar) but NONE shows the full set — key gaps: no true duality of patterning, very limited productivity/syntax.
★ Bee dance = genetic, non-productive; vervet calls = learned, predator-specific, no syntax; Washoe (132 signs) & Kanzi (lexigrams) = trained, not spontaneous full language.
★ Bipedalism (lowered larynx → long pharynx) is the MOST important physical adaptation for human speech.
★ Speech is ancient; WRITING is recent (cuneiform ~5,000 yrs) and must be taught — reading/writing are SECONDARY to spoken/signed language.
★ Human language ≠ animal communication: ~half of human speech is grammatical items, and grammar yields infinite sentences from finite words.
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

notes.title: Humans, Animals, and the Evolution of Language
notes.body:
Why humans can speak (physical adaptations):
• Upright, even teeth; muscular lips; smaller mouth; smaller, more muscular tongue; velum that raises/lowers.
• MOST IMPORTANT: bipedalism → head sits directly above the spinal column and the larynx is lower, creating a longer pharynx for air resonance.

Conclusions on animal vs. human communication:
• Many animals learn signs that stand for things; some learn rudimentary grammar.
• But even a 5-year-old human's language is far more advanced.
• Human language isn't just lexical (nouns/verbs) — about HALF of typical speech is grammatical items (prepositions, conjunctions, articles, auxiliaries). Grammar builds infinite sentences from finite words.

Evolution & writing:
• Language origin is controversial — perhaps ~60,000 years ago, around when humans began making art (abstract cognition).
• Writing is recent: cuneiform (Mesopotamia) ~5,000 years ago; Egyptian hieroglyphs about the same time; Maya developed writing independently; Phoenicians are credited with the first alphabet → Greek → Latin & Cyrillic.
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

notes.title: Animal Communication — Case Studies
notes.body:
HONEY BEES:
• Round dance = food is present; waggle dance = distance, direction, quantity.
• Communication? Yes — systematic and rule-based, with limited displacement. But NOT really arbitrary, NO duality of patterning, essentially non-productive (no innovation), and GENETIC, not learned → not a full language.

VERVET MONKEYS:
• Most sophisticated monkey system studied; at least ~10 predator-specific alarm calls (snake → stand & look down; eagle → hide in bush; leopard → run up a tree).
• Appears LEARNED, not instinctive; may be used for 'lying' (deception → theory of mind?).
• BUT lacks discreteness/recombination, limited productivity, no syntax (no duality of patterning).

APES:
• Vicki (chimp): spoke only mama, papa, up, cup.
• Washoe (chimp): produced 132 ASL signs; understood ~3× as many.
• Kanzi (bonobo): understood complex verbal commands/questions; answered via a lexigram keyboard (~74% correct on 600 questions).
• Ape vocal tracts aren't built for human speech.

DOLPHINS:
• Some learned rudimentary grammar — can use WORD ORDER to code differences in meaning.
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

notes.title: Arbitrariness & Its (Partial) Exceptions
notes.body:
• Language is a system of ARBITRARY signs — signs indicate something else and are used by convention (like a traffic light or wedding ring), with no causal/inherent form–meaning relationship.
• Most words have no direct relationship to their meanings (cross-linguistic 'bread', or a dozen/twelve/12/XII).
• Rare representational (ICONIC) exceptions:
   – Onomatopoeia: words imitating sounds (buzz, slurp, clank, woof, meow).
   – Sound symbolism: sound clusters linked to meanings (English gl-: glisten, gleam, glare, glimmer, glow, glitter).
• Kiki–Bouba effect: people cross-culturally match 'kiki' to a spiky shape, 'bouba' to a round one.
• BUT both onomatopoeia and sound symbolism are still only PARTLY motivated — language remains largely arbitrary.
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

notes.title: The Eight Hallmarks of Human Language
notes.body:
1. Arbitrariness — no inherent link between form and meaning; signs used by convention (bread/pain/xleb/mian bao/kenyér).
2. Discreteness — words break into elemental units (tap = t–a–p).
3. Duality of patterning (complex patterns at multiple levels) — meaningless sounds combine into meaningful units (t,a,p → tap, apt, pat).
4. Displacement — talk about things/events not present.
5. Productivity — infinite messages from finite elements & patterns.
6. Cultural transmission — the code must be learned from the environment; shared by a community; no individual can change it alone.
7. Reflexivity — use the code to talk about the code itself (metalanguage).
8. Interchangeability — users can both transmit AND receive messages.
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

notes.title: What Language IS
notes.body:
Language is:
• A complex, RULE-BASED system for organizing and expressing information.
• Inherently INTERACTIONAL — used to share knowledge, coordinate actions, make requests/complaints.
• CREATIVE — we coin and understand new forms (supercalifragilistic…, bae, YOLO, FOMO).
• An expression of SOCIAL IDENTITY — word choice, pronunciation, registers (formality), regional dialects, social dialects.
• SPOKEN or SIGNED — not necessarily written. Writing is recent in human history; children must be TAUGHT to write, but not to speak/sign.
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

notes.title: Course Objectives & Subfields of Linguistics
notes.body:
Objectives:
• Examine your own beliefs/attitudes about language and language use.
• Become aware of the diversity of language systems AND their similarities.
• Get introduced to the subfields of linguistics and to tools for linguistic analysis.

Subfields (what linguists do):
• Phonetics — sounds: production & perception.
• Phonology — how sounds pattern together in a language.
• Morphology — how words are formed.
• Syntax — how words combine into clauses and sentences.
• Semantics — meaning.
• Pragmatics — meaning in context.
• Sociolinguistics — language in social contexts.
• Historical linguistics — how language changes.
• Also: psycholinguistics, computational linguistics, applied linguistics, etc.
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

notes.title: Prescriptive vs. Descriptive Grammar
notes.body:
DESCRIPTIVE grammar:
• Absolutely necessary for effective communication.
• Not explicitly taught; never forgotten.
• Known SUBCONSCIOUSLY.
• No one 'decides' these rules — they emerge from use.

PRESCRIPTIVE grammar:
• Communication can still happen without these rules.
• Must be taught explicitly; we forget them all the time.
• Must be consciously thought about.
• Grammar 'experts' decide on them.
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

notes.title: What Is Linguistics? (Empirical & Descriptive)
notes.body:
• Linguistics = the SCIENTIFIC study of natural human language.
• Empirical: relies on / derives from OBSERVATION — language is treated as scientific data to be analyzed objectively.
• The study of language structure and language use = GRAMMAR (in the linguistic sense).
• Linguistics is NOT about prescriptive grammar (telling people what they "should" do / what is "correct").
• Linguistics IS about DESCRIPTIVE grammar: the goal is to describe and explain what people ACTUALLY do — study of language WITHOUT judgment.
notes.source: [Brotherton, LIN 1 Lecture 1: What Is Language & Linguistics? (adapted from Zellou & Greer)]

notes.title: ★ KEY EXAM POINTS — Chapter 14
notes.body: ★ HISTORICAL LINGUISTICS = how languages change + how related languages share an ancestor. All languages change at every level. ★ LEXICAL change incl. BORROWING (falcon ← faucon). ★ SOUND CHANGE: REGULAR (systematic, often CONDITIONED by environment) vs. SPORADIC (irregular). GREAT VOWEL SHIFT = English long-vowel chain (PUSH/PULL chains); why spelling ≠ pronunciation. ★ MORPHOLOGICAL change via ANALOGY (rare→common pattern; fewer allomorphs). SYNTACTIC change incl. GRAMMATICALIZATION (word → grammatical marker; 'stille' → 'still'). ★ SEMANTIC change: broadening/narrowing/amelioration/pejoration. ★ COMPARATIVE METHOD compares SOUND CORRESPONDENCES in related languages to reconstruct a PROTO-LANGUAGE (* = reconstructed). COGNATES share an ancestor (gift/Gift); beware FALSE FRIENDS. A LANGUAGE FAMILY = daughters of one proto-language.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

notes.title: 14.8-14.9 Reconstructing the past
notes.body: The comparative method compares multiple related languages and their regular sound correspondences to reconstruct their common ancestor, a proto-language (reconstructed forms marked with *, unknown ones temporarily with ?). Evidence comes from cognates — words descended from the same ancestor (English 'gift' and German 'Gift' are true cognates despite different meanings) — but analysts must beware false friends, similar-looking words with different meanings. The chapter's case study reconstructs aspects of Proto-Chinese. Languages sharing a proto-language form a language family.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

notes.title: 14.6 Semantic change
notes.body: Word meanings change over time: broadening (a word covers more), narrowing (less), shift, and evaluative changes (amelioration = more positive; pejoration = more negative). Semantic change is pervasive and interacts with lexical and cultural change.
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

notes.title: 14.4-14.5 Morphological & syntactic change
notes.body: Morphological change often proceeds by analogy: a word shifts to match a pattern in other words (rare → common), commonly reducing the allomorphs in a paradigm; analogy can also regularize inflectional affixes. Syntactic change alters sentence structure/word order over time. A key syntactic process is grammaticalization, where an ordinary word becomes a grammatical marker (e.g., the adjective 'stille' → Modern English 'still').
notes.source: [Anderson et al. (2022), Essentials of Linguistics, 2nd ed., Ch. 14]

notes.title: 14.3 Phonological (sound) change
notes.body: A change affecting a spoken language's phonology is a sound change. It can be regular (systematic across all eligible words, often conditioned by a specific environment), or sporadic (irregular, affecting only some words). Sound change may add, lose, or merge phonemes, or merely re-pronounce them (e.g., English [sk] > [ʃ]). The Great Vowel Shift reshaped English long vowels — analysed as push and/or pull chains — and is a key reason English spelling and pronunciation mismatch.
